  • Rough conventions (Cohen): .10 small, .30 medium, .50 large. In test-retest reliability the same number would be poor, so interpret against the context.

12.2 Pearson's product-moment correlation (r)

Formulas.
Definitional: r = Σ(zX zY) / n, the average product of the paired z scores. (This is where "product-moment" comes from: a moment is a deviation from the mean.)
Covariance form: r = cov(X,Y) / (sX sY), where cov = Σ(X−MX)(Y−MY)/(n−1).
Raw score: r = [nΣXY − ΣXΣY] / √{[nΣX² − (ΣX)²][nΣY² − (ΣY)²]}
Significance: t = r√(n − 2) / √(1 − r²), with df = n − 2.
Why covariance alone is not enough. Covariance already captures whether X and Y move together, but its size depends on the units the variables are measured in, so it cannot be compared across studies. Dividing by the two standard deviations standardises it onto a fixed −1 to +1 scale. A correlation is a standardised covariance. That one sentence answers a whole family of questions.

Coefficient of determination

r² is the proportion of variance in one variable that is shared with (accounted for by) the other. 1 − r² is the coefficient of non-determination or the coefficient of alienation is √(1 − r²). So r = .60 means 36% shared variance, not 60%. This non-linearity matters: doubling r from .30 to .60 multiplies the shared variance by four (from 9% to 36%).

Worked example

Five students, hours studied (X) and score (Y): (2,4), (4,6), (6,7), (8,9), (10,11). MX = 6, MY = 7.4.
x deviations: −4, −2, 0, +2, +4. y deviations: −3.4, −1.4, −0.4, +1.6, +3.6.
Σxy = 13.6 + 2.8 + 0 + 3.2 + 14.4 = 34.0. Σx² = 16+4+0+4+16 = 40. Σy² = 11.56+1.96+0.16+2.56+12.96 = 29.2.
r = 34.0 / √(40 × 29.2) = 34.0 / √1168 = 34.0/34.18 = .995. Almost perfect positive. r² = .99, so 99% of the variance in score is shared with study hours in this (artificially tidy) data.

12.3 The assumptions and limitations of Pearson's r

  1. Both variables interval or ratio. Otherwise use a rank or categorical coefficient.
  2. Linearity. r measures linear relationship only. A perfect U-shaped relationship gives r = 0. Always look at the scatterplot first.
  3. Bivariate normality, for significance testing.
  4. Homoscedasticity: the spread of Y is roughly the same at every value of X.
  5. Independence of pairs, and continuity of the underlying variables.
  6. No extreme outliers, to which r is very sensitive.

The four things that distort r

DistortionWhat happensFix
CurvilinearityA strong non-linear relation produces r near 0Inspect the scatterplot. Use eta (the correlation ratio) or polynomial regression
OutliersA single extreme pair can create or destroy a correlation, especially with small nInspect, then justify removal or use Spearman's rho, which is robust
Restriction of rangeSampling only a narrow slice of X attenuates (shrinks) r. The classic case: correlating entrance-exam scores with performance among admitted students onlySample the full range, or apply a correction for restriction of range
Heterogeneous subgroupsPooling two groups with different means creates a correlation that exists in neither groupPlot by subgroup; compute r within each
Attenuation due to unreliabilityMeasurement error in either variable pulls r towards zero, so the observed r underestimates the true relationSpearman's correction for attenuation: rtrue = rxy / √(rxx ryy)
Correlation is not causation. Say it, then say why, because the "why" is the mark. Three alternatives always remain: (1) reverse causation, Y may cause X; (2) the third-variable problem, a confound Z may cause both, which is why ice cream sales correlate with drowning (the confound is summer); (3) coincidence, especially in large datasets where spurious correlations are guaranteed. Only a randomised experiment licenses a causal claim, because randomisation is what removes the third variable.

12.4 The other correlation coefficients

CoefficientSymbolVariable XVariable YNotes
Pearson product-momentrInterval/ratio, continuousInterval/ratio, continuousThe parametric standard
Spearman's rank-order (rho)ρ or rsOrdinal (ranks)Ordinal (ranks)ρ = 1 − [6ΣD² / n(n² − 1)], where D is the difference between the two ranks for each case. It is simply Pearson's r computed on ranks. Robust to outliers and to non-linear but monotonic relations
Kendall's tauτOrdinalOrdinalBased on concordant vs discordant pairs. Better than ρ for small samples and many tied ranks; gives smaller values than ρ for the same data
Point-biserialrpbTrue dichotomy (male/female, pass/fail)Interval/ratioMathematically identical to Pearson's r with the dichotomy coded 0/1. The basis of item-total discrimination in item analysis
BiserialrbArtificial dichotomy (a continuous variable that has been split, e.g. pass/fail cut from a continuous score)Interval/ratioEstimates what r would be if the dichotomy were left continuous. Can exceed 1.0, which point-biserial cannot
Phi coefficientφTrue dichotomyTrue dichotomyPearson's r on two 0/1 variables. Related to chi-square: φ = √(χ²/N). Used for 2×2 tables
TetrachoricrtArtificial dichotomyArtificial dichotomyEstimates the correlation between the assumed underlying continuous normal variables
Contingency coefficientCNominal, any number of categoriesNominalC = √[χ²/(χ² + N)]. Cannot reach 1.00, and its ceiling depends on table size, which is why Cramér's V is now preferred
Cramér's VVNominal, r×cNominalV = √[χ² / (N × min(r−1, c−1))]. Ranges properly from 0 to 1
Eta (correlation ratio)ηNominal / categoricalIntervalMeasures any relationship, linear or not. Equals r when the relation is perfectly linear, exceeds it otherwise
Kendall's coefficient of concordanceWAgreement among three or more sets of ranks (e.g. several judges ranking the same candidates)Ranges 0 (no agreement) to 1 (perfect agreement)
The memory hook for choosing. Both continuous → Pearson. Both ranks → Spearman. One dichotomy + one continuous → point-biserial (real dichotomy) or biserial (artificial). Two dichotomies → phi (real) or tetrachoric (artificial). Both nominal with many categories → contingency C or Cramér's V. The word "artificial" always points to biserial or tetrachoric.

Worked Spearman example

Five candidates ranked by two interviewers.
Judge A: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5. Judge B: 2, 1, 4, 3, 5. D = −1, +1, −1, +1, 0. D² = 1, 1, 1, 1, 0. ΣD² = 4.
ρ = 1 − [6(4) / 5(25 − 1)] = 1 − 24/120 = .80. Strong agreement.

12.5 Partial and semi-partial correlation

Partial correlation (pr)Semi-partial / part correlation (sr)
NotationrY1.2rY(1.2)
What is removedThe effect of X₂ is removed from both X₁ and YThe effect of X₂ is removed from X₁ only, not from Y
Question"What is the relation between X₁ and Y among people who are equal on X₂?""How much does X₁ add to the prediction of Y over and above X₂?"
DenominatorOnly the part of Y that X₂ did not explainAll of Y's variance
SizeAlways the larger of the two in absolute valueAlways the smaller
Where it appearsControlling a confound conceptuallysr² is the unique contribution of a predictor to R² in multiple regression
First-order partial formula: rY1.2 = (rY1 − rY2r12) / √[(1 − r²Y2)(1 − r²12)]. Zero-order correlation = ordinary r, nothing controlled. First-order = one variable controlled. Second-order = two controlled (rY1.23). The order is simply the number of variables held constant.
The classic illustration: the correlation between shoe size and reading ability in children is about .60. Partial out age and it drops to roughly zero. Age was driving both. Partial correlation is the statistical version of "holding everything else constant", and it is what makes non-experimental data interpretable.

13 Regression

13.1 Simple linear regression

Correlation asks how strongly two variables go together. Regression asks a different question: given X, what is my best prediction of Y? It fits a straight line through the scatterplot and uses it to predict.

The regression equation. Ŷ = a + bX, where Ŷ (Y-hat) is the predicted score, b is the slope or regression coefficient (the change in Y per one-unit change in X), and a is the intercept (the predicted Y when X = 0).

b = r (sY / sX)  ·  a = MY − b MX
In standardised (z) form the intercept vanishes and the slope is the correlation: zŶ = r · zX.

The least squares criterion

The line is chosen so that the sum of the squared vertical distances from each point to the line, Σ(Y − Ŷ)², is as small as possible. Those vertical distances are the residuals or errors of prediction. Note that they are vertical, not perpendicular, and that this is exactly the same least-squares logic that made the mean the balance point in section 3.

Worked example

Using the study-hours data from 12.2: r = .995, sX = 3.16, sY = 2.70, MX = 6, MY = 7.4.
b = .995(2.70/3.16) = 0.85. a = 7.4 − 0.85(6) = 2.30.
So Ŷ = 2.30 + 0.85X. A student studying 7 hours is predicted to score 2.30 + 5.95 = 8.25.

Standard error of estimate. SY.X = sY√(1 − r²) is the standard deviation of the residuals: the typical size of a prediction error, in the units of Y. When r = 0 it equals sY (you predict the mean and do no better than chance); when r = ±1 it is zero (perfect prediction). It is the single most useful number for saying how good a regression actually is.

Facts about the regression line worth memorising

  • The line always passes through the point (MX, MY).
  • There are two regression lines: Y on X (for predicting Y) and X on Y (for predicting X). They coincide only when r = ±1 and are perpendicular when r = 0. r is the geometric mean of the two slopes: r = √(bYX · bXY).
  • The residuals sum to zero and are uncorrelated with X.
  • Regression towards the mean (Francis Galton's original discovery): unless r = 1, extreme scores on X are followed by less extreme predicted scores on Y. This is a statistical necessity, not a psychological finding, and it is the reason uncontrolled pre-post designs appear to show improvement in the most severe cases. Naming regression to the mean as a threat to internal validity is worth a mark on its own.

13.2 Assumptions of regression (the LINE acronym)

AssumptionCheckIf violated
LLinearity of the X–Y relationScatterplot; residuals vs fitted plotTransform, or add polynomial terms
IIndependence of residualsDurbin–Watson statistic (about 2.0 is fine, under 1 or over 3 is a problem)Time-series or multilevel models
NNormality of residualsHistogram or Q–Q plot of residualsTransform; large n gives robustness
EEqual variance of residuals (homoscedasticity)Residual plot: an even band, not a fanTransform Y, or use robust standard errors / weighted least squares

13.3 Multiple regression

Ŷ = a + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + … + bkXk. Two or more predictors, one continuous criterion.

StatisticMeaning
R (multiple correlation)The correlation between the observed Y and the predicted Ŷ. Always positive, ranges 0 to 1
R² (coefficient of multiple determination)The proportion of variance in Y explained by all the predictors together
Adjusted R²R² penalised for the number of predictors and the sample size. Always ≤ R². Report this one, because R² mechanically rises every time you add any predictor, even a useless one
b (unstandardised coefficient)The change in Y per one-unit change in that X, holding the others constant. In the original units, so it cannot be compared across predictors
β (beta weight, standardised coefficient)The same thing in z-score units. These are comparable across predictors, so the largest |β| identifies the strongest unique predictor
sr² (squared semi-partial)The unique proportion of Y's variance that this predictor explains and no other does. The honest measure of a predictor's contribution
F test of the modelTests whether R² differs from zero overall. Individual predictors are tested by t

Methods of entry

MethodHow it worksUse when
Simultaneous / enter / standardAll predictors entered at once; each is evaluated for its unique contributionNo theoretical ordering; the default and safest choice
Hierarchical / blockwisePredictors entered in blocks in an order the researcher chooses, with the change in R² (ΔR²) tested at each stepTheory-driven: enter demographics first, then the variable of real interest, to show it predicts over and above them. The preferred method in psychology
Stepwise (forward, backward, or both)The software selects predictors by statistical criteria aloneDiscouraged. It capitalises on chance, is unstable across samples, and produces results that rarely replicate. Purely exploratory use only

13.4 Multicollinearity

Definition: predictors that are highly correlated with each other, so they carry largely the same information.

  • Consequences: R² stays high, but the individual b and β weights become unstable, their standard errors inflate, real predictors test non-significant, and coefficients can flip sign between samples. You lose the ability to say which predictor matters.
  • Detection: VIF (variance inflation factor) above 10 (strict: above 5); tolerance (= 1/VIF) below .10; bivariate r above .80 between predictors; a condition index above 30. Singularity is the extreme case, where one predictor is a perfect linear combination of others (for example, entering all subscales and the total score).
  • Remedies: drop one of the pair, combine them into a composite or factor score, centre the variables when the collinearity comes from interaction terms, or use ridge regression or principal-components regression.
  • Suppressor variable: a predictor that correlates near zero with Y but nevertheless increases R² by removing irrelevant variance from another predictor. Counter-intuitive, and a favourite distractor.
Sample size rules of thumb for multiple regression: Tabachnick and Fidell suggest N ≥ 50 + 8k for testing the overall model and N ≥ 104 + k for testing individual predictors, where k is the number of predictors. A cruder and very quotable rule is at least 10 to 15 cases per predictor.

13.5 Logistic regression

Used when the dependent variable is categorical, most often binary (relapsed / did not relapse, admitted / not admitted). Ordinary regression cannot be used because it would predict impossible values below 0 and above 1, and because the residuals could not possibly be normal or homoscedastic.

The chain of transformations.
Probability P → odds = P / (1 − P) → logit = ln(odds), which is unbounded and can be modelled linearly:
ln[P / (1 − P)] = a + b₁X₁ + b₂X₂ + …
Exponentiating a coefficient gives the odds ratio: OR = eb, printed by SPSS as Exp(B). OR > 1 means the predictor raises the odds of the outcome, OR < 1 lowers them, OR = 1 means no effect.
FeatureLinear (OLS) regressionLogistic regression
DVContinuousCategorical (binary, or multinomial / ordinal)
EstimationOrdinary least squaresMaximum likelihood
Coefficient testt testWald statistic (or the likelihood-ratio test, which is better with small n)
Model fitR², F test−2 log likelihood, Cox & Snell R², Nagelkerke R² (a "pseudo R²" rescaled to reach 1.0), classification accuracy table
Goodness of fit test–Hosmer–Lemeshow: a non-significant result means good fit
AssumptionsLinearity, normality, homoscedasticity of residualsNo normality or homoscedasticity required. Needs a linear relation between predictors and the logit, independence, no multicollinearity, and a decent number of cases per predictor (at least 10 in the smaller outcome category)
Where you meet it clinically: predicting diagnosis from symptom scores, predicting dropout from therapy, predicting readmission, predicting suicide attempt from risk factors. Logistic regression has largely replaced discriminant function analysis for these problems, because it makes far weaker distributional assumptions and its odds ratios are directly interpretable to clinicians.

13.6 The rest of the multivariate family, in one glance

TechniqueQuestion
Discriminant function analysisWhich combination of continuous variables best predicts membership of known groups? (MANOVA reversed)
Canonical correlationWhat is the relationship between a set of predictors and a set of criteria? The most general of the linear models
Path analysisDoes this specified pattern of directional relationships among measured variables fit the data?
Structural equation modelling (SEM)Path analysis with latent (unmeasured) variables. Combines a measurement model (confirmatory factor analysis) with a structural model
Multilevel / hierarchical linear modellingHow do you analyse data that is nested (pupils within classes, patients within therapists) and therefore not independent?
Cluster analysisDo the cases fall into natural groups? (Factor analysis groups variables; cluster analysis groups people)
Survival analysis / Cox regressionHow long until an event occurs, and what predicts the timing? Handles censored data (people who never relapse during the study)
Recap of sections 12 and 13: a correlation is a standardised covariance running from −1 to +1, whose sign is direction and absolute value is strength, and whose square is shared variance. Pearson's r needs interval data, linearity, bivariate normality and homoscedasticity, and it is distorted by curvilinearity, outliers, restriction of range, pooled subgroups and unreliability. Choose the coefficient by the scales: Spearman for ranks, point-biserial for a real dichotomy, biserial for an artificial one, phi for two real dichotomies, tetrachoric for two artificial ones, Cramér's V for nominal tables. Partial correlation removes a third variable from both X and Y, semi-partial from X only, and sr² is a predictor's unique contribution. Regression fits Ŷ = a + bX by least squares, where b = r(sY/sX), the residual SD is the standard error of estimate, and the line always passes through the two means. Multiple regression adds predictors, reports adjusted R² and comparable beta weights, prefers hierarchical over stepwise entry, and is undermined by multicollinearity (VIF over 10). Logistic regression models a categorical outcome through the logit, estimates by maximum likelihood, and reports odds ratios.

14 Non-parametric tests

14.1 When you switch, and what you give up

Parametric testsNon-parametric (distribution-free) tests
AssumeA specified population distribution (usually normal), homogeneity of variance, and interval or ratio dataVery little about the population distribution
Work onMeans and variances, using the actual valuesRanks, signs, medians and frequencies
Scale requiredInterval or ratioNominal or ordinal (and interval data can be ranked down to use them)
PowerHigher, when assumptions holdLower. The classic figure is about 95% efficiency for Mann–Whitney relative to the t test under normality, meaning you would need roughly 5% more participants
Sample sizePrefers larger nUsable with very small n
OutliersBadly affectedRobust, since only rank order matters
InteractionsCan test themMostly cannot
Switch to a non-parametric test when: the DV is nominal or ordinal; the distribution is badly skewed or has serious outliers and cannot be transformed; the sample is too small to trust the central limit theorem; the variances are wildly unequal; or the data are ranks to begin with. Stay parametric when the assumptions are reasonable, because you keep the extra power and the ability to test interactions.
The precision cost. Ranking throws information away. If four people score 10, 11, 12 and 40, the ranks are 1, 2, 3 and 4; the fact that the fourth person was enormously higher disappears. That robustness is exactly the same property as the information loss, which is why non-parametric tests are less powerful when the parametric assumptions actually hold.

14.2 The chi-square family

Karl Pearson introduced chi-square in 1900, arguably the first modern statistical test. Frank Yates added the continuity correction in 1934, and R. A. Fisher gave us the exact test for small tables.
χ² = Σ[(O − E)² / E], where O is the observed frequency in a cell and E the expected frequency under H₀.
For a test of independence, E = (row total × column total) / grand total.
df: goodness of fit = k − 1  ·  test of independence = (r − 1)(c − 1).
TestQuestionData
χ² goodness of fit (one variable)Do the observed frequencies across categories match a hypothesised distribution?One nominal variable, k categories
χ² test of independence / association (two variables)Are the two categorical variables related, or independent?An r × c contingency table
χ² test of homogeneityDo several populations have the same distribution across categories?Same arithmetic as independence, different sampling logic

Worked example

Does treatment completion differ by therapy type? Observed:

CompletedDropped outRow total
CBT401050
Psychodynamic302050
Column total7030100

Expected: each cell = (row × column)/100, so 35, 15, 35, 15.
χ² = (40−35)²/35 + (10−15)²/15 + (30−35)²/35 + (20−15)²/15
= 25/35 + 25/15 + 25/35 + 25/15 = 0.714 + 1.667 + 0.714 + 1.667 = 4.76.
df = (2−1)(2−1) = 1. Critical χ² at .05 = 3.84. Reject H₀: completion is associated with therapy type.
Effect size φ = √(4.76/100) = .22, a small-to-medium association.

Assumptions and cautions for chi-square

  1. Frequencies, not percentages or means. Running chi-square on percentages is a common and fatal error.
  2. Independence of observations: each case contributes to exactly one cell. This is why a repeated-measures design needs McNemar, not chi-square.
  3. Expected frequency of at least 5 in every cell (a common relaxation: no cell below 1, and at most 20% of cells below 5). If violated, combine categories or use Fisher's exact test.
  4. Yates's correction for continuity subtracts 0.5 from each |O − E| before squaring, in 2×2 tables with small n. It makes the test more conservative; many statisticians now consider it over-conservative and prefer Fisher's exact test.
  5. Chi-square tells you whether there is an association, not its strength or direction. Report phi (2×2) or Cramér's V (larger tables) alongside it.
  6. Like every test, chi-square grows significant with large N, so a trivial association becomes significant at N = 10,000.

14.3 The rank-based tests, matched to their parametric partners

DesignParametric testNon-parametric equivalentNamed forLogic
One sample vs a hypothesised valueOne-sample tSign test / one-sample Wilcoxon / Kolmogorov–SmirnovWilcoxon; Kolmogorov, SmirnovCounts how many scores fall above vs below the hypothesised median
Two independent groupsIndependent-samples tMann–Whitney U (= Wilcoxon rank-sum)Henry Mann and Donald Whitney (1947)Pools and ranks all scores, then asks whether one group's ranks are systematically higher. U = n₁n₂ + n₁(n₁+1)/2 − R₁
Two independent groups (medians)–Median testMoodSplits at the combined median and runs a chi-square. Less powerful than Mann–Whitney
Two related samplesPaired-samples tWilcoxon signed-rank testFrank Wilcoxon (1945)Ranks the absolute difference scores, reattaches the signs, and sums the positive and negative ranks. Uses both the direction and the magnitude of the change
Two related samples, direction only–Sign test–Counts only pluses and minuses. Uses direction only, so it is weaker than Wilcoxon
Two related dichotomiesMcNemar's χ²McNemar testQuinn McNemar (1947)For before-and-after yes/no data on the same people. Uses only the cells that changed
Three or more independent groupsOne-way ANOVAKruskal–Wallis HWilliam Kruskal and W. Allen Wallis (1952)The rank version of one-way ANOVA: ranks everything, compares mean ranks. Distributed as χ² with df = k − 1
Three or more related samplesRepeated-measures ANOVAFriedman testMilton Friedman (1937)Ranks the conditions within each participant, then compares the mean ranks. χ² with df = k − 1
Three or more related dichotomies–Cochran's QWilliam CochranThe extension of McNemar to more than two occasions
CorrelationPearson rSpearman's ρ / Kendall's τSpearman; KendallCorrelation computed on ranks
Agreement among many judgesICCKendall's W (coefficient of concordance)Maurice KendallConcordance among three or more sets of ranks
Randomness of a sequence–Runs test (Wald–Wolfowitz)Abraham Wald, Jacob WolfowitzTests whether a binary sequence is randomly ordered
Small 2×2 tables–Fisher's exact testR. A. FisherComputes the exact probability of the table; used when expected frequencies are below 5
The mapping to learn cold, because it is asked directly every single year:
independent t → Mann–Whitney U  ·  paired t → Wilcoxon signed-rank
one-way ANOVA → Kruskal–Wallis H  ·  repeated-measures ANOVA → Friedman
Pearson r → Spearman's rho  ·  two related dichotomies → McNemar
Two names, two groups: Mann and Whitney for two independent groups; Wilcoxon for two related ones. Two names again for three or more independent groups: Kruskal and Wallis. One name for three or more related: Friedman.

Worked Mann–Whitney example

Group A: 12, 15, 18. Group B: 9, 11, 14.
Pooled and ranked ascending: 9(1), 11(2), 12(3), 14(4), 15(5), 18(6).
RA = 3 + 5 + 6 = 14. RB = 1 + 2 + 4 = 7.
UA = (3)(3) + 3(4)/2 − 14 = 9 + 6 − 14 = 1. UB = 9 + 6 − 7 = 8. (Check: UA + UB = n₁n₂ = 9. It does.)
The obtained U is the smaller value, 1. For non-parametric tests the decision rule reverses: you reject H₀ when the obtained value is less than or equal to the critical value.

The reversed decision rule. For t, F, χ² and z you reject H₀ when the obtained value is bigger than the critical value. For Mann–Whitney U and the Wilcoxon T you reject when the obtained value is smaller than or equal to the critical value, because a small U or T means the two rank distributions barely overlap. Kruskal–Wallis H and Friedman go back to the ordinary direction, because they are read against the chi-square table.

15 Psychometrics: reliability, validity, item analysis, factor analysis and norms

Entrance papers do not separate statistics from psychometrics. Reliability coefficients are correlations, item discrimination is a point-biserial, factor analysis is a correlation matrix decomposed, and norms are standard scores. This section is worth as much as ANOVA in most of these papers and is usually the least prepared.

15.1 Classical test theory, in one equation

X = T + E: every observed score (X) is the sum of a true score (T) and an error component (E). Errors are assumed to be random, to have a mean of zero across many testings, and to be uncorrelated with true scores. From this one model the whole of reliability theory follows.

Reliability rxx = σ²T / σ²X: the proportion of observed-score variance that is true-score variance. It runs from 0 to 1, and it is a correlation, not a percentage.

15.2 Reliability: the five types

TypeProcedureSource of error it detectsWeakness
Test-retest
(coefficient of stability)		Administer the same test to the same people on two occasions; correlateTime sampling. Instability over timeCarryover, practice and memory effects inflate it; real change deflates it. Interval matters: too short inflates, too long deflates
Parallel / alternate / equivalent forms
(coefficient of equivalence)		Two equivalent forms of the test given to the same people; correlateContent sampling. Which particular items were chosenBuilding two genuinely parallel forms (equal means, variances and intercorrelations) is expensive and often impossible. Considered the strongest single method
Split-halfSplit into two halves (usually odd vs even items), correlate the halves, then correct with Spearman–BrownContent sampling, from a single administrationThe correlation is between two half-length tests, so it underestimates the full test's reliability. That is exactly what the Spearman–Brown correction repairs. Different splits give different answers
Internal consistency
(Cronbach's alpha, KR-20, KR-21)		Computed from item variances in a single administration; equivalent to the mean of all possible split-halvesContent sampling and item heterogeneityDepends on test length and on how homogeneous the items are. Alpha is not a measure of unidimensionality
Inter-rater / inter-scorer
(coefficient of agreement)		Two or more raters score the same responses; compute Cohen's kappa (categorical) or the intraclass correlation, ICC (continuous)Scorer varianceEssential for projectives, observational coding and clinical interviews; irrelevant for objectively scored tests
Formulas to know.
Spearman–Brown prophecy: rfull = 2rhalf / (1 + rhalf). General form for changing test length by a factor of k: rnew = kr / [1 + (k−1)r]. This is the formula that answers "how many items must I add to reach reliability of .90?"
Cronbach's alpha: α = [k/(k−1)][1 − Σs²i / s²t], where k is the number of items.
KR-20: the special case of alpha for dichotomously scored items (right/wrong): [k/(k−1)][1 − Σpq / s²t].
KR-21: a quicker approximation to KR-20 that assumes all items are equally difficult; always gives a slightly lower value.
Cohen's kappa: κ = (po − pe)/(1 − pe), agreement corrected for chance agreement.
Lee J. Cronbach published coefficient alpha in 1951; it is the most-cited paper in the history of psychometrics. G. Frederic Kuder and Marion Richardson published the KR formulas in 1937. Charles Spearman and William Brown independently derived the prophecy formula in 1910. Jacob Cohen gave us kappa in 1960, and the effect-size conventions in 1969.

Interpreting reliability

CoefficientVerdictUse
.90 and aboveExcellentRequired for individual clinical decisions (IQ tests, diagnostic instruments)
.80 to .89GoodAcceptable for most research and for group comparisons
.70 to .79AcceptableThe usual minimum for a research scale
Below .70Questionable to unacceptableNot usable for individual decisions
Two traps about alpha. (1) Alpha rises simply because a test is longer, so a high alpha on a 60-item scale is much less impressive than the same value on a 10-item scale. (2) A very high alpha (above .95) is a warning, not a triumph: it usually means the items are near-redundant paraphrases of each other, which narrows construct coverage. Alpha also does not establish that a scale is unidimensional; only factor analysis can do that.

Standard error of measurement

SEM = s√(1 − rxx), where s is the SD of the test and rxx its reliability. It is the standard deviation of the errors of measurement, so it tells you how much an individual's observed score would bounce around on repeated testing.

It is used to build a confidence band around a person's obtained score: 68% band = X ± 1 SEM, 95% band = X ± 1.96 SEM.

Worked example: WAIS-IV, SD = 15, reliability = .96. SEM = 15√(1 − .96) = 15(0.2) = 3.0. An obtained IQ of 105 gives a 95% confidence band of 105 ± 5.88, that is 99 to 111. This is the number that stops clinicians over-interpreting a 4-point difference between two testings.

Note the inverse relation: as reliability rises, SEM falls. Perfect reliability gives SEM = 0.

15.3 Validity

Validity is the degree to which a test measures what it claims to measure, and more precisely, the degree to which the inferences drawn from the scores are justified. Modern theory (Messick) treats it as a unitary concept with different lines of evidence, but exams still want the traditional types.

TypeQuestionHow it is established
Face validityDoes it look like it measures the thing, to a lay test-taker?Subjective inspection. Not a real form of validity, but it affects motivation and cooperation. Sometimes deliberately avoided, as in the MMPI's subtle items
Content validityDo the items adequately sample the whole domain?Expert judgement against a table of specifications or a syllabus blueprint. Central for achievement tests. Quantified by Lawshe's content validity ratio
Criterion-related: concurrentDoes it agree with an established criterion measured at the same time?Correlate with an existing accepted test or current diagnosis
Criterion-related: predictiveDoes it predict a criterion in the future?Correlate with later outcome (entrance score with later course performance). The coefficient is the validity coefficient
Construct validityDoes it measure the theoretical construct it claims to?The overarching type. Built from convergent and discriminant evidence, factor analysis, group differentiation, developmental change and experimental manipulation. Named by Cronbach and Paul Meehl (1955)
   Convergent validityDoes it correlate highly with measures of the same construct?Correlate with other measures of the same thing
   Discriminant (divergent) validityDoes it correlate weakly with measures of different constructs?The multitrait-multimethod matrix of Campbell and Fiske (1959) tests convergent and discriminant evidence together
   Factorial validityDoes its factor structure match the theory?Exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis
Incremental validityDoes it add predictive power over and above existing measures?Hierarchical regression: is ΔR² significant when it is entered last? The key question for any new clinical instrument
Ecological validityDo the results generalise to real-world settings?Field replication
Differential validityDoes it predict different criteria differently, and does it work equally well across subgroups?Compare validity coefficients across groups; central to test bias and fairness
The relationship between reliability and validity, which is asked constantly. Reliability is a necessary but not sufficient condition for validity. A test can be perfectly reliable and completely invalid (a bathroom scale that consistently reads 10 kg too high; measuring head circumference as an index of intelligence). But a test that is unreliable cannot be valid, because it is not consistently measuring anything at all. Quantitatively, reliability sets the ceiling on validity: the maximum possible validity coefficient is √rxx. So a test with reliability .64 can never correlate more than .80 with any criterion.
Threats to internal and external validity (Campbell and Stanley, 1963) belong to research design rather than test theory, but papers mix them in. Internal validity threats: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression to the mean (Francis Galton), selection, experimental mortality (attrition), and selection-maturation interaction. External validity threats: interaction of selection and treatment, interaction of setting and treatment, interaction of testing and treatment, and multiple-treatment interference. Note that statistical regression appears on the internal list, which links straight back to section 13.

15.4 Item analysis

IndexFormulaRangeInterpretation
Item difficulty (p)p = number who answered correctly / total number0 to 1Confusingly, a higher p means an EASIER item. Optimal p is about .50 for maximum discrimination and variance; for a 4-option multiple-choice item the optimum is about .625, halfway between chance (.25) and 1.00. Keep a spread of difficulties across the test
Item discrimination (D)D = pupper − plower, using the top and bottom 27% of scorers−1 to +1.40 and above = excellent; .30 to .39 = good; .20 to .29 = marginal, needs revision; below .20 = reject or rewrite. A negative D means poor scorers did better than good scorers, which signals a miskeyed or ambiguous item
Item-total correlationPoint-biserial between the item (0/1) and the total score−1 to +1The continuous version of D. Items below about .20 are dropped. Use the corrected item-total correlation, which excludes that item from the total
Distractor analysisThe proportion choosing each wrong option–Every distractor should attract someone, and should attract more low scorers than high scorers. A distractor nobody selects is dead weight and should be replaced
Why the top and bottom 27%? Truman Kelley (1939) showed that 27% is the split that maximises the difference between the groups while keeping each group large enough to be stable. It is a genuine optimum, not an arbitrary convention, and knowing that is a nice detail to include.

Item response theory (IRT), also called latent trait theory

Classical test theory (CTT)Item response theory (IRT)
FocusThe whole test scoreThe individual item
Item statisticsSample dependent: item difficulty changes with the group testedSample invariant: item parameters are on the same scale as ability
Ability estimateTest dependent: a score means something only relative to that testTest-free: θ is comparable across different sets of items
ErrorOne SEM for the whole testError varies with ability level (the test information function)
Models–1PL / Rasch: difficulty (b) only. 2PL: difficulty and discrimination (a). 3PL: adds a guessing parameter (c)
ApplicationTraditional paper testsComputer adaptive testing, item banking, differential item functioning (test bias) analysis
The Rasch model is named for the Danish mathematician Georg Rasch (1960). Frederic Lord and Melvin Novick (1968) wrote the foundational text of modern test theory. In an item characteristic curve, b is the point on the ability scale where the probability of a correct answer is .50 (difficulty, left-right position), a is the steepness at that point (discrimination), and c is the lower asymptote (pseudo-guessing).

15.5 Factor analysis

Purpose: to reduce a large set of correlated variables to a small number of underlying dimensions (factors) that explain the pattern of correlations among them. It answers "how many things is this scale actually measuring?"

Charles Spearman invented factor analysis in 1904 and used it to argue for g, the general factor of intelligence (his two-factor theory: g plus specific factors s). L. L. Thurstone developed multiple factor analysis and centroid extraction, proposed the seven primary mental abilities, and introduced simple structure and rotation. Raymond Cattell gave us the scree test, and applied factor analysis to build the 16PF. Henry Kaiser gave us the eigenvalue-greater-than-one rule, varimax rotation, and (with Meyer and Olkin) the KMO sampling adequacy measure.

The steps

  1. Check that the data are factorable. Bartlett's test of sphericity must be significant (it tests whether the correlation matrix is an identity matrix, and you need it not to be). The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin (KMO) measure of sampling adequacy should be at least .60, and preferably above .80. Note that Bartlett's test of sphericity here is a different test from Bartlett's test of homogeneity of variance, and papers exploit that.
  2. Extract the factors. Principal components analysis (PCA) analyses total variance and is technically a data-reduction method, not a factor model. Principal axis factoring (PAF) and maximum likelihood analyse only the shared (common) variance and are true factor analysis. Others: centroid (Thurstone), image, alpha factoring.
  3. Decide how many factors to retain. Kaiser criterion: retain factors with eigenvalue greater than 1.0 (tends to over-extract). Cattell's scree test: retain the factors above the elbow. Horn's parallel analysis: retain factors whose eigenvalues beat those from random data of the same size, which is the most accurate method. Or retain enough to explain a target percentage of variance (often 60% or more).
  4. Rotate to achieve simple structure (Thurstone): each variable loading strongly on one factor and near zero on the others, so the solution is interpretable. Rotation does not change the total variance explained, only how it is distributed among factors.
  5. Interpret and name the factors from the variables that load highly on them (a loading of .30 or .40 is the usual cut-off).
Rotation familyMethodsAssumesUse when
OrthogonalVarimax (maximises the variance of squared loadings within each factor: the most common), quartimax (simplifies the variables), equamax (a compromise)Factors are uncorrelated (at 90°)You want clean, independent dimensions and easy interpretation
ObliqueDirect oblimin, promaxFactors may correlatePsychological constructs, which almost always do correlate. Produces a pattern matrix (unique contributions, used for interpretation) and a structure matrix (correlations including shared variance)
TermMeaning
Factor loadingThe correlation between a variable and a factor. Squared, it is the proportion of that variable's variance explained by the factor
EigenvalueThe total variance explained by a factor, expressed in units of one variable's variance. Sum of the squared loadings down a column
Communality (h²)The proportion of a variable's variance explained by all the retained factors. Sum of the squared loadings across a row
Uniqueness1 − h²: the variance specific to that variable plus its error
Factor scoreAn individual's estimated standing on a factor
Simple structureThurstone's criterion for an interpretable solution: high loadings on one factor, near-zero on the rest
EFA versus CFA. Exploratory factor analysis asks "what structure is in these data?", imposes no prior model, and lets every variable load on every factor. Confirmatory factor analysis tests a pre-specified model, fixes most cross-loadings at zero, and reports fit indices (χ², CFI and TLI above .95, RMSEA below .06, SRMR below .08). CFA is the measurement half of structural equation modelling. Use EFA when developing a scale, CFA when validating it in a new sample.
Sample size for factor analysis: commonly cited rules are at least 10 cases per variable and an absolute minimum of about 200 to 300 cases. Comrey and Lee's scale is quotable: 100 poor, 200 fair, 300 good, 500 very good, 1000 excellent.

15.6 Standardisation and norms

Standardisation has two meanings, and papers use both. (1) Uniformity of procedure: identical instructions, materials, time limits and scoring for every test-taker, so that differences in scores reflect differences in the person and not in the administration. (2) Establishing norms: administering the test to a large, representative standardisation sample so that individual scores can be interpreted against the group.

Steps in constructing and standardising a test

  1. Define the construct and plan the test, producing a table of specifications (a blueprint of content areas by cognitive level).
  2. Write the item pool, usually two to three times more items than the final test needs.
  3. Expert review for content validity, clarity, and cultural or gender bias.
  4. Pilot / try-out on a sample resembling the target population.
  5. Item analysis: compute difficulty, discrimination and item-total correlations; run distractor analysis; drop and revise items.
  6. Assemble the final form, ordering items from easy to difficult and balancing content.
  7. Standardisation: administer to a large representative sample and develop norms.
  8. Establish reliability and validity on that data.
  9. Write the manual: administration, scoring, norms tables, reliability and validity evidence, and the limits of interpretation.

Types of norms

NormMeaningCaution
Age normsThe typical performance of each age group. Gives a mental age (Alfred Binet's original device)Assumes steady growth with age, so it breaks down after adolescence
Grade normsTypical performance at each school gradeMeaningful only for subjects taught in a fixed sequence; grade-equivalent scores are widely misread
Percentile normsPercentage of the norm group scoring below a given raw scoreEasy to explain, but ordinal: unequal units, compressed at the centre. Do not average them
Standard score normsz, T, deviation IQ, stanine, stenEqual units, so arithmetic is legitimate. The preferred form
Local normsBuilt on the specific institution or region using the testOften more relevant than national norms for selection decisions
Norm-referenced vs criterion-referenced. A norm-referenced test compares a person to other people, and must therefore spread people out (items of about .50 difficulty, high variance). Examples: IQ tests, entrance examinations. A criterion-referenced test compares a person to a fixed standard of mastery regardless of what others scored, and can legitimately produce a distribution where everybody passes. Examples: a driving test, a licensing examination, a mastery test in school. Almost every entrance you are sitting is norm-referenced, which is why your rank matters more than your raw score.
The Flynn effect and why norms expire. IQ scores in the standardisation population rose by roughly 3 points per decade through the twentieth century (James Flynn). This means an old norm table makes people look smarter than they are, which matters most at diagnostic cut-offs for intellectual disability. Norms must be periodically re-established, which is why tests are revised (WAIS to WAIS-R to WAIS-III to WAIS-IV to WAIS-5). Naming the Flynn effect when asked why tests are restandardised is a strong answer.

16 Which test to use

Almost every "which statistical test would you apply" item in an entrance paper is a single path down the tree below. Work left to right: what kind of question, what kind of data, how many groups or variables, related or independent.

The four questions to ask, in order.
1. What is the question? Difference between groups, association between variables, or prediction and structure?
2. What is the scale of the DV? Nominal means frequencies means chi-square. Ordinal means ranks means the non-parametric family. Interval or ratio opens the parametric family.
3. How many groups, conditions or variables? Two means t or its rank equivalent. Three or more means ANOVA or its rank equivalent.
4. Are the groups independent or related? Different people means independent (independent t, one-way ANOVA, Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis). Same people means related (paired t, repeated-measures ANOVA, Wilcoxon, Friedman).
Answer those four and there is only one test left standing.

How to attack Part I (statistics) from here

  1. Learn section 1.2 (Stevens's scales) and section 16 (the decision tree) first, and learn them perfectly. Between them they answer more marks per minute of study than anything else in this book, because "identify the scale" and "which test would you use" are the two most repeated question forms across all these papers.
  2. Memorise the fixed numbers. 68 / 95 / 99.7 percent; 1.96 and 2.58; χ² critical of 3.84 at df 1; Cohen's .20 / .50 / .80 for d and .10 / .30 / .50 for r; η² at .01 / .06 / .14; alpha of .70 acceptable, .80 good, .90 for individual decisions; item discrimination D of .20 as the reject line and the 27% split. These get asked as bare recall.
  3. Drill the parametric-to-non-parametric mapping in section 14.3 until it is reflexive. It appears as a direct matching item in nearly every paper.
  4. Drill the assumption tables. The commonest ANOVA question is not how to compute F, it is which assumptions ANOVA rests on, which test checks each one, and what to do when one fails. Remember that for Levene, Shapiro–Wilk, Box's M, Mauchly and Hosmer–Lemeshow, a non-significant result is the good news.
  5. Learn the names. Section 17.3 is pure marks: every one of these papers asks who developed which test. Fisher, Pearson, Spearman, Gosset, Tukey, Levene, Mauchly, Wilks, Cronbach and Stevens are the ten that recur most.
  6. Do not skip section 15. Reliability, validity, item analysis and factor analysis carry as many marks as the whole inferential-testing block, and most candidates prepare them last and worst. The reliability-caps-validity-at-√rxx point, the SEM confidence band, and the EFA-versus-CFA distinction are all repeat offenders.
  7. Then sit the real papers. Work the statistics items in the IHBAS 2025, IHBAS 2024, RML and PYQ Real 2025 mocks, and any item you miss will map straight back to a numbered section above.
Part II: Research methods. Part I taught you how to analyse data. Part II teaches how the data get made: how a question becomes a design, what makes a study valid, the experimental, quasi-experimental, non-experimental and single-case designs, how observations, interviews and scales are collected, qualitative and mixed methods, clinical trials and meta-analysis, and research ethics. Every design is judged by the same yardstick, the validity of the study (section 19), which is a different thing from the validity of a test (section 15.3).

18 The research process: science, problems, hypotheses and variables

Sections 1 to 17 taught you what to do with numbers once you have them. This half of the book is about how the numbers are produced: how a clinical hunch ("I think group CBT helps our first-episode patients") becomes a question, a hypothesis, a set of measured variables, a design and finally a defensible conclusion. A brilliant ANOVA on a badly designed study is still a bad study, and entrance papers test design at least as hard as arithmetic.

How this half is organised. 18 lays the foundations (science, problems, hypotheses, variables); 19 asks when a study's conclusion can be trusted and how extraneous variables are controlled; 20 to 22 are the designs; 23 data collection; 24 qualitative and mixed methods; 25 clinical trials and meta-analysis; 26 ethics; 27 the decision guide and name index.

18.1 What makes psychology a science

What distinguishes science is not its subject matter but its method of fixing belief. The classic statement is by the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce, in his 1877 essay "The Fixation of Belief" (Popular Science Monthly), which described four ways people settle what they believe. Fred N. Kerlinger opened his Foundations of Behavioral Research (1964) with the same four, which is how they entered research-methods syllabi.

Method of knowing (Peirce, 1877)How belief is fixedClinical exampleWeakness
TenacityYou hold a belief because you have always held it; repetition makes it feel true"Schizophrenia is caused by bad mothering", repeated in a ward for decadesImmune to evidence; contrary facts are ignored
AuthorityYou believe it because a respected source says so (a guru, a textbook, a senior consultant)"Dr X says ECT never works, so it does not"Authorities disagree and can be wrong; no way to settle the dispute
A priori (intuition, reason)It "stands to reason" or "is agreeable to reason"; it feels self-evidently true"Talking about suicide must put the idea in a patient's head"What seems reasonable differs between people and is often false (this one is: asking about suicide does not increase risk)
ScienceBelief is settled by observation that is public, repeatable and self-correcting, independent of what anyone wants to be trueA randomised trial comparing CBT with treatment as usualSlow and provisional, but the only method that corrects itself

Behind this sit two philosophical camps: rationalism (reason is the source of knowledge) and empiricism (John Locke's mind as a tabula rasa, 1690: sensory experience is the source of knowledge). Science is empiricism disciplined by reason: theories are reasoned out, then judged by observation.

The assumptions and characteristics of science

  • Empiricism: claims are settled by systematic observation and measurement, not by argument, authority or introspection alone.
  • Determinism: behaviour has causes, so it is lawful and in principle predictable. In psychology this is probabilistic determinism: causes raise the probability of an outcome rather than guaranteeing it, which is why inferential statistics is needed.
  • Parsimony: of two explanations that fit the facts equally well, prefer the one that assumes less. In philosophy this is Occam's (Ockham's) razor, after the 14th-century English friar William of Ockham ("entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity"); in psychology its special form is Lloyd Morgan's canon.
  • Testability (falsifiability): a claim must be stated so that some possible observation could show it false (Popper, 18.2).
  • Replicability: another researcher following the same procedure should get the same result.
  • Objectivity: findings should not depend on who observes; in practice, intersubjective agreement secured by standardised procedures and operational definitions (18.8).
  • Science is also systematic, public (methods published so others can check them), tentative and self-correcting. Its goals are to describe, explain, predict and control behaviour.
Conwy Lloyd Morgan, An Introduction to Comparative Psychology (1894): "In no case may we interpret an action as the outcome of the exercise of a higher psychical faculty, if it can be interpreted as the outcome of the exercise of one which stands lower in the psychological scale." It was aimed at George Romanes's anecdotal animal psychology, which credited dogs and cats with reasoning where trial-and-error learning sufficed. Morgan's canon is parsimony applied to minds; Occam's razor is parsimony applied to everything.
Replication is not a formality. In 2015 the Open Science Collaboration (led by Brian Nosek) repeated 100 studies from three leading psychology journals: about 97% of the originals had been significant, only about 36% of the replications were. Know the three kinds of replication: direct (exact), repeating the procedure as closely as possible; conceptual, testing the same hypothesis with different operations; systematic, changing one feature at a time to find a finding's limits.

18.2 Induction, deduction and how science actually moves

Induction reasons from particular observations to a general conclusion: you see 40 panic patients who all catastrophically misinterpret bodily sensations and conclude that this is a general feature of panic. Francis Bacon's Novum Organum (1620) made induction the method of the new science. Its weakness is the problem of induction (David Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature, 1739–40): no finite number of observations guarantees a universal conclusion. Every swan Europeans had seen was white, until black swans were found in Australia.

Deduction reasons from a general premise to a particular conclusion that must be true if the premise is: "All anxiety disorders involve overestimation of threat; social anxiety disorder is an anxiety disorder; therefore it involves overestimation of threat." It is certain but adds no new information. Abduction (Peirce's term) is inference to the best explanation, from a surprising observation to the hypothesis that would best explain it; clinical formulation is abductive. Research combines induction and deduction in the hypothetico-deductive method: from a theory deduce a testable hypothesis, collect observations, and see whether the prediction holds. In psychology it is most associated with Clark L. Hull, whose Principles of Behavior (1943) was built as a formal system of postulates and derived theorems.

InductionDeduction
DirectionParticular → general ("bottom-up")General → particular ("top-down")
Starts withObservations, dataA theory or premise
ProducesEmpirical generalisations, new theoryTestable hypotheses, predictions
CertaintyProbable only (Hume's problem)Certain, if the premises are true
Typical ofExploratory and qualitative research, grounded theory, theory developmentExperimental, hypothesis-testing research

Karl Popper: falsification

Karl Popper, in Logik der Forschung (1934; English The Logic of Scientific Discovery, 1959), turned Hume's problem round. Verification and falsification are asymmetric: a million white swans cannot prove "all swans are white", but one black swan disproves it. So science advances by trying to refute theories, and a theory is scientific only if it is falsifiable, that is, it forbids some observable outcomes. This is his answer to the demarcation problem (what separates science from non-science). His examples were Sigmund Freud's and Alfred Adler's theories, which could explain any behaviour after the fact, against Einstein's relativity, which made a risky prediction (starlight bending, checked at the 1919 eclipse) that could have failed. A theory that survives attempts at refutation is corroborated, never proved; this is the logic of testing the null hypothesis (section 8.1).

Thomas Kuhn: paradigms and revolutions

Thomas S. Kuhn, in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), argued that most of the time scientists work inside a paradigm: a shared framework of theory, methods, model studies and assumptions about which questions matter. Work within it is normal science ("puzzle-solving"). Results that do not fit, anomalies, are at first set aside; when they accumulate the field enters crisis, and a scientific revolution replaces the old paradigm: a paradigm shift. Rival paradigms are incommensurable, so the change is partly conversion rather than pure logic. The "cognitive revolution" against behaviourism in the 1950s and 1960s is the usual psychology example, though psychology is often called pre-paradigmatic or multi-paradigmatic because several schools coexist.

Popper vs Kuhn. Popper is falsifiability, demarcation, conjectures and refutations: a normative account of how science should work. Kuhn is paradigm, normal science, anomaly, revolution: a historical account of how science does work. Two later names occasionally appear as distractors: Imre Lakatos (research programmes with a protected "hard core", 1970) and Paul Feyerabend (Against Method, 1975, "anything goes").

Walter Wallace's wheel of science

The sociologist Walter L. Wallace, in The Logic of Science in Sociology (1971), drew the cycle as a wheel: theories yield hypotheses by deduction; hypotheses become observations through operationalising, sampling and measuring; observations are summarised into empirical generalisations; generalisations are built back into theory. Comparing generalisations with hypotheses is the test. The right half is deductive, the left inductive; the top half is theorising, the bottom half doing research. Induction and deduction are not rivals: a research programme goes round the whole wheel and can enter it anywhere.

18.3 Research paradigms: positivism to pragmatism

Before choosing a method a researcher already holds, often unknowingly, a research paradigm: beliefs about what is real and how it can be known. Egon Guba and Yvonna Lincoln (1994) framed every paradigm as answers to three linked questions; a fourth term completes the ladder.

TermThe question it answersExample answers
OntologyWhat is the nature of reality? What exists to be known?One objective reality (realism) vs multiple constructed realities (relativism)
EpistemologyWhat is the relationship between the knower and the known? What counts as knowledge?The researcher stands apart and observes objectively vs the researcher and participant create the knowledge together
MethodologyWhat is the overall strategy and logic for finding things out?Experimental hypothesis testing vs naturalistic, interpretive inquiry
MethodWhich specific technique collects and analyses the data?A questionnaire, a structured interview, a t test, thematic analysis
Methodology is wider than method. A method is a tool (an interview, a scale, an ANOVA); methodology is the reasoned study of methods: why these tools, in this design, answer this question, and with what limits. A past paper: "the scope of research methodology is wider than that of research methods."
ParadigmOntology and epistemologyTypical methodsAim
Positivism (Auguste Comte coined the term in the 1830s; logical positivism of the Vienna Circle in the 1920s–30s)One objective reality that can be observed and measured directly; the researcher is detached and value-free; only verifiable statements are meaningfulExperiments, structured measurement, statisticsDiscover general laws; explain and predict
Post-positivismReality exists but can be known only imperfectly and probabilistically; all observation is theory-laden and fallible; we falsify rather than verify (Popper)Quantitative designs fixed before data collection, hypothesis testing, multiple measuresApproximate truth through repeated, fallible testing. The stance behind most modern quantitative psychology
Constructivism / interpretivismReality is socially and personally constructed; multiple realities; knower and known are inseparableIn-depth interviews, participant observation, narrative and phenomenological analysisUnderstand meaning from the participant's point of view (verstehen)
Critical / transformativeReality is shaped by power, gender, caste, class and history; knowledge is never neutralParticipatory action research, critical ethnography, feminist researchExpose and change injustice; empower participants
Pragmatism (Peirce, William James, John Dewey)Truth is "what works"; the research question, not a philosophy, decides the methodMixed methods (section 24)Solve practical problems with whatever combination of methods answers the question
Exam shorthand. Quantitative = positivist or post-positivist; qualitative = constructivist/interpretivist; mixed methods = pragmatist; participatory and emancipatory = critical/transformative. "Which does not apply to qualitative research?" wants "emphasis on objective truth".

Nomothetic and idiographic approaches

The German philosopher Wilhelm Windelband, in his 1894 rectorial address at Strasbourg, distinguished nomothetic sciences (Greek nomos, law), which seek general laws, from idiographic sciences (idios, one's own), which seek to understand the unique case, as history does. Gordon W. Allport brought the pair into psychology in Personality: A Psychological Interpretation (1937), arguing that personality psychology needed both. Nomothetic work studies groups, averages and laws: the experiment, the survey, factor-analytic trait theories. Idiographic work studies one person in depth: the case study, personal documents (Allport's Letters from Jenny), the Q-sort, single-case designs (section 22), much qualitative research. Allport later suggested morphogenic as a better word for his idiographic method.

Past-paper fact: "Nomothetic approach of study is involved in" → the experimental method. Nomothetic = general laws, groups, quantitative, experimental. Idiographic = the unique individual, case study, qualitative.

18.4 Types of research

Research is classified along several independent axes, and one study sits somewhere on each: a randomised trial of yoga for anxiety in a Bengaluru hospital is applied, explanatory, quantitative, experimental and longitudinal at once.

AxisTypesWhat distinguishes them
PurposeBasic (pure, fundamental) vs appliedBasic research seeks knowledge for its own sake (how does fear extinction work in the amygdala?). Applied research solves a practical problem (does exposure therapy reduce phobic avoidance in our clinic?). Basic findings usually feed later applications
Depth of the questionExploratory, descriptive, explanatory (causal)Exploratory: a new area, no clear hypotheses; it is hypothesis-generating. Descriptive: describes what exists (prevalence, characteristics) without manipulating variables. Explanatory: asks why, tests causal hypotheses
Control over the IVExperimental, quasi-experimental, non-experimental (correlational, ex post facto, survey, observational)Whether the researcher manipulates the IV and randomly assigns participants (sections 20 and 21)
Kind of dataQuantitative, qualitative, mixedNumbers and statistics vs words and meanings (section 24)
TimeCross-sectional vs longitudinalOne occasion vs repeated measurement of the same people (section 21)
SettingLaboratory vs fieldControl vs realism (section 19.1)
Number of participantsGroup (large-N) vs single-subject (small-N)Section 22

Action research, a term introduced by Kurt Lewin ("Action research and minority problems", 1946), is research done by or with practitioners to solve a specific, local problem in their own setting, in cycles of planning, acting, observing and reflecting. A ward team studying why patients miss follow-up appointments, changing the reminder system and re-measuring is doing action research: applied, but aimed at improvement here rather than generalisation (section 24).

Evaluation research (programme evaluation) judges the worth of a programme, policy or service. Michael Scriven (1967) distinguished formative evaluation, carried out while a programme is being developed or delivered, to improve it (piloting a school mental-health curriculum and revising it), from summative evaluation, carried out at the end to judge whether it worked and should be continued or scaled up. The analogy usually credited to Robert Stake: when the cook tastes the soup, that is formative; when the guests taste it, that is summative.

18.5 From a problem to a report: the steps of research

Kerlinger defined scientific research as a systematic, controlled, empirical and critical investigation of hypothesised relations among natural phenomena. Textbooks number the steps differently, but each exists to make the work systematic, controlled, empirical or critical.

  1. Identify and select a research problem: an area of difficulty or ignorance worth investigating.
  2. Review the literature: find out what is already known, what methods have been used and where the gaps are.
  3. Define the problem precisely and state the research question and, where appropriate, the hypotheses (18.6).
  4. Identify the variables and give each an operational definition (18.7, 18.8).
  5. Choose the research design: experimental, quasi-experimental, correlational, qualitative and so on (sections 20 to 24).
  6. Select the sample (section 7.2) and obtain ethical approval (section 26).
  7. Select or construct the tools and collect the data (section 23).
  8. Analyse the data: editing, coding, classification, tabulation, then statistical analysis (sections 2 to 14).
  9. Interpret the results against the hypotheses and the earlier literature; state limitations.
  10. Report the study (APA format: introduction, method, results, discussion) so it can be evaluated and replicated.

Where research problems come from

  • Theory: deducing an untested implication (if the cognitive model of depression is right, negative automatic thoughts should precede, not just accompany, low mood).
  • Previous research: the "suggestions for further research" section, contradictory findings, failures to replicate, untested populations (does a Western finding hold in rural Indian samples?).
  • Practical and clinical problems: high dropout from a de-addiction programme, long waiting lists, a new law such as the Mental Healthcare Act, 2017.
  • Personal experience and observation, including serendipity (an accidental finding, like Ivan Pavlov noticing his dogs salivating before the food arrived).
  • Replication of an important study, and social issues (farmer suicides, exam stress, screen use).

Criteria of a good research problem

Kerlinger gave three formal criteria for a problem statement: it should (1) express a relation between two or more variables, (2) be stated clearly and unambiguously in question form, and (3) imply the possibility of empirical testing. "Is psychoanalysis good?" fails all three; "Does 12 weeks of group CBT reduce BDI-II scores more than treatment as usual in first-episode depression?" passes all three. Practical criteria: the problem should be significant, novel, feasible (time, money, access, the researcher's competence), ethical and interesting. Clinical researchers use the acronym FINER (feasible, interesting, novel, ethical, relevant) and shape the question with PICO (population, intervention, comparison, outcome).

The review of literature

The literature is the body of prior work related to a research problem (a past paper asked for exactly this word). The review shapes the study; its purposes are to establish what is known and locate the gap (avoiding needless duplication), sharpen and delimit the problem, supply the theoretical framework from which hypotheses are deduced, learn from the methods, tools, sample sizes and mistakes of earlier studies, identify the extraneous variables to control, and provide the context for interpreting the findings. Primary sources are original reports by the people who did the study; secondary sources (textbooks, reviews) describe others' work. Searches run through PsycINFO and PubMed; Indian theses are archived in Shodhganga (INFLIBNET). A narrative review is a selective summary; a systematic review follows a pre-specified, reproducible protocol (PRISMA); a meta-analysis pools effect sizes statistically (section 25).

18.6 Hypotheses

A hypothesis (Greek hypo, under, and thesis, placing) is a tentative, testable statement about the relationship between two or more variables; Kerlinger's standard definition is "a conjectural statement of the relation between two or more variables." It is the researcher's informed guess at the answer to the research question, stated so that data can support or contradict it. Its main function is to guide the study: which variables to measure, which design, sample and analysis to use. It is never formulated to prove the researcher right.

Characteristics of a good hypothesis

The list examiners quote is from William J. Goode and Paul K. Hatt, Methods in Social Research (1952). A usable hypothesis must (1) be conceptually clear, its concepts defined, preferably operationally; (2) have empirical referents, so it can be tested against observation (no moral judgements such as "bad parents produce bad children"); (3) be specific about the expected relationship, population and conditions; (4) be related to available techniques for testing it; (5) be related to a body of theory. Other texts add testable/falsifiable, parsimonious, consistent with known facts and stated as a relationship between variables.

Types and forms of hypotheses

TypeWhat it isExample (CBT trial)
Research (substantive, scientific) hypothesisThe prediction in words, in terms of constructs and variablesGroup CBT will reduce depressive symptoms more than treatment as usual
Statistical hypothesisThe same prediction restated about population parameters, so a test can decide itH₀: μCBT = μTAU; H₁: μCBT < μTAU (post-treatment BDI-II)
Null hypothesis (H₀)No difference, no relationship; the hypothesis actually tested (section 8.1)There is no significant difference in BDI-II scores between CBT and TAU
Alternative hypothesis (H₁, Hₐ)There is a difference or relationship; the researcher's real predictionThere is a significant difference between CBT and TAU
Directional (one-tailed)States which way the difference or correlation will goCBT patients will score lower than TAU patients
Non-directional (two-tailed)Predicts a difference but not its directionCBT and TAU patients will differ
Descriptive / relational / causalDescribes a characteristic / predicts an association / predicts that one variable causes anotherMost first-episode patients are under 30 / rumination correlates with relapse / CBT causes symptom reduction
Working hypothesisA provisional hypothesis that guides the early stage of an investigation and is revised as data come in"Dropout may be linked to travel distance": checked, then refined
Universal vs existentialUniversal: the relationship holds for all values of the variables, at all times and places. Existential: it holds for at least one case"All reinforced responses increase in rate" vs "There exists at least one patient who improves without treatment"

Hypotheses are also written in three forms: declarative ("There will be a significant difference in anxiety between yoga and control groups"), question ("Is there a difference in anxiety between yoga and control groups?", strictly a research question) and null ("There is no significant difference..."). Two past-paper items: "Reinforcement will have a positive effect on performance" is an alternative, directional hypothesis (it predicts an effect and its direction); "There is no difference between male and female incomes in the population" is the one that "sounds like a null hypothesis".

A directional hypothesis needs a reason before the data. It must be justified by theory or earlier findings and tested one-tailed; choosing a one-tailed test after seeing which way the data went is cheating (section 8.3).

Where hypotheses come from, and when there are none

Hypotheses are deduced from theory, generalised from previous findings, suggested by clinical observation, borrowed by analogy (animal learned helplessness suggesting a hypothesis about human depression), and sometimes reached by intuition. Not every study has one. Exploratory research, descriptive surveys (what is the prevalence of internet gaming disorder among Delhi college students?) and most qualitative research (grounded theory enters the field without hypotheses and builds theory from the data) state research questions or objectives instead; they are hypothesis-generating, not hypothesis-testing.

Concept, construct, hypothesis, theory, law, model

TermMeaningExample
ConceptAn abstraction formed by generalising from particulars; a word that names a class of things"Weight", "reward", "aggression"
ConstructA concept deliberately invented for scientific purposes; not directly observable, inferred from behaviour, and tied into a theoryAnxiety, intelligence, self-efficacy, ego strength
HypothesisA specific, testable prediction about the relation between variablesSelf-efficacy at intake predicts abstinence at six months
TheoryKerlinger: "a set of interrelated constructs, definitions and propositions that presents a systematic view of phenomena by specifying relations among variables, with the purpose of explaining and predicting the phenomena"Albert Bandura's social cognitive theory (1986); Aaron T. Beck's cognitive theory of depression (1967)
LawA highly confirmed statement of a regular relationship, usually narrow and often mathematical; describes rather than explainsErnst Weber's law (1834), the Yerkes–Dodson law (1908), Edward Thorndike's law of effect
ModelA simplified representation, often an analogy or diagram, of how a system might work; narrower and more concrete than a theoryThe diathesis–stress model; Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin's multi-store model of memory (1968)
"It's just a theory" is a misuse. A scientific theory is the broadest, best-supported kind of explanation; the guess-like thing is the hypothesis. Order of generality: hypothesis (one prediction) < law (a confirmed regularity) < theory (an explanatory system).

18.7 Variables

A variable is any characteristic that can take two or more values; one that takes a single value in a study is a constant. Section 1.1 gave one-line definitions; here each type is built properly, because papers test them through applied items.

Independent and dependent variables

The independent variable (IV) is the presumed cause, the variable the experimenter manipulates (or, in non-experimental research, selects or classifies by). The dependent variable (DV) is the presumed effect, measured and expected to change with the IV. In "Does mindfulness training reduce relapse in recurrent depression?", training is the IV and relapse the DV. The values of an IV are its levels or conditions: placebo, 50 mg and 100 mg is one IV with three levels. An IV is manipulated by presence vs absence (therapy vs none), amount (4, 8 or 12 sessions) or type (CBT vs interpersonal therapy). A manipulation check verifies that the manipulation produced the intended state (did the stress induction raise self-rated stress?). A good DV is reliable, valid and sensitive: a task so easy that everyone scores near the top has a ceiling effect, one so hard that everyone scores near the bottom a floor effect, and both hide real effects.

ContextName for the cause sideName for the effect side
ExperimentIndependent variable, treatment, factorDependent variable
Regression, correlational researchPredictor, explanatory variableCriterion, response variable, outcome
EpidemiologyExposure, risk factorOutcome, disease
Classic S-O-R scheme (Robert S. Woodworth)Stimulus variables (features of the environment or task, e.g. light intensity: always an IV) and organismic variables (features of the person, e.g. age)Response variables (the behaviour measured, e.g. response rate: always a DV)
Find the IV by asking "what is presumed to cause what?", not by word order. Past paper: "Old age home residents who have heart disease die at an earlier age than the ones who do not have heart disease." The IV is having heart disease; the DV is age at death; living in an old age home is a constant (everyone in the study lives in one). Note that heart disease cannot be manipulated, which makes it an attribute variable and the study non-experimental.

Manipulated (active) vs measured (attribute) variables

Kerlinger divided variables into active variables, which the researcher manipulates (therapy type, dose, instructions), and attribute variables, which participants bring with them and which can only be measured or selected. Attribute variables are also called organismic or subject variables: age, sex, diagnosis, IQ, personality, socioeconomic status, caste, childhood trauma. When the "IV" is an attribute (schizophrenia vs healthy controls), people cannot be randomly assigned to its levels, the groups differ in countless other ways, and no causal conclusion is possible; such studies are quasi-experimental or ex post facto (sections 20 and 21).

Extraneous, confounding and control variables

An extraneous variable is any variable other than the IV that could affect the DV. They are grouped as participant (subject) variables (age, intelligence, motivation, severity), situational (environmental) variables (noise, temperature, time of day, the room), task variables (difficulty, instructions, item order) and experimenter variables (sex, manner, expectations; section 19.5). An extraneous variable that varies randomly across conditions only adds noise (error variance) and lowers power. One that varies systematically with the IV becomes a confounding variable, whose effect cannot be separated from the IV's; a past paper's definition is a variable that influences both the independent and the dependent variable. A control variable is one deliberately held constant or adjusted for.

Example: a clinic compares patients who chose CBT with patients who chose medication, and CBT patients improve more. But people who choose weekly talking therapy are, on average, less severely ill and more motivated, so severity and motivation are confounded with treatment. Random assignment (section 19.6) is the cure.

Intervening variables and hypothetical constructs

Intervening variable is used in two senses. In research-methods texts (Bruce Tuckman's scheme of independent, dependent, moderator, control and intervening variables) it is a process between IV and DV that explains their link but cannot be directly observed, measured or manipulated, only inferred: learning, fatigue, motivation. Practice (IV) improves performance (DV) through learning (intervening).

Kenneth MacCorquodale and Paul E. Meehl, "On a distinction between hypothetical constructs and intervening variables" (Psychological Review, 1948), sharpened the term. An intervening variable (Edward Tolman's term from the 1930s; Clark Hull's habit strength is a textbook example) merely summarises the relation between observable inputs and outputs, with no surplus meaning. A hypothetical construct carries surplus meaning: it asserts that something real exists (a memory trace, a neural process, the ego) with properties beyond the data that introduced it, so it can be wrong in new ways.

Mediators and moderators

Both are "third variables" in an X–Y relation, doing completely different jobs. The definitive statement is Reuben M. Baron and David A. Kenny, "The moderator–mediator variable distinction in social psychological research" (Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 1986).

  • A mediator (M) explains how or why X affects Y. It lies on the causal path: X causes M, and M causes Y. CBT (X) reduces negative automatic thoughts (M), which lowers depression (Y). Paths: a (X → M), b (M → Y, controlling for X), c (total effect of X on Y), c′ (direct effect once M is controlled). The indirect effect is a × b, and c = c′ + ab.
