  • A moderator (Z) explains when, for whom or how strongly X affects Y. It is not caused by X; it changes the size or even the direction of the X–Y relationship. CBT helps mild-to-moderate depression much more than severe depression: severity moderates the treatment effect. Statistically a moderator is an interaction (X × Z; sections 10.4 and 13.3).

Baron and Kenny's four steps for mediation: (1) X predicts Y (path c); (2) X predicts M (path a); (3) M predicts Y with X also in the equation (path b); (4) the effect of X on Y drops when M is controlled. If c′ falls to zero, mediation is full; if it shrinks but stays significant, partial. The indirect effect was traditionally tested with the Sobel test (Michael Sobel, 1982); current practice uses bootstrapped confidence intervals for a × b (Kristopher Preacher and Andrew Hayes, 2004; Hayes's PROCESS macro), and step 1 is no longer considered essential.

The classic mix-up. "Social support buffers the effect of stress on depression" is moderation ("buffer" signals an interaction). "Stress leads to depression through rumination" is mediation (rumination is the mechanism). Test: if the third variable is caused by X and sits between X and Y, it is a mediator; if it exists before X, is unaffected by X, and the effect of X differs across its levels, it is a moderator. Hook: mediator = mechanism, moderator = "more for some". Neither is a confound, which causes both X and Y and makes their link spurious.

Suppressor variables

A suppressor variable correlates with a predictor but hardly at all with the criterion, yet adding it to a regression increases prediction, because it partials out criterion-irrelevant variance in the predictor. The concept is credited to Paul Horst (1941). Illustration: a written symptom questionnaire predicts clinician-rated severity, but part of its score reflects reading ability. Adding a reading test (correlated with the questionnaire, not with severity) removes that irrelevant part and raises R. The signature is a substantial regression weight, sometimes with an unexpected sign, for a variable whose simple correlation with the criterion is near zero (sections 12.5 and 13.3).

Continuous, discrete and the rest

Continuous variables can take any value in a range (reaction time); discrete ones only separate values (number of admissions). Quantitative variables differ in amount (dose, anxiety score); categorical ones differ in kind (diagnosis, therapy type), and a categorical variable with two values is dichotomous (relapsed or not). Sections 1.1 and 1.2 cover these and the scales of measurement. An IV can be quantitative (three doses) or categorical (three therapies), which decides whether trends or only group differences can be tested.

18.8 Operational definitions

Constructs such as anxiety, aggression or intelligence cannot be observed directly. An operational definition defines a concept by the procedures (operations) used to measure or manipulate it.

Percy W. Bridgman, Harvard physicist (Nobel Prize, 1946), introduced operationism in The Logic of Modern Physics (1927), reflecting on Einstein's redefinition of simultaneity: "we mean by any concept nothing more than a set of operations; the concept is synonymous with the corresponding set of operations." Stanley Smith (S. S.) Stevens brought it into psychology with "The operational definition of psychological concepts" (Psychological Review, 1935), and it became part of neobehaviourist method. "Who gave operational definition / operationism?" → Bridgman; who imported it into psychology → Stevens.
ConstructOne possible operational definition
AnxietyScore on the State–Trait Anxiety Inventory (STAI; Charles Spielberger and colleagues, 1970); or heart rate and skin conductance during a speech task
Aggression in childrenNumber of hits, kicks and punches delivered to a Bobo doll in a 20-minute observation (Albert Bandura, Dorothea Ross and Sheila Ross, 1961)
Severe depressionA score of 29 or more on the Beck Depression Inventory-II
Hunger (manipulated)Hours of food deprivation: 0, 12 or 24
LearningNumber of trials needed to reach a criterion of two errorless runs
Treatment adherenceProportion of prescribed doses taken, from pill counts

Kerlinger distinguished the constitutive (conceptual) definition, which defines a construct with other constructs ("anxiety is a diffuse, unpleasant apprehension about future threat"), from the operational definition, which gives it meaning through activities. Operational definitions are either measured (how a variable will be measured: anxiety as an STAI score) or experimental (how it will be manipulated: stress induced by a five-minute speech before two evaluators).

Why they matter, and their limits. Operational definitions make research objective and replicable: another researcher can repeat exactly what you did. But no single operation captures a construct, and strict operationism implies every new test defines a new concept (Edwin Boring's 1923 remark that intelligence is "what the tests test"). Modern practice is multiple operationism: measure the construct several ways and look for convergence. Relying on one operation is mono-operation bias, a threat to the construct validity of a study (section 19.1); whether a test measures its construct is test validity (section 15.3).
The operational definition is not the construct. "Depression = BDI-II of 29 or more" is a measurement rule for one study, not what depression is. A drug that only improves sleep can lower BDI scores, which is why construct validity asks whether the operations represent the construct you claim to have studied.
Recap of section 18: Peirce (1877) named four ways of fixing belief: tenacity, authority, a priori and science. Science assumes empiricism, (probabilistic) determinism, parsimony (Occam's razor; Lloyd Morgan's canon, 1894), testability, replicability and objectivity. Induction runs particular → general (Bacon; Hume's problem), deduction general → particular, and the hypothetico-deductive method (Hull) combines them, as Wallace's wheel (1971) shows. Popper (1934/1959) made falsifiability the mark of science; Kuhn (1962) gave paradigm, normal science, anomaly and paradigm shift. Ontology, epistemology, methodology and method define a paradigm: positivist/post-positivist = quantitative, constructivist = qualitative, critical = participatory, pragmatist = mixed. Windelband (1894) coined nomothetic and idiographic; Gordon Allport (1937) brought them into psychology. Research is basic or applied; exploratory, descriptive or explanatory; action research is Kurt Lewin (1946); formative vs summative evaluation is Scriven (1967). A good problem (Kerlinger) relates variables, is a clear question and is testable. A hypothesis is a conjectural statement of the relation between variables; Goode and Hatt (1952) listed its criteria; know research vs statistical, null vs alternative, directional vs non-directional, universal vs existential. IV = manipulated cause with levels, DV = measured effect; attribute variables cannot be manipulated; a confound varies with the IV; MacCorquodale and Paul Meehl (1948) separated intervening variables from hypothetical constructs; mediator = mechanism (ab), moderator = interaction (Baron and Kenny, 1986); suppressor = Horst (1941). Operational definitions come from Bridgman (1927) via Stevens (1935).

19 Validity of a study and the control of extraneous variables

A study is run to support a conclusion of the form "X caused Y in these people, and would do so in others like them". This section asks when that conclusion deserves to be believed, what can make it false, and what researchers do about it. The whole of experimental design (sections 20 to 22) is a set of answers to the problems listed here, so this is the section that makes the designs make sense.

Validity of a STUDY is not validity of a TEST. Section 15.3 asked whether a test measures what it claims to (content, criterion-related, construct validity of a measure; the MTMM matrix). This section asks whether a study's conclusion is sound: internal, external, statistical conclusion and construct validity of a study. The word "construct validity" appears in both, with related but different meanings, and "ecological validity" appears in both lists. When a question mentions history, maturation, attrition, generalising to settings or causal inference, it is about the study.

19.1 The four kinds of validity of a study

The distinction between internal and external validity was introduced by Donald T. Campbell in 1957 ("Factors relevant to the validity of experiments in social settings") and made famous by Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley (1963), "Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for research on teaching", a chapter in N. L. Gage's Handbook of Research on Teaching, reprinted as a slim book in 1966. Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell, in Quasi-Experimentation (1979), split each in two, giving the four types still used; William R. Shadish, Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell, Experimental and Quasi-Experimental Designs for Generalized Causal Inference (2002), is the current standard.

Validity of a studyThe question it asksTypical threatsStrengthened by
Statistical conclusion validityIs there really a relationship (covariation) between X and Y, and how strong is it, or did the statistics mislead?Low power, violated test assumptions, "fishing" through many tests (inflated Type I error), unreliable measures, restriction of range, inconsistent treatment deliveryAdequate n (power analysis, section 8.5), reliable measures, correct tests, corrections for multiple testing
Internal validityGiven that X and Y covary, did X cause the change in Y, or would it have happened anyway?History, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression, selection, attrition and their interactions (19.2)Random assignment, control groups, holding conditions constant, blinding
Construct validity (of causes and effects)Do the operations really represent the constructs named? Was it "CBT" that worked, or therapist attention? Was "depression" measured, or sleep?Poor definition of constructs, mono-operation and mono-method bias, demand characteristics, experimenter expectancy, novelty effects, reactivityMultiple operational definitions (18.8), attention-placebo controls, manipulation checks, blind assessment
External validityDoes the causal relationship generalise to other people, settings, treatments, outcome measures and times?Unrepresentative samples, artificial settings, pretest sensitisation, multiple-treatment interference (19.4)Random selection, field settings, replication in new populations, heterogeneous samples
The order of business. Campbell and Stanley called internal validity the sine qua non: "the basic minimum without which any experiment is uninterpretable." There is no point asking whether a causal effect generalises (external validity) until you know there is one (internal validity), and no point asking about cause until you know there is a reliable covariation (statistical conclusion validity). Cook and Campbell's order is therefore statistical conclusion → internal → construct → external.

The trade-off between internal and external validity

Every step taken to raise internal validity tends to lower external validity, and vice versa. A laboratory study of fear conditioning in healthy, right-handed undergraduates, with a fixed script and a single computer task, controls almost everything, so a difference between conditions can confidently be blamed on the IV; but the participants, setting and task are unlike a phobic patient in a crowded Mumbai train. A naturalistic study of patients in community clinics has realism but no control. The resolution is programmatic: establish the effect under control, then test its generality in the field and in new populations, and replicate.

Population validity and ecological validity

Glenn Bracht and Gene Glass (1968) divided external validity into population validity (can the results be generalised from this sample to the wider population of people?) and ecological validity (can they be generalised from the conditions the researcher created to other settings and conditions?). A trial run only on male inpatients with first-episode schizophrenia at a tertiary centre may have poor population validity for women or outpatients; a memory study using lists of nonsense syllables may have poor ecological validity for remembering medication instructions at home.

Ecological validity is a borrowed and stretched term. It was coined by Egon Brunswik in his lens model of perception (collected in Perception and the Representative Design of Psychological Experiments, 1956), where it meant how well an environmental cue (such as retinal size) correlates with the real property it signals (an object's distance). His demand that experiments sample situations as representatively as they sample people he called representative design. Later writers turned "ecological validity" into "how true to real life is the study", and it is now loosely used as a synonym for external validity, a drift Kenneth Hammond (1998) protested. For exams: ecological validity = generalisability to real-world settings, one component of external validity, not the whole of it (section 15.3 uses it in the same loose sense).

Mundane and experimental realism

Elliot Aronson and J. Merrill Carlsmith (1968, Handbook of Social Psychology) separated mundane realism, the extent to which the laboratory situation resembles everyday life, from experimental realism, the extent to which it is involving and believable to participants, so they react spontaneously. Stanley Milgram's obedience experiment (1963) had low mundane realism (no one is asked to shock a stranger in a memory study) but very high experimental realism (participants sweated, trembled and laughed nervously). Aronson and Carlsmith argued that experimental realism matters more. Later texts add psychological realism: whether the processes triggered are the same as in real life.

19.2 Threats to internal validity

A threat to internal validity is any rival explanation for a change in the DV other than the IV. Campbell and Stanley (1963) listed eight, and the eight are what papers ask about. Each is easiest to understand in the weakest design, the one-group pretest–posttest design (O X O, section 20): a clinic measures anxiety, gives eight weeks of relaxation training and measures again. Scores fall. Every threat below is a reason the fall might have happened without the training.

  1. History: specific external events, other than the treatment, occurring between pretest and posttest: exam results, a festival, the end of a lockdown, a new prescription from the psychiatrist.
  2. Maturation: processes within participants that change with the passage of time: growing older, spontaneous remission, fatigue, hunger, boredom. Depressive episodes often remit on their own; young children with autism gain some language over a year with or without ABA.
  3. Testing: taking a test changes scores on a later testing, through practice, familiarity with the items or sensitisation to the topic.
  4. Instrumentation: changes in the measuring instrument or the observers rather than the participants: rater drift, leniency or fatigue, a different version of the scale at posttest.
  5. Statistical regression: groups selected for extreme scores score closer to the mean on retest with no treatment at all (19.3).
  6. Selection: the groups differed before treatment because of how people got into them (volunteers for therapy vs patients who declined).
  7. Experimental mortality (attrition): differential dropout. If the most severely ill leave the treatment group, its posttest mean improves without anyone getting better. ("Mortality" means dropping out, not dying.)
  8. Selection–maturation interaction (and other selection interactions): groups that would change at different rates anyway, such as recent-onset patients treated and chronic patients as controls. Selection can likewise interact with history, instrumentation or regression.

Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell (1979) added threats that arise when there is a control group, because the groups can affect each other, plus one from correlational research: ambiguous temporal precedence (does low social support cause depression, or does depression drive friends away?); diffusion or imitation of treatment (control patients on the same ward pick up the breathing exercises); compensatory equalisation (staff give the deprived control group extra services); compensatory rivalry (the control group works harder to keep up, the John Henry effect, after the folk hero who raced a steam drill and died winning, popularised by Gary Saretsky in 1972; some sources credit Robert Heinich with first use); and resentful demoralisation (controls who know they missed the desirable treatment give up and do worse, exaggerating the effect).

Where textbooks disagree. Campbell and Stanley list eight internal threats; some textbooks give seven (omitting the interaction) and others ten or more (adding diffusion, experimenter bias and so on). Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002) list internal threats as ambiguous temporal precedence, selection, history, maturation, regression, attrition, testing, instrumentation, and additive and interactive effects, and they moved diffusion, compensatory equalisation, compensatory rivalry and resentful demoralisation to the list of threats to construct validity, on the grounds that they change what the treatment and control conditions actually consist of. If an option list offers "resentful demoralisation" as an internal threat, accept it (Cook and Campbell, 1979); if it asks for Campbell and Stanley's original list, it wants the eight.
ThreatWhat it isClinical exampleWhat controls it
HistoryExternal events between measurementsA 12-week anxiety programme coincides with board exams endingA control group measured over the same period (it experiences the same history); short intervals; laboratory isolation
MaturationInternal change with time: growth, spontaneous remission, fatigueDepressed patients improve over 6 months untreatedControl group (matures at the same rate); random assignment
TestingThe pretest changes posttest scoresPractice on a neuropsychological testControl group (also pretested); alternate forms; posttest-only design; Solomon four-group design (Richard L. Solomon, 1949) to measure it
InstrumentationThe measure or the raters changeA clinician-rater becomes lenient at follow-upStandardised instruments; trained, blind raters; inter-rater reliability checks; automation
Statistical regressionExtreme scorers drift toward the meanOnly the most anxious students are enrolledA control group drawn from the same extreme pool by random assignment; reliable measures; selecting on one test and using another as pretest
SelectionGroups differ before treatmentVolunteers vs refusers comparedRandom assignment; failing that, matching and pretest comparison
Experimental mortalityDifferential dropoutSevere cases leave the exposure groupMinimise burden, track and compare dropouts, intention-to-treat analysis (section 25)
Selection × maturationGroups would change at different ratesRecent-onset vs chronic patientsRandom assignment
Ambiguous temporal precedenceUnclear which came firstSupport and depression measured togetherManipulate the IV; longitudinal measurement
Diffusion / imitationControl group gets the treatmentWard-mates share techniquesSeparate sites (cluster randomisation); instructions not to discuss
Compensatory equalisationStaff compensate the control groupNurses give controls extra timeBlind staff; monitor what each group receives
Compensatory rivalry (John Henry)Control group tries harderControl teachers out-teach the programmeKeep groups unaware of each other; blinding
Resentful demoralisationControl group gives upWait-listed patients lose hopeCredible attention-placebo control; delayed treatment offered; blinding
"Which threat is controlled by a control group?" A comparable control group, measured at the same times, controls history, maturation, testing and instrumentation, because both groups experience them equally and they cancel in the comparison. It controls regression only if both groups come from the same extreme pool. It does not control selection unless the groups were formed by random assignment, and nothing fully protects against differential attrition. This is why the randomised control-group design is called a true experiment (section 20).

19.3 Regression to the mean, in depth

Sir Francis Galton, "Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature" (Journal of the Anthropological Institute, 1886). Galton compared the heights of 928 adult children with those of their parents (205 sets). Children of very tall parents were tall, but on average less extreme than their parents; children of very short parents were short, but less so. The children's deviation from the population mean was roughly two-thirds of the parents' deviation. He first called it "reversion" (in his earlier sweet-pea experiments) and then "regression towards mediocrity", and the word regression has stuck to the statistical technique ever since (section 13).

Regression to the mean is not a psychological process and not a biological force. It is a consequence of imperfect correlation. Every observed score contains some error (section 15.1: X = T + E). People who obtain extreme scores on one occasion are, on average, people whose true score is high and whose error that day happened to push them further out. On a second occasion the error is independent and averages zero, so the group's mean moves back toward the population mean, even though nobody's true score has changed. The less reliable the measure (the lower the test–retest correlation), the larger the regression.

Predicted retest score for a group selected on X:
predicted mean on retest = M + r × (mean of selected group on X − M),
where M is the population mean and r is the test–retest correlation (with equal SDs on both occasions). If r = 1 there is no regression; if r = 0 the selected group is expected to fall all the way back to M.

Worked example, computed

The figure below was simulated, not drawn by hand. One thousand people have a symptom score with mean 50 and SD 10; the scale's test–retest reliability is .60, so 60% of the variance is true score and 40% is error. Everyone is tested twice and nobody is treated. The clinic enrols the most severe 10% at the first testing (pretest above 62.8). Their pretest mean is 67.8. At retest, with no treatment, their mean is 60.2: a fall of 7.6 points, about three-quarters of a standard deviation. The formula predicts it: 50.1 + 0.60 × (67.8 − 50.1) = 60.7. Their average true score was 60.6 all along; the extra 7 points at pretest were error that did not repeat.

Had this clinic given those 100 patients eight weeks of a useless herbal remedy and run a one-group pretest–posttest study, it would have reported a 7.6-point "improvement" with a large effect size and a tiny p value. That is the danger. Regression to the mean contaminates any study that selects people because they are extreme, which in clinical work is nearly every study, since people seek treatment when their symptoms are at their worst.

  • Untreated improvement in clinical samples: part of the "improvement" in uncontrolled case series, and part of the placebo response in drug trials, is regression.
  • Matching across different populations: if a treatment group from a low-scoring population is matched on pretest with a control group from a higher-scoring population, each matched group regresses toward its own population mean on retest, manufacturing a spurious difference. Donald Campbell and Albert Erlebacher (1970) showed how this could make the American Head Start compensatory education programme look harmful.
  • Reward and punishment: Daniel Kahneman (Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011) recalled Israeli Air Force flight instructors who were convinced that praise after an excellent landing made the next one worse and criticism after a bad landing made the next one better. Both were regression: an exceptional landing is usually followed by a more ordinary one, whatever the instructor says.
How to control regression. Not by matching, and not by testing more people. The cure is a control group drawn from the same extreme pool and formed by random assignment: both groups regress equally, and only the difference between them reflects treatment. Other safeguards: use highly reliable measures; take two baseline measurements, selecting on the first and using the second as the pretest; and never interpret improvement in a group selected for extremity without a control.

19.4 Threats to external validity

Campbell and Stanley (1963) listed four factors that limit generalisation (they called them "factors jeopardising external validity or representativeness"):

  1. Reactive or interaction effect of testing (pretest sensitisation): the pretest may make participants more or less responsive to the treatment, so the result holds only for pretested people. A pretest questionnaire about stigma may sensitise participants to an anti-stigma film; unpretested audiences in the real world would not respond as strongly. The Solomon four-group design was built to detect exactly this.
  2. Interaction of selection and treatment: the treatment works only for the kind of people who happened to be sampled. A mindfulness programme tested on motivated, educated, urban volunteers may not work for rural patients with low literacy.
  3. Reactive effects of experimental arrangements: the experimental setting itself (being observed, the laboratory, knowing one is in a study) produces effects that will not occur outside it. The Hawthorne effect and demand characteristics (19.5) are the classic cases.
  4. Multiple-treatment interference: when the same participants receive several treatments, the effects of earlier ones persist and interfere with later ones, so the result applies only to people who received that sequence. This is the external-validity face of the carry-over problem in within-subject designs (19.7).

Cook and Campbell (1979) restated external validity threats as interactions of the treatment with selection, setting and history: the effect may hold only for these people, only in this kind of setting, or only at this point in time (a programme evaluated before smartphones may not work after them). Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002) generalised this to interactions of the causal relationship with units, treatment variations, outcomes and settings. The common remedies are random sampling from the target population (section 7.2), heterogeneous samples and settings, field replication and, ultimately, meta-analysis across many studies (section 25).

19.5 Reactivity and bias: participants and experimenters

People who know they are being studied do not behave like people who do not, and researchers who know what they expect do not observe like researchers who do not. Any influence that systematically distorts results is a bias. Behaviour changed by the act of measuring it is reactivity. Both threaten the construct and external validity of a study, and, when they differ between groups, its internal validity.

Participant effects

The Hawthorne effect. Between 1924 and 1932 the Western Electric Company's Hawthorne Works near Chicago studied worker productivity (later associated with Elton Mayo, and written up by Fritz Roethlisberger and William Dickson in Management and the Worker, 1939). In the illumination experiments output rose when lighting was increased, but also in the control group, and sometimes when the light was dimmed. The interpretation that output rose because the workers knew they were being studied was named the Hawthorne effect by Henry A. Landsberger (Hawthorne Revisited, 1958): participants change their behaviour because they know they are being observed, independent of the intervention. Reanalyses (Steven Levitt and John List, 2011) found the original data much weaker than the legend, but the term is established.

Martin T. Orne, "On the social psychology of the psychological experiment: with particular reference to demand characteristics and their implications" (American Psychologist, 1962). Demand characteristics are the totality of cues in an experimental situation (rumours, the instructions, the setting, the procedure, the experimenter's manner) that convey the hypothesis to participants and so influence their behaviour. Orne showed how powerful the role of "experimental subject" is: participants given page after page of random numbers to add, and told to tear up each completed sheet and continue, kept going for hours. Orne proposed quasi-controls to detect demand: a careful post-experimental inquiry, a pre-inquiry (asking people to imagine they were in the study and predict their behaviour) and simulators (participants asked to fake being hypnotised or treated, to see whether the "effect" can be produced by role-playing alone).
  • Good-subject effect: Orne's observation that most participants want to help science and the experimenter, so they try to work out the hypothesis and confirm it.
  • Evaluation apprehension: Milton J. Rosenberg (1965): participants are anxious to be judged favourably (as psychologically healthy, intelligent, normal) and behave so as to look good.
  • Stephen Weber and Thomas Cook (1972) classified participant roles as good, negativistic (deliberately working against the hypothesis, sometimes called the "screw-you" effect), faithful (scrupulously following instructions) and apprehensive.
  • Social desirability: the tendency to answer in the way that will be viewed favourably by others, a major bias in self-report (Allen L. Edwards, 1957; the Marlowe–Crowne Social Desirability Scale, Douglas Crowne and David Marlowe, 1960). Controlled by anonymity, forced-choice items matched for desirability, lie or validity scales, and indirect measures (section 23).
  • John Henry effect (19.2) and novelty effect: a new treatment, gadget or app produces improvement partly because it is new and exciting; the effect fades as the novelty wears off, so short trials overestimate benefit.

Placebo and nocebo

A placebo (Latin, "I shall please") is an inert treatment (sugar pill, sham procedure) given so that expectation is held constant between groups; the placebo effect is improvement produced by the expectation of treatment and the ritual of care. Henry K. Beecher's "The Powerful Placebo" (JAMA, 1955) pooled 15 studies and reported about 35% of patients satisfactorily relieved by placebo. Later analyses (Asbjørn Hróbjartsson and Peter Gøtzsche, 2001) showed much of that was natural recovery and regression to the mean, though placebo responses on subjective outcomes such as pain are real. The nocebo effect (Latin, "I shall harm"), named by Walter Kennedy in 1961, is the reverse: negative expectations produce symptoms, as when patients warned of headaches report more headaches on placebo.

Experimenter effects

Oskar Pfungst (1907) investigated Clever Hans, a Berlin horse owned by Wilhelm von Osten that apparently answered arithmetic questions by tapping its hoof. Pfungst showed that Hans answered correctly only when the questioner knew the answer and was visible: the horse was reading tiny, involuntary cues (a slight lift of the head or relaxation of posture when the correct number of taps was reached). Nobody was cheating; the cue was unconscious. Clever Hans is the founding example of the experimenter expectancy effect, and the reason for blind testing.

Robert Rosenthal made the experimenter expectancy effect a research programme. In Rosenthal and Kermit Fode (1963), students were each given rats to train in a maze; some were told their rats were specially bred "maze-bright", others "maze-dull". The rats were in fact randomly assigned from the same stock, yet the "bright" rats learned faster, presumably because of differences in how the students handled and observed them. In Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson's Pygmalion in the Classroom (1968), teachers at an elementary school were told that a test had identified certain children (actually chosen at random, about 20%) as "bloomers" who would show an intellectual spurt; after about eight months those children, especially in the first and second grades, had gained more IQ points than their classmates. This Pygmalion or Rosenthal effect is the self-fulfilling prophecy in the classroom. Later replications found the effect real but smaller and less consistent than the 1968 study suggested.

Keep the sources of expectancy apart. Demand characteristics (Orne): cues that make the participant guess and play to the hypothesis. Experimenter expectancy (Robert Rosenthal; Clever Hans): the experimenter's expectation leaks into the participant's behaviour or into the recording of it. Hawthorne effect: change because one is observed. Placebo effect: change because one expects to be treated. John Henry effect: the control group competes. The past-paper answer to "a double-blind study is used to minimise the impact of" is both experimenter bias and expectancy effects.

19.6 Techniques of control

Control means holding constant, or otherwise neutralising, the influence of extraneous variables so that only the IV differs between conditions (a past paper defined it as "the process of holding constant the possible influence" of extraneous variables). Fred N. Kerlinger, in Foundations of Behavioral Research (1964 and later editions), summed up the aim of design in the MAXMINCON principle: maximise systematic (experimental) variance, by making the levels of the IV as different as possible; minimise error variance, by reliable measurement and controlled conditions; and control extraneous systematic variance, by the techniques below. Ronald A. Fisher's The Design of Experiments (1935) gave the three classic principles of experimental design: randomisation, replication (more than one unit per condition, so error can be estimated) and local control (blocking similar units together).

Randomisation

Random assignment (randomisation) gives every participant an equal chance of being placed in any condition, typically by computer-generated random numbers. It is the most powerful control technique because it equalises groups, within the limits of chance, on every extraneous variable at once, known and unknown, measured and unmeasured: severity, motivation, genes, life events. It is the defining feature of a true experiment and the main protection against selection bias and confounding. With small samples chance imbalance remains possible, which is why trials use block and stratified randomisation and keep the sequence hidden from recruiters (allocation concealment, section 25).

Random selection and random assignment are different things. Random selection (random sampling, section 7.2) decides who gets into the study; it makes the sample representative and buys external validity. Random assignment decides which condition each participant receives; it makes the groups equivalent and buys internal validity. A study can have either without the other. Most clinical trials use a convenience sample of consenting patients (no random selection) but assign them randomly (strong internal validity, limited generality); a national survey uses random selection but assigns nobody to anything (representative, but no causal claim). Past papers: "randomisation is not possible in" purposive sampling (it refers to selection); "the principle that ensures every participant has an equal chance of being assigned to any group" is randomisation; "the main reason for randomly assigning subjects" is to make the groups as similar as possible so the only systematic difference is the treatment.

Matching

In matching, participants are paired on a variable known to affect the DV (baseline severity, IQ) and the members of each pair are placed in different conditions, ideally by random assignment within the pair (the matched-pairs approach, combining matching with randomisation). It reduces error variance and guarantees balance on the matched variable. Its problems: you can match only on variables you know about and can measure; matching on several at once soon becomes impossible and discards participants; without random assignment every unmatched variable can still differ; and matching groups from different populations creates regression artefacts (19.3).

Elimination and holding constant

An extraneous variable can be eliminated (a sound-proof room removes noise) or held constant (only right-handed participants, only first-episode patients, always 10 a.m., the same experimenter and instructions), so it cannot differ between conditions. The cost is external validity: the result strictly applies only to people and conditions like those.

Building it into the design, and statistical control

Instead of removing a variable, make it a factor: a 2 (treatment vs control) × 2 (male vs female) factorial design measures the effect of sex and its interaction with treatment instead of leaving it as noise (section 10.4). When the variable is a nuisance, this is blocking: participants are grouped into homogeneous blocks (mild, moderate, severe) and randomly assigned within each, so block-to-block variation leaves the error term (the randomised block design, Fisher's local control). A variable that cannot be controlled by design can be measured and removed statistically: ANCOVA (section 11.2) adjusts posttest means for a covariate such as pretest severity, and partial correlation (12.5) and multiple regression (13.3) remove a third variable's influence. Statistical control is weaker than randomisation: it adjusts only for what was measured, and only as well as it was measured.

Participants as their own controls

In a within-subjects (repeated-measures) design every participant experiences every condition, so stable individual differences drop out of the error term and power rises (sections 9.4 and 10.5). The price is order effects (19.7).

Blinding

  • Single-blind: the participants do not know which condition they are in. Controls participant expectancy, placebo responses and demand.
  • Double-blind: neither the participants nor the people administering the treatment and assessing the outcome know who is in which condition. Controls participant expectancy and experimenter bias.
  • Triple-blind: additionally, those analysing the data (and in trials the monitoring committee) do not know which coded group is which until the analysis is done.
  • In psychotherapy trials the therapist and patient cannot be blind to the therapy delivered, so the realistic standard is a blind outcome assessor (single-blind assessment).

Other procedural controls

  • Deception and cover stories: a plausible false account of the purpose keeps participants from guessing the hypothesis, reducing demand characteristics; ethically permissible only when necessary, low-risk and followed by debriefing (section 26).
  • Standardised instructions and procedures: every participant receives the same script, timing and setting, which reduces both error variance and experimenter influence.
  • Automation: presenting stimuli and recording responses by computer removes experimenter cues and recording errors.
  • Unobtrusive (non-reactive) measures, where ethical, to reduce reactivity.
  • Placebo controls hold expectation constant in drug trials. In psychotherapy research the equivalent is the attention-placebo (attention control) condition: participants receive the same amount of therapist contact and a credible rationale without the active ingredient, so that any advantage of the real therapy cannot be due to attention, warmth or expectancy alone. A wait-list control controls for time, history and maturation but not for attention or expectancy.
TechniqueWhat it controlsMain limitation
Random assignmentAll participant variables, known and unknown; selection biasCan fail by chance in small samples
MatchingThe matched variables onlyUnknown variables uncontrolled; loss of participants; regression artefacts
Elimination / holding constantThe variable held constantReduces generality
Blocking / factorial inclusionThe blocked variable, and its interaction with the IVNeeds more participants and cells
Statistical control (ANCOVA)Measured covariatesOnly what was measured; assumes homogeneous regression slopes
Within-subjects designAll stable individual differencesOrder and carry-over effects
CounterbalancingOrder (position) effectsFails with asymmetric carry-over
BlindingExpectancy, placebo, experimenter biasOften impossible for therapists and patients in psychotherapy
Placebo / attention controlExpectancy, attention, the ritual of treatmentHard to make a credible psychological placebo

19.7 Order effects and counterbalancing

When the same participants serve in several conditions, the order in which they meet the conditions can affect their scores. Section 10.5 introduced these briefly; here they are treated properly.

  • Practice effects: performance improves with repetition (familiarity with the task, warming up).
  • Fatigue effects: performance declines with time and repetition (tiredness, boredom).
  • Carry-over effects: the effect of one condition persists into the next (a drug still active, a strategy still in use, a mood still lingering).
  • Sensitisation: after experiencing several conditions, participants work out what is being varied and guess the hypothesis.

Practice and fatigue are position effects: they depend on where in the sequence a condition falls, whichever condition it is. Carry-over is a sequence effect: it depends on which condition came before. In psychophysics the same logic applies to primacy and recency effects and to the order of ascending and descending series, and the standard answer to "primacy and recency effects in a psychophysics experiment are controlled by" is counterbalancing.

The counterbalancing schemes

  • Complete counterbalancing: use every possible order, with equal numbers of participants in each. With n conditions there are n! orders: 2 conditions give 2, 3 give 6, 4 give 24, 5 give 120. Practical only for small n.
  • Partial (incomplete) counterbalancing: use a subset of orders chosen so that position effects still balance out.
  • Latin square: n orders, arranged so that each condition appears exactly once in each ordinal position (and once in each row). It balances position (practice and fatigue) but not sequence: in the simple cyclic square A is always immediately followed by B.
  • Balanced Latin square (Williams design, after E. J. Williams, 1949): additionally, each condition immediately precedes and follows every other condition exactly once, which balances first-order carry-over. For an even number of conditions n rows suffice; for an odd number two squares (2n rows) are needed.
  • ABBA (reverse) counterbalancing: each participant receives the conditions in one order and then in the reverse (A B B A), so that each condition has the same average position. It assumes practice effects are linear; if most practice happens early, ABBA fails.
  • Randomised orders: each participant receives an independently randomised order. Simple and effective with many participants or many trials; with few participants imbalance can remain.
Why counterbalancing works, and when it fails. Counterbalancing does not remove order effects; it spreads them equally across conditions, so they add the same amount to every condition mean and cancel in the comparison (they still inflate error variance, and order can be entered as a factor to measure it). That logic requires the order effect to be symmetric: doing A first must help B exactly as much as doing B first helps A. When carry-over is asymmetric (differential), counterbalancing fails, a problem E. C. Poulton and P. R. Freeman (1966) documented as "unwanted asymmetrical transfer". Examples: participants taught an imagery mnemonic in condition A will keep using it in the "rote rehearsal" condition B, but not the reverse; a drug with a long half-life contaminates the placebo period that follows it; insight, once gained, cannot be unlearned. The remedies are a washout period between conditions (standard in crossover drug trials) or abandoning the within-subjects design for a between-subjects design.
Recap of section 19: validity of a study (not of a test, section 15.3) has four types (Cook and Campbell, 1979; Shadish, Cook and Campbell, 2002): statistical conclusion, internal (Campbell's sine qua non), construct and external; internal and external trade off. External validity splits into population and ecological validity (Bracht and Glass, 1968); ecological validity is Brunswik's term stretched to mean real-world realism; Aronson and Carlsmith (1968) separated mundane from experimental realism. Campbell and Stanley's (1963) eight internal threats: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, statistical regression, selection, experimental mortality, selection–maturation interaction; Cook and Campbell added ambiguous temporal precedence, diffusion, compensatory equalisation, compensatory rivalry (John Henry) and resentful demoralisation, the last four moved to construct validity in 2002. A control group controls history, maturation, testing and instrumentation; only random assignment controls selection. Regression to the mean (Francis Galton, 1886): in our simulation (r = .60) the untreated top 10% fell from 67.8 to 60.2. External threats: pretest sensitisation, selection × treatment, reactive arrangements, multiple-treatment interference. Reactivity: Hawthorne (named by Landsberger, 1958), demand characteristics (Orne, 1962), evaluation apprehension (Rosenberg, 1965), placebo (Beecher, 1955), nocebo (Kennedy, 1961); expectancy: Clever Hans (Pfungst, 1907), Robert Rosenthal and Fode (1963), Pygmalion (1968). Control: MAXMINCON (Kerlinger); randomisation, replication, local control (Fisher, 1935); random assignment buys internal validity, random selection external; matching, holding constant, blocking, ANCOVA, own controls, blinding, placebo and attention controls. Counterbalance order effects: n! orders, Latin square, balanced Latin square (Williams, 1949), ABBA, random orders; asymmetric carry-over defeats them all.

20 Experimental and quasi-experimental designs

A research design is the plan that decides who is studied, what is done to them, when they are measured and what they are compared with. Section 19 listed the threats that can make a conclusion wrong; this section ranks the designs by how many of those threats each one rules out, from the true experiment (a causal claim), through the quasi-experiment (a cautious one), down to the pre-experimental designs (mostly none). Section 21 covers designs that manipulate nothing.

20.1 What makes an experiment

  1. Manipulation. The researcher deliberately changes the independent variable (IV): CBT for some patients and not others. A variable you merely measure (gender, diagnosis, childhood trauma) is not manipulated, and a study built on it is not an experiment however controlled it looks.
  2. Control. Everything except the IV is held constant or balanced: same assessor, instructions and timing, and a control group treated identically except that it does not receive the IV (the experimental group does).
  3. Random assignment. Every participant has an equal chance of landing in any condition, decided by a random process, not by the researcher, clinician or participant. It balances the groups on every variable at once, including ones nobody thought of, so any remaining difference is chance, which is exactly what the significance test (section 8) allows for.
Random assignment is not random sampling. Random sampling (section 7.2) decides who gets into the study and protects external validity. Random assignment decides which condition each person goes to and protects internal validity. Most clinical trials randomly assign a convenience sample: strong internal, limited external validity. A survey can have a perfect random sample and no assignment at all.
Ronald A. Fisher built the logic of the modern experiment at the Rothamsted agricultural station and set it out in The Design of Experiments (1935). His three principles are asked by name: randomisation, replication (several units per treatment, so that error can be estimated) and local control (grouping similar units into blocks to remove their differences from error). The randomised block, Latin square and factorial designs below are all his.

20.2 What a causal claim needs: three criteria, Mill's methods and MAXMINCON

Three conditions must hold before you can say X causes Y. They go back to John Stuart Mill's A System of Logic (1843) and are stated the same way in modern texts such as William R. Shadish, Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell (2002).

CriterionMeaningHow an experiment secures it
1. CovariationX and Y vary togetherThe groups differ significantly on the DV
2. Temporal precedenceThe cause comes before the effectX is applied first and Y measured afterwards, so the order is known by construction
3. Elimination of alternative explanations (non-spuriousness)No third variable or artefact could produce the covariationRandom assignment plus a control group removes the threats of section 19

A correlational study can meet the first, sometimes the second, rarely the third; that gap is why correlation does not imply causation (section 12.1).

Mill's methods of induction. Of Mill's five methods, two are the logic of all design. The method of agreement: if every case showing the effect shares only one circumstance, that circumstance is probably the cause (weak, because the shared factor may not be the only one). The method of difference: if a case with the effect and a case without it differ in only one circumstance, that circumstance is the cause. This is the logic of the experiment: experimental and control groups made identical except for X. The other three are the joint method of agreement and difference, the method of residues (subtract the effects of known causes; what remains belongs to the remaining cause) and the method of concomitant variation (Y changes in degree whenever X does), which is the logic of correlation.

Kerlinger's MAXMINCON. Fred N. Kerlinger, in Foundations of Behavioral Research (1964), reduced the purpose of design to the control of variance, in one acronym (Indian guides also write Max-Min-Con or Max-Kon-Min).

InstructionWhich varianceHow
MAXimiseSystematic (experimental) variance produced by the IV; Indian texts call it primary varianceMake the levels of the IV as different as possible (a full course of CBT, not one session); deliver it well
MINimiseError variance: individual differences and measurement errorReliable measures (section 15.2), standardised procedures, within-subjects or blocked designs
CONtrolExtraneous systematic variance from other variables; also called secondary varianceRandomisation, elimination (hold constant), matching, building the variable in as a factor or block, ANCOVA (section 11.2)
It is the F ratio in words. F = between-groups variance / within-groups variance (section 10.1). Maximising systematic variance enlarges the numerator, minimising error shrinks the denominator, and controlling extraneous variance stops a confound impersonating the treatment in the numerator. In the item "maximisation of ____, minimisation of ____, control of ____ variance", the answer is primary, error, secondary.

20.3 Reading and writing Campbell and Stanley's notation

Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley wrote "Experimental and quasi-experimental designs for research on teaching" as a chapter of N. L. Gage's Handbook of Research on Teaching (1963), reprinted as a book in 1966. They described 16 designs (3 pre-experimental, 3 true experimental, 10 quasi-experimental) and rated each against 8 threats to internal validity and 4 to external validity (section 19), using a compact notation.

X = exposure to the treatment; a blank where X would be = no treatment (different treatments: X₁, X₂).
O = an observation or measurement of the DV, numbered O₁, O₂ ...
R = random assignment, written at the start of each row.
Each row is one group; left to right is time; symbols in the same vertical column happen at the same time.
A dashed line between rows = groups not equated by randomisation (intact groups). Later authors write NR at the start of such rows, and C for assignment by a cut-off score.

"Thirty inpatients with schizophrenia are randomly split; both groups are rated on the PANSS; one receives eight weeks of social skills training; both are rated again" is written R O₁ X O₂ over R O₃ O₄, the pretest-posttest control group design. If ward A got the training and ward B did not, the R's disappear and a dashed line separates the rows. To place any design, ask in order: is there an R, is there a row without X, and is there an O before X?

20.4 Pre-experimental designs

Campbell and Stanley called these "pre-experimental" because they cannot rule out rival explanations. Examiners ask exactly which threats each one fails, and they are the designs most hospital audits and student projects use without realising it.

Design 1, the one-shot case study (X O). A group is treated, then measured once. A deaddiction centre runs a new relapse-prevention group and reports that craving scores at the end are "low". Low compared with what? With no pretest and no comparison group, there is no comparison at all. It fails history, maturation, selection and mortality; Campbell and Stanley said such studies have "such a total absence of control as to be of almost no scientific value", and that piling up careful detail on one group is the "error of misplaced precision"; the effort would be better spent on a comparison group.

Design 2, the one-group pretest-posttest design (O X O). Twenty patients with panic disorder score 31 on the Beck Anxiety Inventory, receive ten sessions of CBT, and score 18. The fall could be history (anything else that happened in between), maturation (spontaneous remission), testing (the pretest changed the posttest), instrumentation (a stricter rater or changed scale), or regression (marked "?": if patients were enrolled because they scored extremely high, they drift towards the mean anyway); the selection-maturation interaction is also uncontrolled. It does control selection and mortality, because the same people are compared with themselves.

Design 3, the static-group comparison (X O over a dashed line over O). Students at a college with a mindfulness programme are compared on stress with students at a college without one. Measuring both groups at the same time controls history, testing, instrumentation and regression (maturation "?"). The decisive weakness is selection: the colleges may have differed before the programme. Mortality and the selection-maturation interaction are also uncontrolled.

Where textbooks disagree. Campbell and Stanley (1963) call these three "pre-experimental". Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002) dropped the label and treat them as the weakest quasi-experiments ("designs without a control group", "without a pretest"). If the question names Campbell and Stanley or offers "pre-experimental", choose it.

20.5 True experimental designs

All three use random assignment and a control group, and Campbell and Stanley rate all three as controlling all eight internal threats. They differ in what they do about the pretest.

Design 4, the pretest-posttest control group design (R O X O over R O O), is the classic randomised controlled trial. History, maturation, testing, instrumentation and regression act equally on both groups and cancel in the comparison; randomisation removes selection; the pretest checks that randomisation worked, shows who dropped out, and adds precision when used as a covariate (ANCOVA, section 11.2). Its one weakness is external: the interaction of testing and X (pretest sensitisation), because the pretest may make people more responsive to the treatment.

The wrong statistic. Running a paired t test inside each group and concluding "the treatment group changed significantly and the control group did not" is the error Campbell and Stanley singled out. Compare the groups directly: ANCOVA on posttests, a t test on gain scores, or the group × time interaction in a mixed ANOVA (section 10.5).

Design 6, the posttest-only control group design (R X O over R O). Randomisation already makes the groups equivalent within the limits the significance test allows for, so the pretest is not essential; most of Fisher's agricultural experiments had none. Dropping it removes testing effects and pretest sensitisation and is necessary when a pretest is impossible or would reveal the purpose. The price: no check on initial equivalence, no covariate, no view of who dropped out, and larger groups are needed. Analysis: independent t (section 9.3) or one-way ANOVA.

Design 5: the Solomon four-group design

Richard L. Solomon proposed it in "An extension of control group design" (Psychological Bulletin, 1949). Campbell and Stanley wrote that it "deservedly has higher prestige" than design 4 and "represents the first explicit consideration of external validity factors". It is designs 4 and 6 run side by side, all four groups randomly assigned:

GroupPretestTreatmentPosttestRole
1O₁XO₂Experimental group of design 4
2O₃–O₄Control group of design 4
3–XO₅Experimental group of design 6
4––O₆Control group of design 6
What it controls: everything design 4 controls, plus pretest sensitisation (the reactive or interaction effect of testing, testing × X), which it not only avoids but measures, along with the main effect of testing. That is the answer to "the Solomon four-group design is used to control for ...".

The comparisons. The effect of X is replicated four ways: O₂ > O₁, O₂ > O₄, O₅ > O₆ and O₅ > O₃; if all agree, the inference is much stronger. O₄ vs O₆ isolates the effect of the pretest alone, and comparing O₆ with the pretest means O₁ and O₃ shows the combined effect of maturation and history.

The analysis. No single test uses all six sets of scores, because groups 3 and 4 have no pretest. Campbell and Stanley set the pretests aside and run a 2 × 2 factorial ANOVA on the four posttests: pretested (yes/no) × treated (yes/no) (section 10.4). Column means give the main effect of X, row means the main effect of pretesting, and the interaction is pretest sensitisation. If both pretest effects are negligible, an ANCOVA of O₂ vs O₄ with the pretest as covariate adds precision.

Worked example. Undergraduates are randomly assigned to four groups to test a 20-minute anti-stigma film; the DV is an attitude-to-mental-illness scale (higher = more accepting). Pretest means O₁ = O₃ = 58; posttest means O₂ = 72, O₄ = 60, O₅ = 66, O₆ = 59. Main effect of the film = (72 + 66)/2 − (60 + 59)/2 = 9.5. Main effect of pretesting = (72 + 60)/2 − (66 + 59)/2 = 3.5. The film's effect is 12 points in pretested students but 7 in unpretested ones, an interaction of 5: the stigma questionnaire primed students to take the message to heart. Testing alone (O₄ − O₆) = 1; maturation plus history (O₆ − 58) = 1. In the real world nobody fills in a questionnaire before the film, so expect about 7 points; design 4 alone would have reported 12.

Its cost: four groups instead of two, roughly double the participants ("more than double effort", said Campbell and Stanley), and an awkward analysis. It is worth it mainly when sensitisation is a real risk: attitude change, health education, prejudice reduction.

Campbell and Stanley's Table 1

+ = controlled, − = definite weakness, ? = possible concern, blank = not relevant. The last two columns are external validity threats.

DesignHist.Mat.Test.Instr.Regr.Sel.Mort.Sel. × Mat.Testing × XSelection × X
1 One-shot case study−−−−−
