Read it as rules. A control group measured at the same time controls history, testing and instrumentation. Random assignment controls selection and its interactions. A pretest creates the testing × X problem, escaped only by design 6 and the unpretested half of design 5. No design fully settles selection × X (generalising beyond the kind of people studied); that needs random sampling or replication.

20.6 Who gets what: between, within, mixed, matched and blocked designs

Between-subjectsWithin-subjects (repeated measures)Mixed (split-plot)
DefinitionEach participant experiences one conditionEach participant experiences every conditionAt least one between and one within factor
ExampleCBT vs waiting listReaction time under placebo, low and high doseGroup (CBT vs control) × time (pre, post, follow-up): the standard trial
ForNo order or carryover effects; the only option when a treatment cannot be undoneFewer participants; each person is their own control, so individual differences leave the error term and power risesA clean group comparison plus the power of repeated measures; the group × time interaction is the treatment effect
AgainstMore participants; individual differences inflate errorOrder effects (practice, fatigue, carryover, sensitisation), controlled by counterbalancing (section 19)Some problems of both; sphericity needed for the within factor
StatisticsIndependent t (9.3), ANOVA (10.2, 10.4)Paired t (9.4), repeated-measures ANOVA (10.5), Wilcoxon, Friedman (14.3)Mixed ANOVA (10.5)

"Split-plot" is Fisher's agricultural term: whole plots got one treatment (between) and each plot was split into subplots for a second (within).

Matched-groups design. Participants are paired on a variable strongly related to the DV (baseline severity, IQ), and one member of each pair is randomly assigned to each condition; the analysis treats the pair as the unit (paired t). Matching equates the groups on the matched variable and cuts error variance, but only on that variable. Matching intact groups without randomisation is dangerous: matched people are atypical of their own populations and regress towards different means on retest, producing a spurious effect. Matching supplements randomisation; it never replaces it.

Randomised block design (RBD). Fisher's local control made concrete: participants are grouped into blocks homogeneous on a nuisance variable (severity, hospital), and randomly assigned to all treatments within each block, so block differences are removed from error. With t treatments and b blocks, error df = (t − 1)(b − 1): four relaxation techniques across five severity blocks gives 3 × 4 = 12. A repeated-measures design is the case in which each person is a block.

Latin square as a design. A t × t arrangement that controls two nuisance variables at once (rows, for example participants; columns, for example order), with each treatment once in every row and column. Its main use is counterbalancing order (section 19); it reappears below as the counterbalanced quasi-experiment. Error df = (t − 1)(t − 2), so 6 for a 4 × 4 square. It assumes the treatments do not interact with the row and column variables.

20.7 Factorial and nested designs

A factorial design studies two or more IVs (factors) at once, every level of each combined with every level of the others: "more than one IV, levels combined in a systematic manner".

2 × 3 = two factors (count the numbers), with 2 and 3 levels (read the numbers), and 6 cells (multiply). 2 × 2 × 3 = three factors, 12 cells. With k factors there are 2k − 1 effects: two factors give 2 main effects + 1 interaction; three factors give 3 main + 3 two-way + 1 three-way = 7.

Therapy (CBT vs counselling) × medication (none, low, high) for depression is a 2 × 3 with six cells. A main effect is one factor's effect averaged over the other; an interaction means one factor's effect depends on the level of the other (CBT helps a lot without medication but adds little at high dose). The statistics are in section 10.4.

Why factorial designs are efficient. Every participant contributes to every main effect, so one study answers several questions; Fisher (1935) showed that a factorial experiment estimates several factors, and their interactions, with the same number of trials needed to estimate one factor alone to the same precision. Only a factorial design can reveal an interaction, often the clinically important finding. And testing one factor across levels of another shows how general its effect is. The cost: cells multiply fast, and three-way interactions are hard to read.

Nested designs. In a nested (hierarchical) design each level of one factor occurs within only one level of another, instead of being crossed with all. Therapists 1 to 3 deliver only CBT and therapists 4 to 6 only interpersonal therapy: therapists are nested within therapy. Pupils within classrooms and patients within wards are the everyday cases. You cannot test the interaction of the nested factor with the factor it sits in, and therapist differences are partly confounded with the therapy comparison, so the nested factor is modelled as a random factor (multilevel models). Campbell and Stanley make the same point about assigning whole classrooms: the classroom, not the pupil, becomes the unit of analysis.

20.8 Quasi-experimental designs

A quasi-experiment keeps manipulation (or a clearly timed intervention) and a comparison but lacks random assignment. Campbell and Stanley (1963) gave it its name; the standard extended work is Thomas D. Cook and Donald T. Campbell, Quasi-Experimentation: Design and Analysis Issues for Field Settings (1979), updated by Shadish, Cook and Campbell (2002). Randomisation is often impossible: patients are already on wards, a policy changes for a whole district, or withholding treatment would be unethical. The strategy is to add design features (pretests, comparison groups, many time points) until each specific rival explanation becomes implausible.

Nonequivalent control group design (design 10)

O X O over a dashed line over O O: two intact groups, both pretested and posttested, one treated. One ward of a government mental hospital introduces a token economy; a similar ward continues usual care; both are rated before and after six months. It is design 4 without the R, and the pretest makes it far better than the static-group comparison: you can see how unequal the groups were and analyse change. Main effects of history, maturation, testing and instrumentation are controlled; what remains are interactions with selection:

  • Selection-maturation: the groups were changing at different rates anyway (an acute ward improves faster than a chronic one).
  • Selection-history (local history): an event affected one group only (ward A got a new charge nurse).
  • Selection-instrumentation: the scale behaves differently in the two groups (a ceiling effect in the better ward).
  • Selection-regression: the treated group was chosen because it scored extremely, so it regresses towards the mean while the comparison does not.

Interrupted time-series design (design 7)

O O O O X O O O O: one unit measured many times before and after an intervention. The pre-intervention points show the series' level, trend and bounce, so the change at X is judged against what the series was already doing; that answers maturation, testing and regression. An effect can be a change in level (an immediate step), in slope (the trend bends), or both, analysed by segmented regression or ARIMA models. Donald T. Campbell and H. Laurence Ross's (1968) study of the Connecticut crackdown on speeding, introduced after a record year of road deaths in 1955, is the classic: the next year's fall looked like success, but the longer series showed how unstable yearly totals were and that a record year is usually followed by a lower one (regression to the mean).

What history looks like in a time series. History is the main remaining threat: another event at the same moment as X. If a new consultant took over the ward in week 25 of panel A, the step would look identical. Next is instrumentation: a new protocol often brings a new definition of an "incident" or a new form, producing a step with no change in behaviour. Seasonal cycles (examinations, festivals, monsoon admissions) can mimic or hide an effect in a short series.

Multiple (controlled) time series (design 14) adds a comparison series from a similar unit that did not receive X (the next ward, a neighbouring state, as Campbell and Ross used). If both series drop at week 25, history is the likely cause; if only the treated one drops, history becomes implausible. In a switching-replications variant, the comparison unit receives X later, so the effect must appear twice at two different times.

Regression discontinuity design (design 16)

Donald L. Thistlethwaite and Donald T. Campbell (1960) introduced it as "an alternative to the ex post facto experiment", asking whether public recognition in the National Merit Scholarship programme affected students' later plans and achievements. Recognition went to students above a cut-off on a qualifying score, so they would have done better anyway. Their solution: assign by a strict cut-off on a quantitative pre-measure, plot the outcome against that pre-measure, and look for a discontinuity (jump) in the regression line exactly at the cut-off. Notation: C O X O over C O O, where C = assignment by cut-off.

A District Mental Health Programme clinic screens adults with the PHQ-9 (0 to 27). Places are scarce, so the rule is strict: 15 or more is offered eight sessions of CBT, below 15 is not; everyone is reassessed at three months. Treated patients started more depressed and are still worse on average at follow-up, so the naive comparison says therapy did harm. But on each side, follow-up rises smoothly with intake score. Fit a line to each side: with no effect the two lines would meet at the cut-off as one line; if CBT works, the treated line drops there, and the drop is the effect.

Why it is the strongest quasi-experiment. The assignment rule is completely known, so it can be modelled exactly, which is what a nonequivalent group design lacks. Regression to the mean does not bias it, because both sides regress along the same line. Ethically it is attractive: treatment goes to those who need it most.
What breaks it. (1) The cut-off must be obeyed; clinicians nudging 14s up to 15 make it "fuzzy". (2) The shape of the relation must be right; a curve fitted with straight lines can fake a jump. (3) The estimate applies only near the cut-off. (4) It needs many more participants than a randomised trial for the same power.

Natural experiments and counterbalanced designs

In a natural experiment the "treatment" is assigned by nature, policy or accident in a way plausibly unrelated to the outcome. In the Dutch Hunger Winter of 1944–45 a blockade caused famine in the western Netherlands for a sharply bounded period; Ezra Susser and colleagues (1996) found that people conceived at its height had about twice the risk of schizophrenia. Nobody could ethically starve pregnant women, but history did, for a precisely dated window. Natural experiments remain quasi-experiments: they are only as good as the argument that exposure was "as if random".

In a counterbalanced (rotation) design (design 11), intact groups that cannot be randomised each receive every treatment, in orders arranged as a Latin square, so that differences among groups and among occasions are balanced out of the treatment comparison. Its weaknesses are carryover (multiple-treatment interference) and treatment-by-group interactions. Its single-group cousin, the equivalent time-samples design (design 8: X₁O X₀O X₁O X₀O), is the ancestor of the ABAB designs of section 22.

FamilyManipulationRandom assignmentComparisonCausal claim
Pre-experimentalYesNoNone, or an intact group without pretestNot defensible
Quasi-experimentalYes, or a timed interventionNoIntact groups, many time points, or a cut-offCautious: each rival ruled out by design
True experimentalYesYesRandomly formed control groupStrongest
Non-experimental (section 21)NoNoMeasured differences or correlationsAssociation only

20.9 Laboratory, field, analogue and simulation studies

Kerlinger distinguished laboratory experiments (IV manipulated in an artificial, controlled setting), field experiments (IV manipulated, ideally with random assignment, in the natural setting), field studies (nothing manipulated; measurement in the natural setting) and survey research (section 21).

Laboratory experimentField experiment
Control of extraneous variablesHighLower
Internal validityHigherLower
External (ecological) validityLower: artificial tasks and settingsHigher
Demand characteristicsHigh: people know they are studied (Martin T. Orne, 1962)Low
EthicsConsent straightforwardCovert manipulation raises consent problems (section 26)
ExampleStanley Milgram's (1963) obedience studies at YaleIrving Piliavin, Judith Rodin and Jane Piliavin (1969): a confederate collapsed in New York subway trains to see who helped

"The advantage of field experiments over laboratory experiments" is higher external validity; internal validity and ease of control are the laboratory's.

Kurt Lewin's field theory held that behaviour is a function of person and environment, B = f(P, E) (Principles of Topological Psychology, 1936), so behaviour stripped of its natural field may not be the same behaviour. With Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White (1939) he created autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire leadership climates in boys' clubs, an early field experiment, and in 1946 he coined action research.

Analogue studies investigate a clinical question under conditions that resemble but are not the real clinical situation: non-clinical or sub-clinical participants (students with high spider fear instead of patients with phobia), a standardised short treatment, a laboratory setting, or analogue measures such as role-plays. Peter J. Lang and A. David Lazovik's (1963) test of systematic desensitisation with snake-fearful students is the classic. Strengths: control, randomisation, easy recruitment, fewer ethical problems. Weakness: generalisation to real patients, who are more severe, comorbid and differently motivated. The exam answer to "analogue research involves" is research on healthy, non-clinical populations.

Simulation reproduces the essential features of a real situation artificially: Philip Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment (1971) simulated a prison, Orne's "simulators" faked hypnosis as a control for demand characteristics, simulated patients are used in interviewing research, and computer (Monte Carlo) simulation, as in this book's computed diagrams, shows how a method behaves when the truth is known. Simulation buys control and safety at the cost of realism.

Recap of section 20: an experiment needs manipulation, control and random assignment (Ronald A. Fisher's randomisation, replication and local control, 1935); a causal claim needs covariation, temporal precedence and elimination of alternatives (John Stuart Mill, 1843, whose method of difference is the experiment). Fred N. Kerlinger's MAXMINCON: maximise systematic (primary), minimise error, control extraneous (secondary) variance. Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley (1963): R, X, O, dashed line for nonequivalent groups; 16 designs (3 pre-experimental, 3 true, 10 quasi) against 8 internal and 4 external threats. One-shot case study (X O) is uninterpretable; one-group pretest-posttest (O X O) fails history, maturation, testing and instrumentation; static-group comparison fails selection and mortality. Pretest-posttest control group controls all internal threats but not pretest sensitisation; posttest-only control group avoids it; Richard L. Solomon's (1949) four-group design measures it through a 2 × 2 ANOVA on posttests (pretested × treated), at about double the cost. Within-subjects designs gain power but need counterbalancing; mixed (split-plot) designs are the standard trial; RBD error df = (t − 1)(b − 1), Latin square (t − 1)(t − 2). A 2 × 3 factorial has two factors and six cells and is the only way to see interactions; nested factors sit inside others. Quasi-experiments (Thomas D. Cook and Campbell, 1979) lack random assignment: nonequivalent control group (selection interactions remain), interrupted time series (history and instrumentation remain; a comparison series helps), regression discontinuity (Donald L. Thistlethwaite and Campbell, 1960; the jump at the cut-off is the effect), natural experiments and counterbalanced designs. Field experiments trade internal for external validity; analogue studies use non-clinical participants.

21 Non-experimental designs: correlational, developmental and epidemiological

In a non-experimental design the researcher manipulates nothing and assigns nobody. Variables are measured as they already exist, and the question is whether, how strongly and in what pattern they go together. Clinical psychology cannot do without these designs: age, sex, diagnosis, childhood trauma, poverty and brain injury cannot be assigned, and many things that could be assigned (neglect, substance use) must not be. Non-experimental designs describe, predict and generate hypotheses; they support a causal claim only through the slow accumulation of evidence described in 21.7.

21.1 Correlational designs

A correlational design measures two or more variables in the same people and quantifies how they covary, with r, regression or their relatives (sections 12 and 13). Sleep quality and depressive symptoms are measured in 300 college students; r = −.45. It can tell you that the variables are related, how strongly, in what direction and in what shape, and it allows prediction: knowing X improves your guess about Y. It cannot, on its own, tell you why, because of two problems (section 12.1).

  • The directionality problem (reverse causation): does poor sleep cause depression, or depression cause poor sleep? A single correlation is symmetrical and cannot say.
  • The third-variable problem (spurious correlation): a third variable may cause both. Heavy social media use and depression in adolescents may both be driven by loneliness or family conflict. Partial correlation (section 12.5) removes third variables you measured; it cannot remove the ones you did not.

The cross-lagged panel design

A partial answer to the directionality problem is to measure both variables on the same people at two (or more) times. Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley (1963) proposed the name "cross-lagged panel correlation", and Donald Pelz and Frank Andrews (1964) developed the same idea. Six correlations result: two synchronous (A and B at time 1; A and B at time 2), two stabilities or autocorrelations (A with itself, B with itself) and two cross-lagged correlations (A₁ with B₂, B₁ with A₂). The logic is temporal precedence: if A causes B, early A should predict later B better than early B predicts later A.

The classic application is Leonard D. Eron, L. Rowell Huesmann, Monroe M. Lefkowitz and Leopold O. Walder (1972), "Does television violence cause aggression?": in their Columbia County sample, boys' preference for violent television at about age 8 predicted their aggression ten years later better than early aggression predicted later viewing preference. The method has known weaknesses. David A. Kenny (1975) showed that unequal stabilities or changing reliabilities can by themselves make one cross-lag larger, and a third variable acting on both can still produce the pattern. Today panel data are analysed with cross-lagged panel models in structural equation modelling (section 13.6), which estimate each path while controlling for the stabilities.

21.2 Survey research

Fred N. Kerlinger's definition (Foundations of Behavioral Research, 1964) is the one examiners quote: survey research studies large and small populations by selecting and studying samples drawn from them, to discover the relative incidence, distribution and interrelations of sociological and psychological variables. Kerlinger classed surveys as non-experimental. So a survey can tell you how common something is (incidence, prevalence), how it is spread across groups (distribution) and what goes with what (interrelations), but not the causal factors of an event, which is the answer to "survey research does NOT ...". A census is a survey of the whole population; a sample survey studies a sample (section 7.2).

TypeWho is measured, and whenExampleMain problem
Cross-sectional surveyOne sample, one occasionA prevalence survey of exam anxiety in Class 12 studentsA snapshot: no change, no time order
Trend studyDifferent samples from the same population at several times (repeated cross-sections)The National Family Health Survey rounds (NFHS-1 to NFHS-5)Shows population change, not individual change
Cohort study (survey sense)Different samples from the same cohort (people born or entering in the same period) at several timesSamples of the 1990 birth cohort surveyed in 2010 and 2020Change within a generation, but not within individuals
Panel studyThe same individuals at every waveThe same 2,000 students surveyed every year of collegeAttrition and panel conditioning (being surveyed changes later answers)

Surveys are collected face-to-face, by telephone, by post, or online, each mode trading cost against response rate, coverage and social desirability; the design of questionnaires, interviews and scales is in section 23. Whatever the mode, the two big threats are coverage and non-response bias (the people who answer differ from those who do not) and self-report bias.

Placing a typical M.Phil or MA dissertation. A single online questionnaire (Google Forms, shared through WhatsApp and Instagram) given once to about 250 college students recruited by convenience and snowball sampling, measuring, say, social media use, loneliness and depressive symptoms, and analysed with Pearson correlations and a binary logistic regression predicting probable depression (PHQ-9 of 10 or more), is a cross-sectional correlational survey design: non-experimental, quantitative, one time point, non-probability sample. Say exactly that in a viva. Its honest limitations are the ones in this section: no temporal order and no causal inference (the odds ratios from the logistic regression, section 13.5, are adjusted associations, and "predict" means only statistical prediction); possible third variables; common-method variance because every measure is self-report on one occasion; and limited external validity because the sample is convenience-based and limited to people online.

21.3 Ex post facto (causal-comparative) research

Ex post facto means "from after the fact". Kerlinger defined it as systematic empirical inquiry in which the scientist does not have direct control of the independent variables, because their manifestations have already occurred or because they are inherently not manipulable; inferences about relations are made, without direct intervention, from the concomitant variation of independent and dependent variables. In practice the researcher starts from groups that already differ on the IV and compares them on the DV, which is why it is also called causal-comparative research. Adolescents who were bullied at school vs those who were not, compared on social anxiety; children of a parent with schizophrenia vs controls, compared on attention.

Why it is not an experiment, however carefully done. There is no manipulation and no random assignment. The decisive problem is self-selection: people end up in the groups for reasons of their own, and those reasons may themselves cause the DV. People who practise yoga daily and report less anxiety may have chosen yoga because they were calmer, healthier or wealthier to begin with. Matching and ANCOVA can equate the groups on measured variables only; the rest of the selection differences remain. Reverse causation is also open (social anxiety may attract bullying). Survey research is ex post facto in this sense, which is exactly why it cannot isolate causes.

21.4 Developmental designs

Developmental questions are about change with age. The difficulty is that age never travels alone. Every observation has an age, a cohort (the generation, defined by year of birth) and a time of measurement (the year of testing, carrying that period's history), and the three are locked together: age = time of measurement − year of birth. Fix any two and the third is fixed, so a simple design can never separate all three.

  • Cross-sectional design: different age groups tested at one time. Quick and cheap, no attrition or practice effects. But age differences are confounded with cohort differences: 70-year-olds and 30-year-olds tested in 2026 differ in schooling, nutrition and technology as well as in age, and it shows age differences, not age changes or individual trajectories. This is the answer to "a disadvantage of cross-sectional studies is ...".
  • Longitudinal design: one cohort tested repeatedly as it ages. It shows real age changes and individual differences in change, and the order of events. But age changes are confounded with time of measurement (a change between 2010 and 2020 might come from the era, not from ageing), and it suffers attrition (selective drop-out, usually of the less healthy), practice effects from repeated testing, ageing instruments, cost, and results that arrive after a career. It describes one cohort only.
  • Time-lag design: people of the same age tested at different times (18-year-olds in 2000, 2010 and 2020). Age is held constant; cohort and time of measurement are confounded. It answers questions like "are today's adolescents more anxious than earlier generations at the same age?"
K. Warner Schaie, "A general model for the study of developmental problems" (Psychological Bulletin, 1965), set out the age-cohort-time model and three sequential designs that combine simple ones so that two of the three factors can be separated (with an assumption about the third):
Cohort-sequential: two or more cohorts followed longitudinally over the same ages; separates age and cohort, assuming no time-of-measurement effect.
Time-sequential: the same age range tested cross-sectionally at two or more times; separates age and time of measurement, assuming no cohort effect.
Cross-sequential: two or more cohorts tested at the same times; separates cohort and time of measurement, assuming no age effect.
Schaie's own Seattle Longitudinal Study, begun in 1956 as his doctoral work and repeated at seven-year intervals with new cohorts added, is the model sequential study. Earlier, Richard Q. Bell (1953) had proposed "convergence", an accelerated longitudinal design in which several cohorts are followed for a short span and the overlapping segments are joined into one long curve, which is the cohort-sequential idea.
Terminology varies. Many developmental textbooks use "sequential", "cross-sequential" and "cohort-sequential" loosely for any design that follows several cohorts over time, and introductory MCQs often define "cross-sequential" as "combining cross-sectional and longitudinal approaches". If the options are only longitudinal, cross-sectional and cross-sequential, the combination answer is cross-sequential; if the question names K. Warner Schaie's three, use the definitions above. And "studying the same people repeatedly over time" is always plain longitudinal.

Famous longitudinal studies

StudyBeganWhoRemembered for
Genetic Studies of Genius (Lewis M. Terman)1921About 1,500 California schoolchildren (usually cited as 1,528) with Stanford–Binet IQs of roughly 135 to 140 and above, the "Termites"Gifted children were on average healthier, better adjusted and more successful than the stereotype of the fragile genius predicted; still followed after Terman's death in 1956. Exam keys add that adjustment problems clustered in children with IQs of about 180 and above in childhood, the group Leta S. Hollingworth described in Children Above 180 IQ (1942)
Grant Study, now part of the Harvard Study of Adult Development1938268 Harvard undergraduates, founded by Arlie V. Bock; later joined by the Glueck sample of inner-city Boston menGeorge E. Vaillant's work on adaptation and the maturity of defences (Adaptation to Life, 1977); warm relationships predicting healthy ageing
Seattle Longitudinal Study (K. Warner Schaie)1956Adults tested every seven years, with new cohorts addedThe cohort-sequential method; most intellectual abilities show little average decline before the 60s, and large cohort differences mean that cross-sectional studies exaggerate decline

Dunedin Multidisciplinary Health and Development Study (founded by Phil A. Silva)1972–731,037 babies born in Dunedin, New Zealand, between April 1972 and March 1973, with very low attritionAvshalom Caspi and Terrie E. Moffitt's gene-environment interaction findings, such as the serotonin transporter gene, life stress and depression (2003)

A shorter classic is H. Rudolph Schaffer and Peggy Emerson's (1964) study of 60 Glasgow infants followed through the first 18 months, which gave the stages of attachment.

Microgenetic design. Robert S. Siegler and Kevin Crowley (1991) described the microgenetic method for watching change as it happens: observe children through a period of rapid change, with a high density of observations relative to the rate of change (often trial by trial over days or weeks), and analyse each response intensively. It shows how a new strategy is discovered and spreads, which widely spaced longitudinal tests miss.

21.5 Epidemiological designs

Epidemiology studies the distribution and determinants of disorders in populations. Its designs are the same logic in a medical vocabulary: the IV is called the exposure and the DV the outcome.

Prevalence and incidence

MeasureDefinitionExample
Point prevalenceExisting cases at one point in time ÷ population at that timeProportion of adults with a current depressive episode on the survey day
Period prevalencePeople who were cases at any time during a period (e.g. the past 12 months) ÷ population12-month prevalence of alcohol use disorder
Lifetime prevalencePeople who have ever been cases, including recovered ones ÷ populationHas ever met criteria for panic disorder
Incidence (cumulative incidence, risk)New cases during a period ÷ people at risk (free of the disorder) at the startNew cases of postpartum depression within a year of delivery
Incidence rate (incidence density)New cases ÷ total person-time at risk12 new cases per 1,000 person-years
Prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration (for a fairly rare, stable condition). Schizophrenia has a low incidence but lasts long, so its prevalence is high relative to incidence; a brief adjustment disorder can have high incidence and low point prevalence. Incidence is what you need for causes (who becomes ill); prevalence is what you need for service planning (how many are ill now). India's National Mental Health Survey 2015–16 (NIMHANS), a cross-sectional prevalence study of adults in 12 states, reported a lifetime prevalence of any mental morbidity of 13.7% and a current prevalence of 10.6% (excluding tobacco use disorder).

The four core designs

A cross-sectional (prevalence) study measures exposure and outcome in a population sample at the same time. It gives prevalence and associations quickly, but cannot show which came first, and it over-represents long-lasting cases (people who recover or die quickly are less likely to be caught on survey day).

A cohort study starts with people who are free of the outcome, classifies them by exposure, and follows them to see who develops the outcome. It gives incidence directly and so the relative risk, establishes temporal order, and can study several outcomes of one exposure. In a prospective cohort the researcher starts now and follows people into the future (the Framingham Heart Study, from 1948; Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's British Doctors Study of smoking, from 1951). In a retrospective (historical) cohort both exposure and outcome have already happened, but the analysis still runs forward, from exposure recorded in old files to outcome recorded later: school records from 2005 that noted bullying, linked to clinic records in 2025. Cohort studies are slow and expensive, need very large samples for rare outcomes, and lose people to attrition.

A case-control study runs the other way. It starts from the outcome: cases who have the disorder and controls who do not, as similar as possible otherwise (often matched on age and sex). It then looks back for differences in past exposure. Doll and Hill's 1950 comparison of lung cancer patients with controls, which found far more smokers among the cases, is the landmark. It is fast, cheap and the most efficient design for rare disorders (autism, early-onset psychosis, suicide), since you begin with the few cases instead of waiting for them, and it can examine many exposures at once. Its weaknesses: it cannot give incidence or relative risk, only the odds ratio; choosing proper controls is hard (hospital controls bring Berkson's bias, Joseph Berkson, 1946); and it is vulnerable to recall bias: mothers of children with a developmental disorder search their memories of pregnancy far harder than mothers of typical children.

A nested case-control study is carried out inside an existing cohort: every case that arises is compared with a sample of cohort members who were still free of the outcome at that time. Exposure data (stored blood, early questionnaires) were collected before the outcome, which removes recall bias, and only a fraction of the stored material has to be analysed.

Retrospective is not the same as case-control. A retrospective cohort uses past data but reasons from exposure to outcome; a case-control study reasons from outcome to exposure. The question "the British Doctors were questioned about smoking in 1951 and followed for decades: what design?" is a prospective cohort (observational, not experimental). "Rare outcome plus past exposure" signals case-control.

Ecological studies and the ecological fallacy

An ecological study uses groups (districts, states, countries) as the units: suicide rates against unemployment rates across Indian states, for example, using National Crime Records Bureau data. The ecological fallacy is drawing conclusions about individuals from a correlation between group averages. William S. Robinson (1950) gave the classic demonstration with 1930 US census data: across the 48 states, the percentage of foreign-born residents correlated +.53 with the literacy rate, yet at the individual level being foreign-born correlated −.11 with literacy. Immigrants had settled in states whose native-born populations were highly literate. A state-level correlation, even a strong one, says nothing certain about the people inside the states. (The reverse error, generalising from individuals to groups, is the atomistic fallacy.)

21.6 Measuring association: relative risk, odds ratio and attributable risk

Arrange any exposure-outcome study as a 2 × 2 table with cells a (exposed, ill), b (exposed, well), c (unexposed, ill), d (unexposed, well).

  • Risk in a group = ill ÷ everyone in that group: a/(a+b) for exposed, c/(c+d) for unexposed.
  • Relative risk (risk ratio), RR = risk in exposed ÷ risk in unexposed. Needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies and trials.
  • Odds = ill ÷ well within a group: a/b and c/d. Odds ratio, OR = (a/b)/(c/d) = ad/bc. The only measure available from a case-control study, and the one logistic regression produces (section 13.5).
  • Reading them: RR or OR = 1 means no association; above 1, the exposure is associated with more of the outcome (a risk factor); below 1, with less (protective). A 95% confidence interval that includes 1 means the association is not significant.
  • Risk difference (attributable risk) = risk in exposed − risk in unexposed: the excess cases due to the exposure, on an absolute scale. Attributable risk percent in the exposed = risk difference ÷ risk in exposed. Population attributable risk percent = (overall risk − risk in unexposed) ÷ overall risk: the share of all cases in the population that would disappear if the exposure did.

Worked example. A cohort of 1,000 adults whose childhood records noted trauma (200 exposed) or not (800 unexposed) is assessed for depression. 60 of the 200 exposed and 80 of the 800 unexposed are depressed.

  1. Risk in exposed = 60/200 = 0.30; risk in unexposed = 80/800 = 0.10. RR = 0.30/0.10 = 3.0: those exposed to childhood trauma were three times as likely to be depressed.
  2. Odds in exposed = 60/140 = 0.429; odds in unexposed = 80/720 = 0.111. OR = (60 × 720)/(140 × 80) = 43,200/11,200 = 3.86.
  3. Risk difference = 0.30 − 0.10 = 0.20: 20 extra cases per 100 exposed people (number needed to harm = 1/0.20 = 5). Attributable risk percent in the exposed = 0.20/0.30 = 67%: two-thirds of the depression among the exposed is attributable to the exposure, if the association is causal.
  4. Overall risk = 140/1,000 = 0.14, so PAR% = (0.14 − 0.10)/0.14 = 29%.
Why the OR is bigger than the RR here, and why case-control studies use it. The OR exaggerates the RR whenever the outcome is common; when the outcome is rare (roughly under 10% in both groups), b ≈ a + b and d ≈ c + d, so OR ≈ RR. That is the rare disease assumption, and it is why case-control studies of rare disorders report ORs as estimates of relative risk. The OR survives case-control sampling because it is symmetrical: the odds of exposure among cases divided by the odds of exposure among controls equals the odds of illness among the exposed divided by the odds among the unexposed, so sampling all cases and only some controls leaves it unchanged (3.86 in the figure), whereas any "risk" from that table depends on how many controls the researcher decided to take.

From association to causation: the Bradford Hill criteria

Austin Bradford Hill, in "The environment and disease: association or causation?" (1965), listed nine "viewpoints" for judging whether an observed association is causal. He insisted they were aids to judgement, not a checklist, and that none except temporality is indispensable.

ViewpointQuestionApplied to childhood trauma and adult depression
StrengthIs the association large?RR = 3 is stronger than most confounders could produce
ConsistencyIs it repeated in different places, samples and designs?Found in cohort and case-control studies across countries
SpecificityDoes the exposure lead to one particular outcome?Weak here: trauma predicts many disorders (Hill himself said this one is often absent)
TemporalityDoes the exposure come first?The trauma was recorded in childhood: the only essential criterion
Biological gradientIs there a dose-response relation?More types or longer duration of trauma, higher risk
PlausibilityIs there a plausible mechanism?Stress-system (HPA axis) sensitisation, negative schemas
CoherenceDoes it fit what else is known?Consistent with stress-diathesis models
ExperimentDoes removing or reducing the exposure reduce the outcome?Prevention and early-intervention evidence
AnalogyDo similar exposures have similar effects?Early adversity in animal studies

21.7 Descriptive designs: observation, case study and archival research

Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its natural setting without intervening: children's play in an anganwadi, interaction on a psychiatric ward. It gives high ecological validity and is often the first step in a new area, but it is open to reactivity (people behave differently when watched) and observer bias, and it cannot explain what it records. Sampling, coding and observer reliability are covered in section 23.

A case study is an intensive, usually long-term study of one person, family, group or institution, using interviews, observation, tests and records. It is idiographic (aimed at understanding the particular), in the sense Wilhelm Windelband (1894) distinguished from the nomothetic search for general laws, a distinction Gordon W. Allport (1937) brought into psychology. It is the right design for rare phenomena, for generating hypotheses, for disconfirming a universal claim with one counter-example, and for illustrating a treatment. Its limits: no control, no generalisation to others, and heavy reliance on the investigator's interpretation and on retrospective reports. (Small-N designs that add experimental control to the single case are section 22.)

CaseWho reported itWhat it is remembered for
Anna O. (Bertha Pappenheim)Josef Breuer, treating her in 1880–82; published in Studies on Hysteria (Breuer and Sigmund Freud, 1895)Hysterical symptoms relieved by talking about their origins; she called it the "talking cure"; the root of the cathartic method
Little Hans (Herbert Graf)Sigmund Freud (1909), "Analysis of a phobia in a five-year-old boy"A horse phobia interpreted as Oedipal anxiety; conducted almost entirely through the boy's father; the first child analysis
Phineas GageJohn Martyn Harlow (1848 and 1868)On 13 September 1848 a tamping iron passed through his left frontal lobe; he survived but his personality changed ("no longer Gage"); frontal lobes and personality
H.M. (Henry Molaison)William Beecher Scoville and Brenda Milner (1957)Bilateral medial temporal lobe removal for epilepsy in 1953 left profound anterograde amnesia with intact procedural learning (mirror tracing); the hippocampus and memory
GenieFound in Los Angeles in 1970 aged 13 after extreme isolation; studied by Susan Curtiss and othersLearned vocabulary but never full grammar: evidence for a critical period for language, and a lasting ethics lesson

Archival research analyses records that already exist and were collected for another purpose: hospital case files, census data, National Crime Records Bureau suicide statistics, court records, letters and diaries. Émile Durkheim's Suicide (1897), built from official suicide statistics, is the founding example. It is unobtrusive (no reactivity), cheap, can cover long periods and large populations, and can reach the past. But the researcher cannot control what was recorded or how carefully, definitions change over time, and missing data are common. Systematically coding the content of texts, media or interviews is content analysis (section 24).

Recap of section 21: non-experimental designs measure without manipulating. Correlational designs show covariation and allow prediction but face the directionality and third-variable problems; the cross-lagged panel design (named by Donald T. Campbell and Julian C. Stanley, 1963; used by Leonard D. Eron and colleagues, 1972) compares A₁→B₂ with B₁→A₂. Survey research (Fred N. Kerlinger) studies the incidence, distribution and interrelations of variables, not causes; trend studies resample a population, cohort studies a generation, panel studies the same people. Ex post facto (causal-comparative) research compares pre-existing groups and is undone by self-selection. A single online questionnaire analysed with correlation and logistic regression is a cross-sectional correlational survey design. Developmental designs juggle age = time of measurement − cohort: cross-sectional confounds age with cohort, longitudinal confounds age with time of measurement (plus attrition and practice), time-lag confounds cohort with time; K. Warner Schaie's (1965) cohort-sequential, time-sequential and cross-sequential designs separate two factors at a time. Remember Lewis Terman (1921), the Grant Study (1938), Seattle (1956), the NYLS (1956) and Dunedin (1972–73), and Robert S. Siegler's microgenetic method. Epidemiology: point, period and lifetime prevalence vs incidence (prevalence ≈ incidence × duration); cohort studies (prospective or retrospective) give incidence and RR; case-control studies start from the outcome, suit rare disorders, give only the OR and suffer recall bias; nested case-control sits inside a cohort. In the worked table RR = 3.0, OR = 3.86, risk difference = 0.20, AR% = 67%, PAR% = 29%; OR approximates RR only for rare outcomes; OR or RR = 1 means no association. William S. Robinson (1950) showed the ecological fallacy; Austin Bradford Hill (1965) gave nine viewpoints for causation, of which only temporality is essential. Descriptive designs are naturalistic observation, the case study (Anna O., Little Hans, Phineas Gage, H.M., Genie) and archival research.

22 Single-subject (small-N) designs

Every design in sections 20 and 21 answers its question by comparing groups: the average of the treated group against the average of the control group. That works when you want to know what happens on average to people like these. It works badly when the question is about this child, this client, this behaviour, which is the question an ABA therapist, a special educator or a rehab counsellor faces every morning. A group mean can improve while half the individuals in the group get worse; a treatment that helps the "average autistic child" may describe no real child at all. Single-subject designs (also called single-case, single-system, N = 1, intrasubject or small-N designs) answer the causal question inside one individual, by measuring that person again and again and switching the treatment on and off in a planned way. They are true experiments: the independent variable is manipulated, the dependent variable is measured repeatedly, and the rival explanations are ruled out by the pattern of the data rather than by a control group.

22.1 Why single-case research exists

Section 18 introduced the two aims a science of persons can have. The nomothetic aim looks for general laws that hold across people (most of experimental psychology); the idiographic aim tries to understand the particular individual in depth. The terms come from the philosopher Wilhelm Windelband (1894) and were brought into personality psychology by Gordon Allport (1937). Single-case designs are a bridge between the two: they study one person intensively (idiographic in method) but in order to establish lawful cause-and-effect relationships that can then be replicated across people (nomothetic in aim).

Psychology actually began with single subjects: Hermann Ebbinghaus (1885) studied memory with himself as the only participant, and Ivan Pavlov's conditioning work used a handful of dogs studied for years. Group comparison with significance testing became dominant only after Ronald A. Fisher's statistics (The Design of Experiments, 1935) reached psychology in the 1930s and 1940s (section 20).

Who built the method. B. F. Skinner (Burrhus Frederic Skinner) studied the moment-to-moment behaviour of individual rats and pigeons in The Behavior of Organisms (1938), recording each animal's responding continuously on a cumulative recorder and showing control by turning contingencies on and off. His approach is the experimental analysis of behaviour, with its own journal, the Journal of the Experimental Analysis of Behavior (1958). Murray Sidman's Tactics of Scientific Research (1960) is the methodological bible: it argued that reliability and generality are shown by replication, not by significance tests, and defined direct and systematic replication. Michel Hersen and David H. Barlow, Single Case Experimental Designs: Strategies for Studying Behavior Change (1976), carried the logic into clinical psychology and psychiatry (third edition, 2009, with Matthew Nock). Alan E. Kazdin, Single-Case Research Designs: Methods for Clinical and Applied Settings (1982), is the other standard text, and Kazdin also wrote the classic papers on social validation (section 22.9).

Applied behaviour analysis and its seven dimensions

When these methods moved from the laboratory to classrooms, hospitals and homes, the field became applied behaviour analysis (ABA), launched with the Journal of Applied Behavior Analysis in 1968. In its first volume Donald M. Baer, Montrose M. Wolf and Todd R. Risley (1968) defined ABA by seven dimensions, still memorised by every behaviour analyst: applied (the behaviour matters to the person and society), behavioural (it is observable behaviour that is measured, not a report of it), analytic (the researcher demonstrates experimental control, which is exactly what the designs in this section do), technological (procedures are described so completely that someone else could replicate them), conceptually systematic (procedures are tied to basic principles such as reinforcement), effective (the change is large enough to matter practically) and generality (the change lasts over time, appears in other settings, or spreads to other behaviours). The same paper described the two core demonstrations of control: the reversal and the multiple baseline.

Case study is not a single-case experiment. A case study (section 21) is an uncontrolled, usually narrative and often retrospective account of one person: Freud's Little Hans, Breuer's Anna O., the amnesic patient H.M. It can generate hypotheses but cannot establish causation, because nothing is manipulated and there is no baseline against which change can be judged. A single-case experimental design has one participant but all the machinery of an experiment: an operationally defined target behaviour, repeated objective measurement, a stable baseline, deliberate manipulation of the independent variable in planned phases, and a demonstration that behaviour changes when, and only when, the treatment changes. "N = 1" describes the sample size, not the level of control. Kazdin also showed that a case study strengthened with objective, repeated measurement and several cases sits between the two: better than an anecdote, still short of an experiment.

22.2 The logic: repeated measurement, baseline, prediction, verification, replication

A group experiment rules out history, maturation and the other threats of section 19 by having a control group experience them too. A single-case design has no control group, so the participant serves as their own control across time. That only works if the behaviour is measured repeatedly (every session, every day) under consistent conditions, so that you can see its natural level, trend and variability before anything is changed.

  1. Baseline (phase A). The target behaviour is measured under ordinary conditions, before treatment, until it is stable: no strong trend and variability small enough that an effect would be visible. The baseline has a descriptive function (how bad is the problem now) and, more importantly, a predictive function: it tells you what the behaviour would probably have looked like in future if nothing were done.
  2. Prediction. Extend the baseline line forward in your mind. That projected path is the counterfactual, the single-case equivalent of a control group.
  3. Affirmation of the consequent. Introduce the treatment (phase B). If behaviour departs from the predicted path, the treatment may be responsible, but so might a coincidental event (history) or growth (maturation). An AB comparison alone stops here.
  4. Verification. Show that the baseline prediction was correct: withdraw the treatment and see behaviour return towards the baseline level (ABA), or show that untreated baselines continue on their predicted path while another tier is treated (multiple baseline).
  5. Replication. Reintroduce the treatment and see the effect again (ABAB), or reproduce it in a second and third tier, participant or setting. Each replication makes coincidence less believable.
Baseline logic (prediction, verification, replication) is the standard name for this reasoning in the applied behaviour analysis text of John Cooper, Timothy Heron and William Heward (1987; later editions). Causal inference in single-case research rests on repeated demonstrations of an effect at different points in time. The single-case standards written for the US What Works Clearinghouse by Thomas Kratochwill and colleagues (2010) require at least three demonstrations of the effect at three different points in time, and phases of at least three data points (five to meet the standard without reservation).

How long a baseline, and what if it is trending?

A single baseline point tells you nothing about trend or variability; two points define a line but cannot show whether it is a fluke. Three data points is the conventional minimum because it is the smallest number that can reveal a trend and a sense of variability, and more is better when the data bounce. The rule is "stability, not a fixed number": keep measuring until the pattern is predictable.

  • Baseline trending in the therapeutic direction (the child's tantrums are already falling): do not start treatment yet. Any later improvement would be indistinguishable from the existing trend. Extend the baseline until it levels, look for what is causing the improvement, or choose a design and analysis that model the trend.
  • Baseline trending in the counter-therapeutic direction (getting worse): you may introduce treatment, and a reversal of the trend is actually a stronger demonstration of effect.
  • Highly variable baseline: extend it, tighten the operational definition and observation conditions, or look for the variable driving the variation (it is often the functional variable you need).
  • Dangerous behaviour (severe self-injury, head-banging, suicide risk): ethics overrides methodology. A short baseline, or none (see the B-A-B design), is acceptable.

22.3 The A-B family: AB, ABA, ABAB, BAB and ABCB

The letters are a notation. A always means baseline (no treatment). B means the first treatment, C a second, different treatment, and BC written together means B and C given at the same time. A1 and A2 number repeated phases.

AB design

Baseline, then treatment. It is the minimum structure and what most clinicians informally do: measure the problem for a week, then start therapy. Its weakness is that there is only one phase change, so only one demonstration of effect. If a 9-year-old's tantrums fall after a token system starts, you cannot tell whether the tokens did it or whether the child's mother returned from hospital that same week (history), the child grew out of it (maturation), or the extreme first week drifted back (regression to the mean). AB is a quasi-experimental design, the single-case analogue of the one-group pretest–posttest design, and Kratochwill's standards do not accept it as evidence of a causal effect. It is still useful as a clinical evaluation tool and when replicated across several clients.

ABA (withdrawal) design

Add a second baseline: treatment is withdrawn and behaviour should return towards its baseline level. Two phase changes now both point the same way, which makes a coincidental external event much less plausible. Its clinical defect is obvious: the study ends in the baseline phase, leaving the client without the treatment that worked.

ABAB (reversal or withdrawal) design

Baseline, treatment, withdrawal, treatment reinstated. This is the strongest single demonstration of experimental control in the single-case family: three phase changes, so three opportunities for the behaviour to change in the predicted direction, satisfying the three-demonstration standard by itself, and it ends with the client on treatment. R. Vance Hall, Diane Lund and Deloris Jackson (1968), in the first article of the first issue of JABA, used reversal designs to show that teacher attention controlled pupils' study behaviour in ordinary classrooms. The figure below shows the same logic with a child with ADHD whose out-of-seat behaviour is treated with a token-and-praise system.

Baseline (A1) is stable around 15.0 episodes per class (range 13 to 17). With tokens and praise (B1) the mean falls to 6.1; on withdrawal (A2) it climbs back to 11.8; on reinstatement (B2) it falls again, faster, to 3.6. Note the graphing conventions: vertical dashed phase-change lines, data points never joined across a phase line, each phase labelled, behaviour on the y axis and sessions on the x axis.

The problems with withdrawal. (1) Ethics. Deliberately removing an effective treatment, especially for dangerous behaviour such as self-injury or aggression, may be unacceptable to parents, staff and ethics committees, and an ABA design that stops in A is worse still. Keep the withdrawal phase brief and end on treatment. (2) Irreversible behaviour. Many targets will not, and should not, return to baseline: once a child has learned to read, to use a picture-exchange card or to tie shoelaces, withdrawing the teaching does not erase the skill, and social behaviours become maintained by the natural reinforcers of peers (a "behavioural trap"). If behaviour does not reverse, the design cannot demonstrate control. (3) Sequence and carryover effects: the second B phase is not a fresh first exposure. For irreversible or dangerous targets use a multiple-baseline or changing-criterion design instead.
Withdrawal versus reversal, strictly. In a true reversal design the second A phase does not just remove the treatment; it reverses the contingency (for example, attention is now given for being out of seat instead of in seat). A withdrawal design simply removes the treatment. Most textbooks and most exam papers use "reversal design" loosely for any ABAB, so accept either name unless the question insists on the distinction.

BAB design

Treatment, withdrawal, treatment. It is used when the behaviour is too serious to leave untreated while a baseline is collected, or when a client arrives already on treatment. It ends on treatment and has two phase changes, but it has no initial baseline, so the natural level of the problem before any intervention is never known.

ABCB and A-B-A-C: comparing treatments or isolating the active ingredient

In an ABCB design the C phase replaces B with a control condition that keeps everything except the hypothesised active ingredient. The classic use: B is attention contingent on appropriate behaviour; C is the same amount of attention given non-contingently (on a timer, regardless of behaviour). If behaviour worsens in C and improves again in B, it was the contingency, not the attention itself, that mattered. This avoids a full return to baseline. A-B-A-C (often extended to A-B-A-C-A) compares two different treatments, each against a baseline. The weakness is multiple-treatment interference: C always follows B, so its effect may be coloured by the earlier treatment (an order effect that cannot be counterbalanced within one person, although it can be counterbalanced across participants, A-B-A-C for one and A-C-A-B for another).

22.4 Multiple-baseline designs

The multiple-baseline design solves the withdrawal problem: it never removes an effective treatment. Instead of verifying the baseline prediction by withdrawal, it verifies it with other baselines that are still running. Baselines are recorded simultaneously on three or more "tiers", and the treatment is introduced to one tier at a time, at staggered points. If each tier changes only when, and not before, the treatment reaches it, coincidence becomes implausible: an outside event (a new teacher, a festival holiday, a medication change) would have hit all tiers at the same calendar time.

  • Across behaviours: one person, several different behaviours (a child's hand-raising, completing worksheets and staying in seat), treated one after another.
  • Across settings: one person, one behaviour, several settings (tantrums at home, in class, in the therapy room), treatment extended to one setting at a time.
  • Across participants (subjects): one behaviour, several people with the same problem, treatment started for each person at a different time. The most common form, and the one drawn below.

Aarav's requests rise from a baseline mean of 1.2 to 8.2 once teaching starts at session 6. On those same days Meera and Kabir, still in baseline, show no change; that is the verification. Meera's requests then rise from session 10 (1.8 to 8.1) and Kabir's from session 14 (0.8 to 6.4): two replications. Three tiers give the three demonstrations the standards ask for.

The two assumptions of a multiple baseline. (1) Independence of baselines: treating one tier must not change the others. If teaching Aarav to request also changes Meera because they share a classroom and she imitates him, or if reducing a child's hitting also reduces kicking (response generalisation), the untreated baselines move early and the design loses its control. (2) Functional similarity: yet the tiers must be similar enough that the same treatment would be expected to work on each. The design walks a line between these. When a baseline changes before its treatment begins, the evidence for that tier is lost.

The concurrent multiple baseline (the original form described by Baer, Wolf and Risley) records all tiers over the same calendar period, which is what lets it rule out history. In a non-concurrent multiple baseline, described by P. J. Watson and E. A. Workman (1981), participants are studied at different times (one client in January, the next in March) and each is randomly assigned a baseline length in advance. It is far more practical in clinics where clients arrive one at a time, but because the tiers do not share calendar time it is weaker against history. A variant for skills that cannot be measured every day without teaching them, the multiple-probe design (Robert Horner and Donald Baer, 1978), replaces continuous baseline measurement with occasional probes. Weaknesses of all multiple baselines: some tiers wait a long time untreated, you need three or more comparable behaviours, settings or people, and the effect is shown only by its timing, not by its removal.

22.5 Changing-criterion design

Some behaviours should not be switched on or off but shifted gradually: cigarettes, caffeine, minutes of exercise, pages read, minutes of on-task work, steps on a fear hierarchy. The changing-criterion design described by Donald P. Hartmann and R. Vance Hall (1976) handles these. After a baseline, the treatment (usually a reinforcement contingency) is applied in a series of phases, each with a stepwise criterion: the client earns the reward only if behaviour meets the current criterion. When behaviour is stable at that level, the criterion is changed again. Hartmann and Hall presented it as a variant of the multiple-baseline logic, in which each phase acts as the baseline for the next.

Experimental control is shown when behaviour tracks the criterion: it changes when, and only when, the criterion changes, and settles close to each new level. In the figure, baseline smoking averages 22.9 cigarettes a day; each criterion phase settles at or just below its limit (17.4, 13.3, 9.8, 5.8 and 3.0 a day against limits of 18, 14, 10, 6 and 3). On the first day of the ≤ 10 and ≤ 3 phases the client overshoots by one cigarette, which is typical of real data. To make the case strong: use at least three criterion changes (each change is a demonstration), vary the length of the phases (5, 4, 6, 4 and 5 days here) so that change cannot simply be following a calendar rhythm, vary the size of the steps, and, if possible, add a brief reversal to an earlier criterion (a "mini-reversal") to show that behaviour follows the criterion in both directions.

Strengths: no withdrawal, one behaviour in one person is enough, and the shaping logic fits clinical goals. Weaknesses: the behaviour must already be in the person's repertoire; if behaviour runs ahead of the criterion (the client simply quits smoking at day 9), control cannot be shown; and it is hard to separate the treatment from the client's own goal-setting.

22.6 Alternating-treatments (multi-element) design and combined designs

The alternating-treatments design (ATD), named and systematised by David H. Barlow and Steven C. Hayes (1979), compares two or more treatments in one person by alternating them rapidly: across sessions, days or parts of a day, in a random or counterbalanced order, each condition usually signalled by a distinct cue (a different therapist, room or colour card) so the person can discriminate them. Barlow and Hayes noted that it had gone by several names before; you will also see it called the multi-element (multielement) design. Each condition is plotted as its own line. If the lines separate clearly and consistently, the conditions have different effects; if they overlap, they do not differ.

In the figure a boy's on-task behaviour averages 34.8% of intervals at baseline. During alternation, praise sessions average 49.0% and token sessions 72.7%, and the two lines never cross, so tokens are the more effective treatment; the last phase uses tokens alone (84.8%). The ATD is the design behind the functional analysis of problem behaviour by Brian Iwata and colleagues (1982), in which a child's self-injury is measured under rapidly alternated attention, demand (escape), alone and play conditions; the condition with the highest line reveals what is maintaining the behaviour.

Strengths: fast (a comparison in days rather than weeks), no withdrawal, can begin without a long baseline, and handles somewhat unstable behaviour because both conditions are equally affected by any drift. Weaknesses: multiple-treatment interference (carryover or contrast between conditions alternated so closely), the conditions must be discriminable, the behaviour must respond quickly, and the rapid switching may be artificial compared with how the treatment would be used in real life.

Combined designs mix these elements to answer more than one question or to shore up a weakness: a multiple baseline in which one tier also gets a brief withdrawal; an ABAB whose B phases contain an alternating-treatments comparison; a changing criterion run inside a multiple baseline across clients. In medicine the same logic appears as the randomised N-of-1 trial (Gordon Guyatt and colleagues, 1986), in which one patient receives drug and placebo in randomised, blinded, repeated periods (section 25).

The designs compared

DesignHow it demonstrates controlBest forMain weakness
ABOnly one phase change; no verificationRoutine clinical monitoring; replicated across many clientsCannot rule out history, maturation, regression. Quasi-experimental
ABAWithdrawal shows return to baseline (verification)Brief research demonstrationsEnds without treatment; behaviour may not reverse
ABABThree phase changes: effect shown, removed, shown againReversible behaviour, e.g. classroom disruption maintained by contingenciesEthics of withdrawal; useless for irreversible skills
BABWithdrawal and reinstatement of an ongoing treatmentDangerous behaviour needing immediate treatmentNo initial baseline
ABCB / A-B-A-CCompares a treatment with a control condition or a second treatmentIsolating the active ingredient (contingent vs non-contingent attention)Order effects, multiple-treatment interference
Multiple baseline (behaviours, settings, participants)Staggered introduction; untreated tiers verify, treated tiers replicateIrreversible behaviour, ethical objection to withdrawal, several clientsBaselines must be independent; long untreated waits; needs 3+ tiers
