22.7 Measuring behaviour in single-case work

Single-case designs stand or fall on measurement, because the whole inference is visual and every session's data point counts. The first step is the operational definition of the target behaviour (the idea of defining a concept by the operations used to measure it is Percy Bridgman's, 1927; see section 18). A good behavioural definition is objective (refers only to observable features), clear (two observers reading it would score the same events) and complete (states what counts, what does not, and where one instance ends and the next begins). "Aggressive" is not a definition; "hitting: any contact of the child's open or closed hand with another person, with enough force to make a sound, counted once per contact" is. Ogden Lindsley's dead-man test is a quick check: if a dead man could do it ("sits quietly", "does not shout"), it is not a behaviour, so define what the person does instead.

The dimensions you can measure

MeasureWhat it recordsExample
Frequency (count)Number of times the behaviour occursNumber of hits in a session
RateCount divided by observation time; needed when sessions differ in length12 hits in 30 min = 0.4 per minute
DurationHow long each episode lasts, or total time engagedMinutes spent crying; minutes on task
LatencyTime from a cue (instruction, stimulus) to the start of the responseSeconds from "pick up your book" to doing it
Inter-response time (IRT)Time between the end of one response and the start of the nextSeconds between bites when eating too fast
Percentage of opportunities / trials to criterionCorrect responses out of trials presented8 of 10 discrete trials correct
Permanent productA lasting result of the behaviour, measured after the factWorksheets completed, cigarette butts, wet bedsheets, Fitbit steps

Frequency, duration and latency are continuous recording: every instance is captured. When behaviour is too frequent or its episodes are hard to separate (hand-flapping, rocking, on-task behaviour), observers use discontinuous methods that divide the session into short intervals and score each one:

  • Partial-interval recording: score the interval if the behaviour occurs at any time during it, however briefly.
  • Whole-interval recording: score the interval only if the behaviour occurs throughout the entire interval.
  • Momentary time sampling (MTS): score the interval only if the behaviour is occurring at the instant the interval ends. Its group version, planned activity check (PLACHECK), counts how many children are engaged at each moment.
Which method over- or under-estimates. Partial-interval overestimates the duration of behaviour (a 3-second burst scores the whole 30-second interval), whole-interval underestimates it (an episode that stops one second early scores nothing), and momentary time sampling is roughly unbiased, erring in both directions, and becomes more accurate with shorter intervals. In the drawn stream the behaviour actually occupies 173 of 300 seconds (57.7%). Partial-interval scores 9 of 10 intervals (90%), whole-interval 4 of 10 (40%), MTS 6 of 10 (60%). Practical rule: use partial-interval for behaviours you want to decrease (overestimating them is the conservative error) and whole-interval for behaviours you want to increase, such as on-task work (underestimating them is conservative). Interval methods give a percentage of intervals, not a true frequency or duration, so do not call them a count.

Inter-observer agreement (IOA)

Because the data come from human observers, a second independent observer records a sample of sessions (conventionally at least 20 to 33% of sessions, in every phase) and the two records are compared. IOA, also called inter-observer reliability, is the observational form of the inter-rater reliability of section 15.2. Agreement of 80% or more is the usual minimum and 90% is preferred; for kappa, the What Works Clearinghouse standards accept 0.60.

  • Total count IOA = (smaller count / larger count) × 100. Observer 1 records 18 out-of-seat episodes, observer 2 records 20: 18/20 = 90%. Simple, but it can hide disagreement: the observers might have counted completely different episodes and still reached similar totals.
  • Interval-by-interval IOA = agreements / (agreements + disagreements) × 100, computed interval by interval. Stricter, because each interval must match.
  • Scored-interval IOA uses only intervals in which at least one observer scored the behaviour (best for low-rate behaviour); unscored-interval IOA uses only intervals in which at least one scored non-occurrence (best for high-rate behaviour). Duration and latency use total duration IOA (shorter/longer) or mean duration per occurrence; discrete trials use trial-by-trial IOA.

Worked example

Two observers score ten 10-second intervals of a child's hand-flapping (+ = occurred, − = did not):

Interval12345678910
Observer 1++−++−++−+
Observer 2++−+−−++++

Interval-by-interval: they agree on 8 intervals and disagree on 2 (intervals 5 and 9): 8/10 = 80%. Scored-interval: at least one observer scored + in 8 intervals (1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10) and both did in 6: 6/8 = 75%. Unscored-interval: at least one scored − in 4 intervals (3, 5, 6, 9) and both did in 2: 2/4 = 50%. Cohen's kappa (Jacob Cohen, 1960; formula in section 15.2) corrects for chance: each observer scored + in 7 of 10 intervals, so chance agreement pe = (.7)(.7) + (.3)(.3) = .58, and κ = (.80 − .58)/(1 − .58) = .22/.42 = .52. The same data give anything from 50% to 80%, and a chance-corrected value of only .52, which is why a report must say which index it used.

Threats to observational data (more in section 23): reactivity (the child behaves differently because an observer is present; let them habituate before baseline), observer drift (observers gradually loosen or tighten the definition over weeks; retrain and recalibrate against a criterion record), observer expectancy bias (observers who know the phase "see" improvement; keep them blind to phase where possible), and complexity of the code. IOA can be high while both observers are wrong together, so agreement is not the same as accuracy.

22.8 Analysing single-case data

Visual analysis

The traditional analysis is visual inspection of the graph. The What Works Clearinghouse standards (Kratochwill and colleagues, 2010) list six features to examine within and between phases:

  1. Level: the mean (or median) of the data within a phase, shown by the level lines in the ABAB figure (15.0, 6.1, 11.8, 3.6).
  2. Trend: the slope of the data within a phase, often drawn as a split-middle or least-squares line. B1 is still falling at its end; A2 is rising.
  3. Variability: how far the points scatter around the level or trend. A1 ranges only 13 to 17, a stable baseline.
  4. Immediacy of effect: how quickly behaviour changes after a phase change, judged by comparing the last three points of one phase with the first three of the next. A1 to B1: 15.7 falls to 9.0. A2 to B2: 13.0 falls to 5.0. The faster the change, the more convincingly it is tied to the intervention.
  5. Overlap: the proportion of data in one phase that falls in the range of the adjacent phase. Less overlap means a clearer effect.
  6. Consistency of data patterns across similar phases: do A1 and A2 look alike, and B1 and B2? Here both baselines are high and both treatment phases low.
Why behaviour analysts prefer visual analysis. It is conservative: only large, clinically obvious effects are visible, so it guards against declaring trivial effects real (fewer Type I errors) at the cost of missing small ones (more Type II errors, section 8). It keeps the analyst close to the individual's data session by session, so a treatment can be changed as soon as it stops working. Its weakness is subjectivity: DeProspero and Cohen (1979) showed that experienced reviewers often disagree about whether the same graph shows an effect, especially with trends and high variability.

Percentage of non-overlapping data (PND)

To combine single-case studies in reviews and meta-analyses, Thomas Scruggs, Margo Mastropieri and Glendon Casto (1987) proposed the simplest overlap index. Find the most extreme baseline point in the direction of improvement (the lowest baseline point for a behaviour you want to reduce, the highest for one you want to increase), then count the percentage of treatment points that are better than it.

PND = (number of treatment points beyond the most extreme baseline point / total treatment points) × 100. Conventional reading: above 90% very effective, 70 to 90% effective, 50 to 70% questionable, below 50% ineffective.

Worked on the ABAB data. Out-of-seat behaviour should decrease, so use the lowest baseline point. A1 = 14, 16, 13, 15, 17, 15: lowest = 13. B1 = 13, 8, 6, 5, 4, 3, 4: points below 13 are 8, 6, 5, 4, 3 and 4, six of seven (the first B1 point equals 13, and a tie counts as overlap). PND = 6/7 = 85.7%, "effective". A2 = 8, 11, 13, 12, 14, 13: lowest = 8. B2 = 7, 5, 3, 3, 2, 3, 2: all seven are below 8, PND = 7/7 = 100%. Pooled, 13/14 = 92.9%, "very effective". In the multiple-baseline figure every intervention point is above that child's highest baseline point, so PND is 100% for all three children.

The weakness of PND. It hinges on a single baseline point. If one A1 session had been a fluke 2 episodes (the child was absent for half the class), no B1 point would fall below it and PND would collapse to 0%, though the graph plainly shows an effect. PND also ignores trend (a baseline already improving gives a high PND with no treatment effect) and has a ceiling at 100%, so it cannot tell a large effect from a huge one.

Other statistics, briefly

  • Other non-overlap indices: percentage of data exceeding the baseline median (PEM), non-overlap of all pairs (NAP), and Tau-U (Richard Parker, Kimberly Vannest and colleagues, 2011), which compares every baseline point with every treatment point and can correct for an existing baseline trend, the main defect of PND.
  • Time-series analysis: repeated measurements of one person are autocorrelated (serially dependent: today's score predicts tomorrow's), which violates the independence assumption of ordinary t tests and ANOVA (section 9.5; the Durbin–Watson check in section 13) and inflates Type I error if you ignore it. Interrupted time-series analysis (ARIMA models of George Box and Gwilym Jenkins, 1970) models the dependency and tests for a change in level or slope at the intervention point, but it needs many data points per phase, often 50 or more.
  • Randomisation tests: if the start point of treatment is chosen at random from several possible sessions, the observed effect can be compared with the effects that would have appeared at every other possible start point.

Clinical versus statistical significance, and the reliable change index

Statistical significance (section 8) says an effect is unlikely to be chance; it does not say the client is better in any way that matters. Applied research asks for clinical significance: did the client move into the range of normal functioning, and is the change bigger than measurement error? Neil Jacobson and Paula Truax (1991), building on Jacobson, Follette and Revenstorf (1984), answered with two criteria that are now standard for evaluating individual therapy outcomes.

Reliable change index: RC = (xpost − xpre) / Sdiff, where Sdiff = √[2(SE)²] and SE = s1√(1 − rxx) is the standard error of measurement (section 15.2), s1 being the pretreatment SD of a normative or clinical sample and rxx the test's test–retest reliability. If |RC| > 1.96, the change is unlikely (p < .05) to be produced by measurement error alone: it is a reliable change.

Worked example. A client attending counselling scores 31 on a depression scale before treatment and 22 after it. The scale's SD is 7.5 and its test–retest reliability .88. SE = 7.5 × √(1 − .88) = 7.5 × 0.346 = 2.60. Sdiff = √(2 × 2.60²) = 3.67. RC = (22 − 31)/3.67 = −2.45. Since |−2.45| > 1.96, the 9-point drop is a reliable improvement. Turned round, any change smaller than 1.96 × 3.67 = 7.2 points on this scale could be measurement noise.

The second criterion is a cut-off for recovery. Jacobson and Truax's preferred cut-off c lies between the dysfunctional and functional populations: c = (s0M1 + s1M0)/(s0 + s1), where 0 is the functional (non-clinical) group and 1 the dysfunctional group. If the clinical mean is 28 (SD 8) and the community mean 7 (SD 5), c = (5 × 28 + 8 × 7)/(5 + 8) = 196/13 = 15.1. Our client, at 22, has reliably improved but is not recovered; a client who reliably improved and crossed below 15.1 would be classed recovered. The four outcome categories are recovered, improved, unchanged and deteriorated (a reliable change in the wrong direction).

22.9 Generality: replication and social validity

One child's ABAB proves the treatment worked for that child. Single-case researchers do not get generality from random sampling (section 7.2); they get it from replication, as Sidman argued.

  • Direct replication: the same researcher repeats the same procedure with the same kind of participant in the same setting. Within one person it is intrasubject replication (the second B phase of an ABAB); across similar people it is intersubject replication (the tiers of a multiple baseline). It establishes reliability of the effect.
  • Systematic replication: the procedure is repeated while deliberately varying one or more features: different therapists, settings, behaviours, ages, diagnoses or cultures. Each success extends the generality of the finding. Barlow and Hersen added clinical replication: a whole treatment package applied by the same clinician to a series of clients with a similar cluster of problems (for example, a series of children with autism).

Effects can be reliable and still trivial. Montrose Wolf (1978), in a paper subtitled "how applied behavior analysis is finding its heart", argued that consumers must judge whether the work is worth doing. Social validity asks three questions: are the goals socially significant (does reducing this behaviour matter to the family and child)? Are the procedures acceptable (would parents and teachers agree to use them, are they ethical and practical)? Are the effects socially important (are the people who live with the child satisfied with the change)? Alan Kazdin (1977) described two methods of social validation: social comparison (compare the client's post-treatment behaviour with that of typical peers, for example how often classmates leave their seats) and subjective evaluation (ask parents, teachers or other significant people to rate the change).

Three different "validities". Social validity is about the acceptability and importance of goals, procedures and outcomes to consumers. It is not the internal or external validity of a study (section 19) and not the content, criterion or construct validity of a test (section 15.3). An exam option offering "construct validity" for a question about whether parents find an intervention acceptable is a distractor.
Recap of section 22: single-case (N = 1, small-N) designs are true experiments on one or a few people, built by B. F. Skinner's experimental analysis of behaviour (1938), Sidman (1960), Hersen and Barlow (1976) and Kazdin (1982), and defined for applied work by Baer, Wolf and Risley's seven dimensions of ABA (1968). Unlike a case study they use operational definitions, repeated measurement and planned phase changes, reasoning by prediction, verification and replication from a stable baseline of at least three points. AB is quasi-experimental; ABA ends untreated; ABAB is the strongest demonstration but raises the ethics of withdrawal and fails with irreversible behaviour; BAB lacks a baseline; ABCB isolates the active ingredient. Multiple baselines (behaviours, settings, participants) stagger treatment and need independent baselines; non-concurrent versions are weaker against history. Changing-criterion designs (Hartmann and Hall, 1976) show control when behaviour tracks stepwise criteria; alternating-treatments designs (Barlow and Hayes, 1979) compare rapidly alternated conditions by line separation. Partial-interval overestimates, whole-interval underestimates, momentary time sampling is roughly unbiased; IOA is smaller/larger count or agreements/total intervals, with kappa correcting for chance. Visual analysis judges level, trend, variability, immediacy, overlap and consistency; PND (Scruggs, Mastropieri and Casto, 1987) above 90% is very effective; autocorrelation rules out ordinary t tests. The reliable change index (Jacobson and Truax, 1991) needs |RC| > 1.96. Generality comes from direct and systematic replication; importance from social validity (Wolf, 1978).

23 Collecting the data: observation, interviews, questionnaires and scaling

Sections 18 to 22 decided what to compare and how to control it. This section is about the instruments that produce the data. There are only a few ways to find out about a person: watch what they do (observation), ask them in conversation (interview), ask them in writing (questionnaire, rating scale, attitude scale), measure their body (psychophysiology), or use traces and records they have already left (archives, diaries, unobtrusive measures). Each has a typical error, and most exam questions here are really about those errors and their names. Whether an instrument is reliable and valid is section 15 (reliability, test validity, item analysis), and what level of measurement a scale yields is section 1.2; they are not repeated here.

23.1 Observation

Observation is the systematic watching and recording of behaviour as it happens. It is the one method that does not depend on what people say they do, which is why it dominates work with young children, people with intellectual disability or autism, and anyone whose self-report is unreliable.

Four distinctions

  • Naturalistic vs controlled (structured, laboratory) observation. Naturalistic observation records behaviour in its usual setting with no interference: a child's play in the school yard, interactions on an inpatient ward. It has high ecological validity but no control, and the behaviour of interest may simply not occur while you watch. Controlled observation arranges the situation so that the behaviour will occur, and records it under standard conditions: the Strange Situation of Mary Ainsworth and colleagues (1978), a parent–child interaction task behind a one-way mirror, the play-based tasks of the ADOS-2 for autism. Standardisation buys comparability and reliability at the price of artificiality.
  • Participant vs non-participant observation. The participant observer joins the group's life (works in the rehab centre, lives in the village); the non-participant observer stays outside it.
  • Overt vs covert (disclosed vs undisclosed). Overt observers are known to be researching; covert observers are not. Covert observation reduces reactivity but raises the ethical problems of deception and lack of informed consent (section 26).
  • Structured vs unstructured recording. Structured observation uses predefined categories and a coding sheet; unstructured observation keeps open, descriptive field notes, typical of qualitative ethnography (section 24).
Raymond L. Gold (1958), in "Roles in sociological field observations", described the four field roles every textbook now repeats. He developed the typology with his supervisor Buford Junker, who set it out in Field Work (1960), so the scheme is sometimes credited to Junker or to both.

Gold's four roles lie on a single continuum from complete involvement to complete detachment:

  1. Complete participant: a fully functioning member of the group whose research role is concealed (covert). A researcher joins a de-addiction support group as a member and never discloses the study.
  2. Participant-as-observer: participates fully but the group knows about the research. A counsellor working in a rehab centre who has told staff and residents she is also studying peer relationships. The usual role in community and ethnographic studies.
  3. Observer-as-participant: mainly an observer, with brief and formal contact; the research role is known. One-visit interviews or a few observation sessions at a school.
  4. Complete observer: no interaction at all; often the observed do not know they are observed. Coding playground behaviour from a distance, or a playroom through a one-way mirror.
Going native is the danger at the participant end: the observer comes to identify so completely with the group that detachment and critical distance are lost. The danger at the observer end is the reverse, misreading what behaviour means to the people doing it (ethnocentrism, in Gold's terms). "Participant observation" in an exam usually means the participant-as-observer role and is linked with ethnography and Bronisław Malinowski's fieldwork in the Trobriand Islands (Argonauts of the Western Pacific, 1922).

Reactivity, habituation and observer error

Reactivity is the change in behaviour caused by the awareness of being observed. The best known form is the Hawthorne effect, named after the Western Electric Hawthorne Works studies of the 1920s and 1930s (the term itself is Henry Landsberger's, 1958; see section 19). Remedies: habituation (the observer visits repeatedly until the novelty wears off before recording starts), unobtrusive positions, one-way mirrors or cameras, and covert observation where ethically permitted. Self-monitoring, in which clients observe and record their own behaviour (a common CBT and ABA technique), is strongly reactive: the act of recording cigarettes often reduces smoking, which is a nuisance for measurement and a gift for therapy.

The observer is also a source of error. Observer bias (observer expectancy) is seeing what one expects, for instance more improvement in a child known to be in the treatment phase; the remedy is keeping observers blind to hypothesis and condition. Observer drift is the gradual, unnoticed change in how an observer applies the definitions over weeks of recording; the remedy is periodic retraining and recalibration against a master coding. Observer fatigue and overly complex codes reduce accuracy. Agreement between observers is quantified as inter-observer agreement, computed exactly as in section 22.7 (total count, interval-by-interval, Cohen's kappa).

Sampling behaviour: what to record and when

No one can record everything a person does, so observation samples behaviour, just as a survey samples people (section 7.2).

MethodWhat is sampledBest forLimitation
Time samplingPre-set time units: behaviour is recorded in short intervals or at set moments (partial-interval, whole-interval and momentary time sampling, drawn in section 22.7). Introduced into child research in the late 1920s by Florence Goodenough and Willard OlsonFrequent, continuous behaviours: on-task, play, hand-flappingBreaks behaviour into fragments; misses rare events; gives percentages of intervals, not true frequency
Event samplingEvery occurrence of a defined event is recorded, with its antecedents, duration and consequences. Classic study: Helen Dawe (1934), 200 quarrels among nursery-school childrenInfrequent, distinct events: tantrums, aggression, seizures, quarrelsObserver must wait for the event; loses the stream of behaviour between events
Situation samplingThe same behaviour is observed across different settings and times (class, playground, home, morning and evening)Generality of findings; improves external validityCostly; settings may not be comparable
Individual (focal) samplingOne participant is observed at a time, in rotation through the groupGroup settings where everyone cannot be watched at onceEach person is seen only briefly

Recording methods

  • Continuous recording: every instance of the target behaviour across the whole session (frequency, duration).
  • Narrative (descriptive) records: a written account of behaviour in sequence. An anecdotal record is a brief factual note of a single significant incident written soon after it happens (a teacher's note that a child bit another child at lunch). A running record (specimen record) is a detailed, continuous, time-stamped description of everything a person does over a period; the classic is Roger Barker and Herbert Wright's One Boy's Day (1951), a whole day of a 7-year-old's life recorded minute by minute.
  • Checklists: a list of behaviours or skills marked present or absent (yes/no). Quick and reliable, but they record occurrence, not quality or frequency. Developmental checklists and autism screening tools (such as the M-CHAT) are of this type.
  • Rating scales: the observer judges the degree or quality of a behaviour on a scale (1 to 5, never to always). They record intensity but bring the rating errors of section 23.5.
  • Coding schemes: a fixed set of mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories into which each unit of behaviour is placed. The classic is Robert F. Bales's Interaction Process Analysis (1950) for small groups: every act in a discussion is coded into one of 12 categories in four areas (positive socio-emotional reactions such as "shows solidarity"; task-area answers such as "gives suggestion"; task-area questions such as "asks for opinion"; negative socio-emotional reactions such as "shows antagonism"). Ned Flanders's interaction analysis does the same for teacher–pupil talk.
Strengths and weaknesses of observation. It records actual behaviour rather than claims about it, captures behaviour people cannot report (infants, non-verbal children, unconscious habits) and preserves context. It cannot reach thoughts, feelings, motives or rare and private behaviour; it is slow and costly; it is vulnerable to reactivity and observer bias; and an observed correlation (children who are hit at home hit others at school) is still only a correlation.

23.2 Interviews

An interview is a purposeful, face-to-face (or voice-to-voice) conversation in which the interviewer asks questions and records answers. Interviews are classified by how much is fixed in advance.

TypeWhat is fixedStrengthWeaknessExamples
Structured (standardised)Exact wording and order of every question; often fixed response options; interviewer may not deviateHighest reliability; comparable across interviewers; lay interviewers can be trained; data easy to quantifyRigid; misses what was not asked; no clinical judgementDiagnostic Interview Schedule (DIS, Lee Robins and colleagues, 1981); WHO's CIDI; the MINI
Semi-structuredA schedule or guide of required topics and questions, with freedom to rephrase, probe and follow upBalances comparability with flexibility; clinical judgement allowedNeeds trained (usually clinical) interviewers; somewhat lower reliabilitySCID; PSE/SCAN; K-SADS; ADI-R; most qualitative research interviews
Unstructured (open, non-directive, in-depth)Only the general aim; the conversation follows the respondentDepth, rapport, discovers the unexpected; ideal for exploration and qualitative workLow reliability; hard to compare or quantify; most open to interviewer biasInitial clinical interview; life-history and phenomenological interviews

Clinical diagnostic interviews

  • SCID (Structured Clinical Interview for DSM), developed by Robert Spitzer, Janet Williams, Miriam Gibbon and Michael First from the 1980s for DSM-III and now the SCID-5. Despite the name it is semi-structured: questions are set, but the clinician judges whether each criterion is met. Separate versions cover clinical disorders and personality disorders. It is the standard answer to "a structured interview commonly used in clinical psychology".
  • MINI (Mini-International Neuropsychiatric Interview), David Sheehan, Yves Lecrubier and colleagues (1998): a short, fully structured interview for DSM and ICD diagnoses taking about 15 minutes, designed for clinical trials and epidemiology. A children's version (MINI-KID) exists.
  • Present State Examination (PSE), John Wing and colleagues (the ninth edition was published by Wing, Cooper and Sartorius in 1974), a semi-structured interview of the patient's mental state over the past month, used in the WHO International Pilot Study of Schizophrenia. Its successor, the WHO's SCAN (Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry), contains the PSE-10.
  • K-SADS (Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia), Joaquim Puig-Antich and William Chambers (1978): a semi-structured interview for children and adolescents (about 6 to 18), given separately to the parent and the child; the widely used K-SADS-PL dates from 1997 (Joan Kaufman and colleagues).
  • For autism, the ADI-R (Autism Diagnostic Interview–Revised; Catherine Lord, Michael Rutter and Ann Le Couteur, 1994) is a semi-structured parent interview, usually paired with the observational ADOS-2.

Interviewer effects and probing

The interviewer is part of the instrument, so interviewer characteristics change the data. Interviewer bias includes the interviewer's expectations and opinions leaking into how questions are asked and answers recorded: in a classic early demonstration, Stuart Rice (1929) found that a prohibitionist interviewer tended to record drink as the cause of destitution among homeless men, while a socialist interviewer tended to record industrial and economic conditions. Interviewer demographics matter too: gender, age, caste, religion, language or perceived status can change what is disclosed (a young female interviewer and an older male respondent discussing alcohol use, or a respondent asked about caste by someone of a different caste). Respondents also give socially desirable answers more readily face to face. Remedies are training, standard wording, matching interviewers to respondents where it matters, and checking for differences between interviewers.

Probes are neutral follow-ups that get a fuller or clearer answer without suggesting one: "Could you tell me more about that?", "What do you mean by 'stressed'?", repeating the question, an expectant pause (the silent probe), or echoing the respondent's last words. Furthering (minimal encouragers such as nodding, leaning forward, "mm-hm", "go on") keeps the respondent talking. A leading probe ("So you felt angry, didn't you?") is the error to avoid. The funnel technique starts with broad, open questions and narrows to specific ones, so that early specifics do not shape later answers.

Interviews compared with questionnaires

InterviewQuestionnaire
Response rateHigh; refusal is harder face to faceOften low, especially by post
Literacy neededNone; usable with illiterate, elderly, child and very ill respondentsReading and writing ability required
Clarification and probingPossible; misunderstandings corrected; non-verbal cues observedImpossible; ambiguous items stay ambiguous
Depth and complex topicsGoodLimited
Cost and timeHigh; one respondent at a time; trained staffLow; large samples quickly
Interviewer biasPresentAbsent
Anonymity on sensitive topicsLow; more social desirabilityHigh; more honest reports of drug use, sexual behaviour, suicidal ideas
StandardisationVaries with typeComplete

Telephone interviews (often computer-assisted, CATI) are cheaper and faster than face-to-face, reach scattered samples and reduce interviewer-appearance effects, but lose non-verbal cues and visual aids, must be shorter, and exclude people without phones. Online and video interviews extend this to video calls, used widely in tele-counselling platforms; they are convenient, but rapport, privacy at the respondent's end, and connectivity become issues.

23.3 Questionnaires and surveys

A questionnaire is a written set of questions that respondents answer themselves. A survey is the research design that uses questionnaires or interviews to collect information from a sample in order to describe a population (its attitudes, behaviours, prevalence of a condition) and the relationships among variables. Surveys can describe distributions and associations; like all non-experimental designs (section 21), they cannot by themselves establish the causes of what they describe.

Open and closed items, and response formats

Open-ended (unrestricted) items let respondents answer in their own words ("What is the most difficult part of caring for your son?"). They give rich, unanticipated answers and suit exploration and pilot work, but they are slow to answer, depend on literacy, and must be coded before analysis. Closed-ended (fixed-alternative, restricted) items provide the answers: dichotomous (yes/no), multiple choice, checklists, rank ordering, and rating formats such as Likert agreement scales and numerical or visual analogue scales. They are quick, easy to score and compare, but can force a choice that does not fit and cannot reveal what the researcher did not think of. A Likert item is "closed-ended with a fixed number of alternative responses". A contingency (filter) question routes respondents ("If you answered No, go to question 12").

Rules for writing items

FaultBad itemBetter
Double-barrelled: two questions in one"How often and how long do you exercise?" / "Is your therapist warm and competent?"Ask each separately
Leading: suggests the expected answer"Don't you agree that therapy should be free?""Should therapy be free of charge?"
Loaded: emotionally coloured words"Should lunatics be allowed to roam the streets?"Neutral, non-stigmatising terms
Double negative"I do not think patients should not be told their diagnosis""Patients should be told their diagnosis"
Jargon or technical terms"Do you experience anhedonia?""Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?"
Ambiguous or vague terms"Do you drink regularly?""On how many days in the past week did you drink alcohol?"
Presuming a fact not established"How has your depression affected your work?"First ask whether the person has been depressed
Hypothetical and memory-taxing items"How many cigarettes did you smoke last year?"Short, recent reference periods

Also keep items short and in the respondent's language (translated and back-translated for Indian regional languages), make response options exhaustive and mutually exclusive, and include a "don't know" or neutral option only when it is a real answer.

Order effects, pilot study and administration

Question order changes answers: earlier questions create a context for later ones (asking about specific worries first raises later ratings of general anxiety), and the position of response options matters (primacy effects favour early options when people read them; recency effects favour the last options heard over the telephone). Howard Schuman and Stanley Presser's Questions and Answers in Attitude Surveys (1981) documented many such context, order and wording effects. Remedies: general before specific (the funnel), sensitive and demographic questions near the end, and rotating or randomising the order of items and options across respondents. A pilot study (pre-test) on a small sample from the same population is essential: it exposes confusing wording, missing response options, timing and skip-pattern errors before they ruin the main study.

Mailed questionnaires are cheap and anonymous but slow, and response rates are often low. Online surveys are cheaper and faster still, allow automatic routing and data entry, but reach only internet users and invite careless responding. Low response rate matters because non-responders usually differ from responders (non-response bias); the problem is not the smaller n but the biased sample. Response rates are raised by advance letters, short and well-designed forms, personalisation, reminders and follow-ups, small incentives and sponsorship by a trusted body: the package Don Dillman systematised as the Total Design Method (1978).

23.4 Response biases and response sets

A response set or response style is a tendency to answer questionnaire items in a particular way regardless of their content. The term "response set" was given by Lee J. Cronbach (1946); Douglas Jackson and Samuel Messick (1958) framed the general problem as content versus style. Every questionnaire score is partly the trait it was written to measure and partly the respondent's style of answering.

  • Acquiescence (yea-saying): agreeing with items irrespective of content; its opposite is nay-saying. Arthur Couch and Kenneth Keniston (1960) described "yeasayers and naysayers" as a stable personality style. It is more common in less educated respondents, children and in cultures that value politeness to the questioner. If all items are keyed in the "agree" direction, acquiescence masquerades as the trait.
  • Social desirability: answering to present oneself favourably rather than accurately. Allen L. Edwards (1957), The Social Desirability Variable in Personality Assessment and Research, showed that the probability of endorsing a personality item is strongly predicted by how socially desirable the item is judged to be. Douglas Crowne and David Marlowe (1960) built the Marlowe–Crowne Social Desirability Scale (33 true/false items describing behaviours that are culturally approved but unlikely, such as "I have never been irked when people expressed ideas very different from my own"). Delroy Paulhus (1984) separated self-deceptive enhancement (honestly believing one's own positive self-image) from impression management (deliberately presenting a good image).
  • Extreme responding: choosing the end points of rating scales (always "strongly agree" or "strongly disagree").
  • Central tendency (midpoint) responding: avoiding the extremes and choosing the neutral middle, often from caution, indifference or fatigue.
  • Faking good and faking bad: deliberate distortion. Faking good is common in job selection and custody assessment; faking bad (exaggerating problems) in compensation claims, disability assessment and forensic settings, and in its extreme clinical form is malingering.
  • Careless or random responding and deviation (choosing unusual answers) complete the list.
BiasHow to reduce or detect it
AcquiescenceBalanced keying: about half the items reverse-keyed (worded in the opposite direction), so agreeing with everything cancels out; check agreement with pairs of opposite items
Social desirabilityAnonymity and confidentiality; neutral wording; forced-choice items that pair statements equal in desirability, as in Edwards's own Edwards Personal Preference Schedule; social desirability scales (Marlowe–Crowne) used as a covariate or screen; indirect and unobtrusive measures
Faking good / badLie and validity scales: the L (lie), F (infrequency, raised by faking bad or confusion) and K (defensiveness, correction) scales of the MMPI (Starke Hathaway and J. C. McKinley, 1943), the Lie scale of Hans and Sybil Eysenck's EPQ (1975); consistency checks; subtle items whose purpose is not obvious
Extreme and midpoint respondingClear anchors on every point; even-numbered scales with no midpoint (forces a lean); standardising scores within the person; forced choice
Careless respondingAttention-check items, inconsistency indices, short questionnaires
Response set vs rating error. Acquiescence, social desirability and extreme responding are errors of the person answering about themselves. Halo, leniency and central tendency error (next subsection) are errors of a rater judging someone else. A high score on a lie scale indicates a tendency to fake or present oneself favourably (social desirability), so for a question like "an elevated Lie scale indicates" every one of faking, social desirability and defensiveness is defensible.

23.5 Rating scales and their errors

A rating scale records a judgement of the degree to which a person shows a characteristic. Formats include numerical (1 to 7), graphic (a line with descriptive anchors along it), descriptive or behaviourally anchored (each point described by a concrete behaviour: the Behaviourally Anchored Rating Scale of Patricia Smith and Lorne Kendall, 1963), and comparative (rank relative to others). In clinical work the key distinction is who rates: clinician-rated scales such as the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (Max Hamilton, 1959) and Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (1960) versus self-report inventories such as the Beck Depression Inventory (Aaron Beck, 1961) and Beck Anxiety Inventory (1988).

Raters make systematic ("constant") errors. The standard list is in J. P. Guilford's Psychometric Methods (1954).

ErrorWhat happensExample
Halo effectA general impression, or one salient trait, colours the ratings of all other, unrelated traits. Named by Edward L. Thorndike (1920), "A constant error in psychological ratings", from officers' ratings of soldiers, whose ratings of physique, intelligence, leadership and character correlated far more highly than the traits could really be relatedAn articulate, well-groomed patient is rated as more insightful, motivated and less ill. The reverse (one bad trait spoils all ratings) is the horns or reverse-halo effect
Leniency (generosity) errorRating everyone too favourablyA supervisor rates all trainees "excellent"
Severity errorRating everyone too harshlyA strict examiner gives no one above 6 of 10
Central tendency errorAvoiding extremes; piling ratings in the middle of the scaleEvery child rated 3 on a 5-point scale
Logical errorRating traits similarly because the rater believes they logically go together, rather than from observationAssuming a child who is good at mathematics must also be good at science
Contrast errorRating others in the direction opposite to oneself on a trait (or relative to the person just rated)A very orderly rater sees others as disorganised; an average candidate after a brilliant one is rated low
Proximity errorTraits placed next to each other on the rating form are rated more alike than traits far apartAdjacent items "punctuality" and "sincerity" get similar ratings
Reducing rating errors: train raters with examples; define every trait and anchor every point behaviourally; rate one trait across all ratees before moving to the next trait (reduces halo); separate related items on the form (reduces proximity error); use forced distributions or rankings (reduces leniency, severity and central tendency); use several independent raters and check their agreement (section 15.2).

23.6 Attitude scaling methods

An attitude is not directly observable, so scaling methods turn agreement with statements into a number on a continuum. The classic methods differ in how the items are chosen and scaled and in how a respondent's score is computed, and those two points are what exam questions test.

Thurstone's method of equal-appearing intervals

Louis Leon Thurstone argued in "Attitudes can be measured" (1928) that attitudes could be placed on a psychological continuum, and with Ernest J. Chave published the method in The Measurement of Attitude (1929), illustrated with attitude toward the church. His earlier law of comparative judgment (1927) is the theory behind the method of paired comparisons.
  1. Write a large pool of statements (often 100 or more) ranging from extremely unfavourable to extremely favourable towards the attitude object.
  2. A large panel of judges sorts each statement into 11 piles (A to K) from most unfavourable to most favourable, judging how favourable the statement is, not whether they agree with it. The piles are meant to look equally spaced, hence "equal-appearing intervals".
  3. Each statement's scale value is the median of the judges' placements.
  4. Each statement's Q value is the interquartile range (Q3 − Q1) of the placements. A large Q means judges disagreed about where it belongs: the statement is ambiguous and is discarded. Thurstone and Chave also applied a criterion of irrelevance, dropping statements endorsed by people with very different attitudes.
  5. A final set of statements is kept, choosing those with low Q values whose scale values are spread evenly along the whole continuum.
  6. Respondents simply mark the statements they agree with. The score is the median (or mean) scale value of the statements endorsed.

Strengths: the intended result is interval-level measurement and each item has a known position. Weaknesses: laborious and expensive to construct; the assumption that judges' own attitudes do not affect their sorting fails (Carl Hovland and Muzafer Sherif, 1952, showed that judges with strong positions displace the neutral items); different patterns of endorsement can give the same score.

Likert's method of summated ratings

Rensis Likert (1932), "A technique for the measurement of attitudes" (Archives of Psychology, No. 140), showed that a much simpler method, in which respondents rate their own agreement with every item, gave reliability at least comparable to Thurstone's, without the panel of judges.
  1. Write statements that are clearly favourable or clearly unfavourable (neutral statements are useless here, unlike in Thurstone's method).
  2. Administer them to a pilot sample with a 5-point response format (Strongly agree, Agree, Undecided, Disagree, Strongly disagree), scored 5 to 1 for favourable items and reversed (1 to 5) for unfavourable items.
  3. Item analysis (section 15.4): keep the items that discriminate between high and low total scorers. The usual procedure compares the top and bottom 25% (or 27%) of total scorers on each item with a t test (Allen Edwards's rule of thumb keeps items with t of 1.75 or more) or uses the item–total correlation.
  4. The respondent's score is the sum (hence "summated rating") or mean of the item scores.

Strengths: easy and cheap to build, every item contributes information about intensity, high reliability. Weaknesses: the same total can arise from very different response patterns; vulnerable to acquiescence (hence balanced keying) and to central tendency responding; the "Undecided" midpoint is ambiguous (neutral, indifferent or not understanding).

Ordinal per item, treated as interval when summed. A single Likert item is ordinal: there is no guarantee that the step from "Agree" to "Strongly agree" equals the step from "Undecided" to "Agree". The summed scale of many items is conventionally treated as approximately interval and analysed with means and parametric tests (section 1.2). Name it correctly: a Likert scale is the summed set of items; a single item with this format is a Likert-type item. "Summated rating scale" = Likert.

Guttman's cumulative scaling (scalogram analysis)

Louis Guttman (1944), "A basis for scaling qualitative data" (American Sociological Review), developed scalogram analysis while working on soldiers' attitudes for the US Army in World War II.

A Guttman scale is unidimensional and cumulative: the items are ordered by difficulty (intensity), so that anyone who agrees with a stronger item also agrees with every weaker one. Like the rungs of a ladder, a score of 3 means the person endorsed exactly the first three items. The total score therefore reproduces the whole response pattern. Real data are never perfect, so Guttman measured how close they come with the coefficient of reproducibility:

CR = 1 − (number of errors / total number of responses), where total responses = respondents × items. A CR of .90 or higher is required to accept the items as a Guttman scale. Because CR can be inflated by items that almost everyone or almost no one endorses, Herbert Menzel (1953) added the coefficient of scalability, conventionally required to be .60 or more.

Sort respondents by total score (rows) and items by popularity (columns, most endorsed on the left). A perfect scale forms a staircase: every row is a run of "yes" followed by a run of "no". R6 has a total of 2 but said no to "neighbour" and yes to the harder "rent my house to". Counting errors as cells that differ from the ideal pattern for that total score (Y Y N N N), R6 contributes 2 errors, so CR = 1 − 2/50 = .96. Guttman's own counting (the fewest responses that must change to make the pattern perfect) gives 1 error and CR = .98. Either way the scale passes .90. Strength: the score has an exact meaning and the scale is demonstrably unidimensional. Weaknesses: very few attitude domains are truly cumulative, the scale works only for the population tested, and it is coarse (only k + 1 possible scores). The Bogardus scale below is the best-known cumulative scale. Guttman scaling is a deterministic forerunner of the probabilistic Rasch model of item response theory (section 15).

Osgood's semantic differential

Charles E. Osgood, George J. Suci and Percy H. Tannenbaum, The Measurement of Meaning (1957), developed the semantic differential to measure the connotative (emotional, associative) meaning of any concept: a person, an illness, a nation, oneself.

The respondent rates a concept on a series of bipolar adjective pairs, usually on a 7-point scale between the two adjectives (good ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ bad). Factor analysis of many such ratings across concepts and languages repeatedly found three dimensions, E P A: Evaluation (good–bad, valuable–worthless, pleasant–unpleasant), by far the largest factor and the one that corresponds to attitude; Potency (strong–weak, large–small, heavy–light); and Activity (active–passive, fast–slow, sharp–dull). The results are shown as a profile, and the difference in meaning between two concepts is measured by Osgood's distance statistic D = √Σd², where d is the difference between the two concepts on each scale.

Strengths: easy to construct and to answer, applicable to any concept, gives a multidimensional picture, and a self versus ideal-self pair of profiles is a ready index of self-esteem. Weaknesses: some adjective pairs do not fit some concepts ("heavy–light" for a person with diabetes); respondents may reach the extremes or the midpoint by style; the polarity of pairs should be alternated so that the favourable adjective is not always on the left (to break acquiescence and position sets). The figure aligns all favourable poles on the left only for reading.

Bogardus social distance scale

Emory S. Bogardus (1925) measured prejudice as the degree of intimacy a person will accept with members of a group. Respondents mark the closest relationship they would accept: (1) to close kinship by marriage; (2) to my club as personal chums; (3) to my street as neighbours; (4) to employment in my occupation; (5) to citizenship in my country; (6) as visitors only to my country; (7) would exclude from my country. Accepting a close relationship implies accepting the more distant ones, so the scale is cumulative (Guttman-type) and ordinal. It is still used for attitudes to castes, religions, migrants and people with mental illness.

Paired comparisons and rank order

In the method of paired comparisons every stimulus is paired with every other and the respondent chooses the preferred (or more favourable) one in each pair. With n stimuli there are n(n − 1)/2 pairs: 10 stimuli need 45 judgements, 20 need 190, which is the method's practical limit. The proportion of times each stimulus is preferred is converted to a scale position using Thurstone's law of comparative judgment, giving an interval scale of preference. The rank-order method asks the respondent to order all stimuli at once, which is quicker but yields only ordinal data and becomes unreliable in the middle of long lists.

Q-sort

William Stephenson introduced Q-technique in 1935 and set it out in The Study of Behavior: Q-Technique and Its Methodology (1953). Ordinary (R-technique) factor analysis correlates tests across many people; Q-technique correlates persons (or one person's different sorts) across many items. The respondent sorts a deck of cards, each with a statement ("I am a responsible person", "I often feel insecure"), into piles from "most like me" to "least like me", with a forced, roughly normal distribution (a fixed number of cards in each pile, typically 9 or 11 piles, with few at the extremes and many in the middle). Because the distribution is fixed, everyone's sort has the same mean and spread, so the method describes the relative importance of traits within one person (ipsative measurement) rather than comparing people's absolute levels. Carl Rogers made it famous in psychotherapy research: in Psychotherapy and Personality Change (Rogers and Dymond, 1954), clients sorted the same statements twice, once for the self and once for the ideal self, and the correlation between the two sorts (John Butler and Gerard Haigh's self–ideal correlation) rose after client-centred therapy, the operational measure of reduced self-ideal discrepancy (incongruence). Jack Block's California Q-set (1961) is the best-known standard deck.

Sociometry and the sociogram

Jacob L. Moreno, founder of psychodrama, introduced sociometry in Who Shall Survive? (1934), from work with girls at the Hudson training school in New York. In the sociometric test each member of a group names the people they would choose (and sometimes reject) as companions for an activity: "Whom would you like to sit next to?", "Whom would you like in your project group?". The choices are drawn as a sociogram, with people as circles and choices as arrows, which shows the group's structure: stars (chosen by many), isolates (chosen by none), mutual pairs, chains, cliques and rejectees. Teachers and school counsellors use it to identify isolated and rejected children; it measures patterns of attraction, choice and social distance within a group, not personality or intelligence.

Visual analogue, forced-choice and checklist methods

  • Visual analogue scale (VAS): a line, usually 100 mm, with anchors only at the ends ("no pain" … "worst pain imaginable"; "not at all anxious" … "extremely anxious"). The respondent marks the line and the score is the distance in mm. Quick, sensitive to small changes, language-light and repeatable many times a day (craving, pain, mood), but each scale is a single item and needs some abstract understanding.
  • Forced-choice method: the respondent must choose between two or more statements, usually matched for social desirability, so that the "good-looking" answer is not obvious. It reduces social desirability and leniency, but produces ipsative scores (a high score on one trait forces lower scores on others), which complicates comparison between people. Edwards Personal Preference Schedule is the textbook example.
  • Checklist method: the respondent (or an observer) ticks every adjective or statement that applies, as in Harrison Gough's Adjective Check List or symptom checklists. Fast and simple, but it records presence or absence, not degree, and the number ticked depends on how many items the respondent tends to tick.

The scaling methods compared

MethodType of scale producedHow it is builtStrengthWeakness
Thurstone (1928; with Chave 1929)Intended interval (equal-appearing intervals)Judges sort statements into 11 piles; scale value = median, ambiguity = Q; respondents tick agreed items; score = median scale valueItems have known positions; interval aimLaborious; judges' attitudes distort scale values; same score from different patterns
Likert (1932)Ordinal per item; summed score treated as intervalAgree–disagree ratings of clearly positive or negative items; item analysis; score = sumEasy, reliable, measures intensityAcquiescence; ambiguous midpoint; same total from different patterns
Guttman (1944)Ordinal, cumulative, unidimensionalItems ordered by intensity; scalogram analysis; CR ≥ .90Score reproduces the response patternFew domains truly cumulative; coarse; sample-specific
