24.12 Quality in qualitative research: trustworthiness and rigour

Yvonna Lincoln and Egon Guba, Naturalistic Inquiry (1985), argued that internal validity, external validity, reliability and objectivity were built for experiments and do not fit naturalistic inquiry, and proposed trustworthiness, made of four parallel criteria. In Fourth Generation Evaluation (1989), Guba and Lincoln added authenticity criteria, which have no quantitative parallel.

Credibility (parallels internal validity) is confidence that the findings truly represent participants' realities. Transferability (parallels external validity) is whether findings apply elsewhere; the researcher cannot prove it, but supplies enough thick description for readers to judge. Dependability (parallels reliability) means the process is consistent and documented well enough to be audited. Confirmability (parallels objectivity) means the findings are shaped by the data rather than the researcher's bias and can be traced back to the data. Authenticity covers fairness (all viewpoints represented) and ontological, educative, catalytic and tactical authenticity (the research enlarged participants' understanding and enabled action).

TechniqueWhat it isCriterion served
Prolonged engagementEnough time in the field to learn the culture and build trust (gives scope)Credibility
Persistent observationFocusing deeply on what is most relevant (gives depth)Credibility
TriangulationChecking findings across sources, investigators, theories or methodsCredibility, confirmability
Peer debriefingA disinterested colleague questions the analysisCredibility
Negative case analysisSeeking cases that do not fit and revising until the analysis covers themCredibility
Member checking (respondent validation)Taking data or findings back to participants for comment; Lincoln and Guba called it the most crucial technique for credibilityCredibility
Thick descriptionRich detail on setting, participants and contextTransferability
Audit trail / inquiry auditA full record of data, notes, coding decisions and memos that an outsider can followDependability, confirmability
Reflexivity and bracketingA reflexive journal on how the researcher shapes the study; in descriptive phenomenology, setting assumptions asideConfirmability

Triangulation. Norman K. Denzin (The Research Act, 1970; the 1978 second edition is the one usually cited) distinguished four types: data triangulation (several sources, varied by time, space and person: patients, carers and nurses on the same ward in different months); investigator triangulation (several researchers code the data); theory triangulation (reading the data through more than one theory, say stigma theory and explanatory models); and methodological triangulation (several methods, within one method type or between methods: interviews plus observation plus case-record review). The idea is older and quantitative: Donald Campbell and Donald Fiske's (1959) case for measuring every construct by more than one method (multiple operationism, the logic of the multitrait-multimethod matrix in section 15.3).

The inter-coder agreement debate. Approaches that treat coding as measurement (quantitative content analysis, codebook TA) report agreement statistics such as kappa. Interpretive approaches (reflexive TA, IPA, constructivist grounded theory) reject them: agreement may only mean shared bias, and one analyst's interpretation is legitimate if transparent and well evidenced. A common middle path is to double-code part of the data and discuss disagreements, without a coefficient. Member checking has critics too: participants may reasonably reject an interpretation pitched at a level they were never asked to reach.

Other frameworks and reporting. Clinical psychologists also meet Lucy Yardley's (2000) four principles (sensitivity to context; commitment and rigour; transparency and coherence; impact and importance) and Robert Elliott, Constance Fischer and David Rennie's (1999) publication guidelines. COREQ (Allison Tong, Peter Sainsbury and Jonathan Craig, 2007) is a 32-item checklist for interview and focus-group studies in three domains: research team and reflexivity, study design, and analysis and findings. SRQR (Bridget O'Brien and colleagues, 2014) has 21 items and covers all qualitative designs. They sit alongside CONSORT and PRISMA (section 25).

Trustworthiness traps. Learn the pairs as a block: credibility–internal validity, transferability–external validity, dependability–reliability, confirmability–objectivity. Member checking serves credibility; thick description transferability; the audit trail dependability and confirmability. Transferability is judged by the reader, not proved by the researcher. Denzin's four triangulations are data, investigator, theory, methodological.

24.13 Mixed-methods research

Mixed-methods research collects and analyses both quantitative and qualitative data in one study or programme and integrates them, so the combination answers the question better than either alone. Integration is the defining feature: a survey and some interviews reported in separate chapters is a multimethod study, not a mixed-methods one. The usual philosophical justification is pragmatism: the question, not a paradigm, decides the methods.

John W. Creswell and Vicki L. Plano Clark, Designing and Conducting Mixed Methods Research (2007; second edition 2011; third 2018), gave the standard classification. The 2007 edition named four designs (triangulation, embedded, explanatory, exploratory); 2011 named six (convergent parallel, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential, embedded, transformative, multiphase); 2018 reduced the core to three (convergent, explanatory sequential, exploratory sequential), treating the rest as complex designs built on them.

Why mix. The original rationale was triangulation: if methods with different weaknesses converge, the answer is more trustworthy. That is Campbell and Fiske's multiple operationism (section 15.3) applied to whole methods. Jennifer Greene, Valerie Caracelli and Wendy Graham (1989) listed five purposes: triangulation (convergence), complementarity (elaboration), development (one method informs the next, as in building a questionnaire), initiation (finding paradoxes that reframe the question) and expansion (breadth).

Notation. Janice Morse (1991) introduced the shorthand: capitals (QUAN, QUAL) mark the dominant strand, lower case (quan, qual) a supplementary one; + means concurrent and → sequential. Later writers added brackets, as in QUAN(qual), for an embedded strand.

DesignNotationPurposeClinical example
Convergent (parallel), once called the "triangulation design"QUAN + QUALCollect both at the same time, usually with equal priority, and compare or merge themIn a trial of yoga for depression, BDI-II scores and interviews about change are collected at the same follow-up and compared
Explanatory sequentialQUAN → qualNumbers first; interviews then explain the results, especially surprising onesA survey of 600 students finds that those with high PHQ-9 scores rarely use the counselling centre; interviews with 15 explain why
Exploratory sequentialQUAL → quanExplore first; then build and test an instrument or intervention, or test how far the findings generaliseCarer interviews generate items for a culturally grounded burden scale, which a large sample then validates (section 15)
EmbeddedQUAN(qual)A supplementary strand inside a design driven by the other, for a question the main design cannot answerInterviews with patients and lay counsellors before, during and after a randomised trial of a lay-counsellor therapy
Transformative, multiphase (2011)AnyA social-justice framing; or a linked programme of studies over yearsDeveloping, piloting and evaluating a district suicide-prevention programme
Mixed-methods traps. (1) Explanatory = quantitative first (QUAN → qual); exploratory = qualitative first (QUAL → quan), usually to build a tool. Students swap these every year. (2) Capitals mean priority; the arrow means order. (3) Convergent designs are concurrent. (4) Two methods without integration is not mixed methods. (5) The paradigm is pragmatism.
Recap of section 24: qualitative research studies meaning, experience, process and context through words and observation; it is inductive, naturalistic, idiographic and emergent, with the researcher as instrument, in the constructivist paradigm. It samples information-rich cases purposively (maximum variation, homogeneous, typical, extreme, critical, criterion, snowball) or theoretically, and stops at saturation, never at a power-analysis number. Data come from in-depth interviews, focus groups (Merton and Kendall 1946; about 6 to 10 people and a moderator), participant observation, documents, photovoice and diaries, coded into categories and themes with memos. Phenomenology (Husserl's bracketing; Heidegger's hermeneutics; Giorgi; Colaizzi's seven steps) seeks the essence of lived experience; IPA (Smith 1996) interprets it through a double hermeneutic, idiographically. Grounded theory (Glaser and Strauss 1967) generates theory by constant comparison and theoretical sampling, coding open → axial → selective (Strauss and Corbin 1990) around a core category; Charmaz (2006) made it constructivist. Ethnography (Malinowski) studies a culture through fieldwork, emic and etic views (Pike 1954) and thick description (Geertz 1973, after Ryle); case studies follow Yin or Stake (intrinsic, instrumental, collective); narrative research keeps stories whole. CA (Sacks, Schegloff, Jefferson) studies turn-taking and adjacency pairs; DA (Potter and Wetherell 1987) studies what talk does; Garfinkel ran breaching experiments. Thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke 2006) has six recursive phases; content analysis (Berelson 1952) counts manifest content; framework analysis (Ritchie and Spencer 1994) charts a matrix; action research (Kurt Lewin 1946) spirals through plan, act, observe, reflect. Trustworthiness (Lincoln and Guba 1985): credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability parallel internal validity, external validity, reliability and objectivity, earned by prolonged engagement, triangulation (Denzin: data, investigator, theory, methodological), member checking, thick description and audit trails; COREQ has 32 items. Mixed methods (Creswell and Plano Clark): convergent QUAN + QUAL, explanatory QUAN → qual, exploratory QUAL → quan, embedded QUAN(qual).

25 Clinical trials, evidence and meta-analysis

Sections 19 and 20 showed that only a true experiment, with random assignment and a control group, can settle a causal question. This section carries that logic into the clinic. When the causal question is "does this treatment work?", the experiment has a special name, the randomised controlled trial, with its own rules for allocation, blinding, analysis and reporting. Then we climb a level. No single trial settles anything, so we need ways of combining trials (systematic review and meta-analysis), of ranking kinds of evidence (the evidence pyramid and evidence-based practice), and of noticing when the published record itself is distorted (publication bias and the replication crisis).

25.1 The randomised controlled trial and where it came from

A randomised controlled trial (RCT) is a true experiment run on patients. Eligible people are recruited, randomly allocated either to the treatment being tested or to a comparison condition, followed for a fixed period, and compared on an outcome that was named in advance (the primary outcome). Each ingredient answers a threat to internal validity from section 19: the control group answers history, maturation, testing and regression to the mean; randomisation answers selection; blinding answers expectancy and experimenter bias; a pre-named outcome answers the temptation to report whichever measure happened to look good.

Why the RCT is the gold standard for treatment questions. Patients improve for many reasons that have nothing to do with treatment: spontaneous remission, regression to the mean (people enrol when they are at their worst), placebo and expectancy, the attention of a kind clinician, life events. An uncontrolled before-and-after study cannot separate these from the treatment. A control group experiences all of them too, so the difference between arms isolates the treatment. Random allocation then makes the arms comparable on every characteristic, measured or unmeasured, so a difference at the end can be blamed on the treatment and not on who received it. No statistical adjustment can do that for confounders nobody measured, which is why observational designs sit lower in the hierarchy of evidence (25.10).

A controlled comparison: James Lind, 1747

On 20 May 1747, aboard the warship HMS Salisbury, the Scottish naval surgeon James Lind took 12 sailors with scurvy whose cases were "as similar as I could have them" and gave six pairs six different remedies: cider, elixir of vitriol, vinegar, sea water, a spicy medicinal paste, or two oranges and a lemon a day. The citrus pair recovered fastest; one was fit for duty within six days. He published it in A Treatise of the Scurvy (1753). This is the classic first controlled clinical trial: similar patients, treatments compared at the same time, under the same conditions. It was not randomised, and each arm had two people.

The first modern RCT: the Medical Research Council streptomycin trial, 1948

The trial usually called the first properly randomised controlled trial is the British Medical Research Council (MRC) trial of streptomycin for pulmonary tuberculosis, published in the British Medical Journal in 1948, whose design came from the statistician Austin Bradford Hill. Streptomycin was in very short supply after the war, so withholding it from a control group was judged ethically acceptable. 107 patients were analysed: 55 received streptomycin plus bed rest and 52 bed rest alone. Allocation came from random sampling numbers kept in sealed envelopes, opened only after a patient had been accepted into the trial (allocation concealment, 25.2), and the radiologists who read the chest X-rays did not know which arm a film came from (blinded outcome assessment). At six months, 4 of 55 streptomycin patients had died (7%) against 14 of 52 controls (27%).

Sir Austin Bradford Hill (1897–1991) also gave epidemiology its criteria for causation from observational data (1965; section 21). The MRC's 1944 patulin trial for the common cold is sometimes called the first double-blind controlled trial, but it allocated by rotation, not randomisation. For the exam: Lind 1747 = first controlled trial; MRC streptomycin 1948 = first modern randomised trial.
Analogue research is not a clinical trial. An analogue study tests a treatment on healthy or sub-clinical volunteers who stand in for patients, for example snake-fearful undergraduates in a study of exposure therapy for phobia. It gives tight control and easy recruitment, at the cost of external validity: mild fear in a student is not a clinical phobia. Papers ask "analogue research involves...": the answer is research on non-clinical populations.

25.2 Randomisation, allocation concealment and blinding

Do not confuse random assignment (who gets which condition; protects internal validity) with random sampling (who gets into the study; protects external validity, section 7.2). Trials almost never sample randomly from the population of patients, but they always assign randomly. There are several ways to generate the allocation sequence.

MethodHow it worksStrengthWeakness
Simple randomisationEach participant is allocated independently by a computer-generated list or random number table (a coin toss in principle)Completely unpredictableIn small trials the arms can end up unequal in size or in key characteristics purely by chance (e.g. 14 vs 6 in a trial of 20)
Block randomisation (restricted)Allocate in blocks, e.g. blocks of 4 containing 2 A and 2 B in random order (AABB, ABAB, ABBA, BAAB, BABA, BBAA)Arms stay equal in size throughout recruitmentIf staff know the block size, the last allocation in each block is predictable; so block sizes are varied at random (4, 6, 8)
Stratified randomisationSeparate randomisation lists (usually blocked) within strata of a strong prognostic factor, e.g. severe vs moderate depression, or each trial siteGuarantees balance on the factors that matter mostOnly a few strata are practical; too many and the cells become nearly empty
Minimisation (Donald Taves, 1974)Each new participant goes to whichever arm would reduce the overall imbalance on several factors, often with a random elementBalances many factors at once in small trialsNot fully random; needs central software
Cluster randomisationWhole groups (schools, wards, villages, clinics) are randomised, not individualsPrevents contamination between arms; fits group-level interventionsNeeds many more participants (25.4)

Allocation concealment

A random sequence is useless if the person enrolling patients can see it coming. A psychiatrist who knows the next envelope says "CBT" may, without meaning to, enrol a more motivated patient now and hold a difficult one back for later. That is selection bias sneaking back in. Allocation concealment means keeping the upcoming assignment hidden from everyone involved in recruitment until the participant is irreversibly enrolled. Methods: central telephone or web randomisation, sequentially numbered opaque sealed envelopes, or identical pre-packed drug containers prepared by a pharmacy. Kenneth Schulz and colleagues (1995), examining 250 trials, found that trials with inadequate concealment exaggerated treatment effects (odds ratios) by about 41%, and trials with unclear concealment by about a third; lack of double-blinding exaggerated them by about 17%.

Allocation concealmentBlinding (masking)
WhenBefore and up to the moment of allocationAfter allocation, during treatment, assessment and analysis
PreventsSelection bias (who gets into which arm)Performance bias, detection (ascertainment) bias, expectancy effects
Always possible?Yes, in every trial, including surgery and psychotherapyNot always: a patient knows whether they are attending therapy

Blinding

LevelWho does not know the allocationWhat it controls
Open labelNobody is blindedNothing; common in psychotherapy and surgery trials
Single-blindUsually the participant (sometimes it means only the outcome assessor)Participant expectancy and placebo responding
Double-blindThe participant and those giving treatment and assessing outcomesExpectancy effects and experimenter (Rosenthal) bias; the standard for drug trials
Triple-blindParticipant, clinicians/assessors and the data analysts (sometimes the data monitoring committee)Also bias in analytic decisions
Psychotherapy trials cannot be truly double-blind. The therapist delivering CBT knows it is CBT, and the patient knows they are in therapy. What such trials can do is blind the outcome assessors (an independent rater who does not know the allocation, often called a "rater-blind" or "assessor-blind" design) and make the control condition credible enough that patients' expectations are similar (25.3). Because single-, double- and triple-blind are used inconsistently, CONSORT 2010 asks authors to state exactly who was blinded rather than use the labels. A drug trial may use an active placebo (a pill with similar side effects but no therapeutic action) so that dry mouth does not unblind the patients.
Concealment is not blinding. The papers' favourite distractor: "Allocation concealment refers to blinding the patient to the assigned arm." Wrong. Concealment hides the upcoming allocation from the recruiter before enrolment; blinding hides the actual allocation from participants, clinicians and assessors after it. And "double-blind controls for?": both participant expectancy and experimenter bias.

25.3 Control conditions in psychotherapy trials

In a drug trial the control is obvious: an identical-looking placebo pill. In psychotherapy there is no inert talk, so the choice of comparison condition decides what question the trial answers. The same therapy can look spectacular against a waitlist and unremarkable against a credible alternative, so always ask "compared with what?" before reading an effect size.

Control conditionWhat the control group getsWhat it controls forWeakness
No-treatmentAssessment onlyTime: spontaneous remission, maturation, history, testing, regression to the meanNo attention or expectancy control; ethically hard when people are suffering; controls may seek help elsewhere
Waitlist (wait-list)Treatment after the trial period, e.g. after 12 weeksSame as no-treatment; everyone is eventually treated, so it is easier to justify ethicallyNo control for attention or expectancy; waiting may make people passive, so waitlists inflate effect sizes; no long-term comparison possible
Treatment as usual (TAU) or enhanced usual careWhatever the service normally providesAnswers the practical question "better than what we already do?"TAU differs between sites and is often badly described
Attention-placebo / psychological placeboEqual time with a warm professional but without the supposed active ingredients: supportive listening, non-directive discussion, general educationNon-specific (common) factors: attention, expectancy, therapeutic alliance, hopeHard to make equally credible; a "placebo" conversation may itself help, which blurs the comparison
Pill placebo (with clinical management)Inert tablet and brief supportive check-insExpectancy and contact in drug or combined trialsOnly possible when a drug is in the design
Active comparator (comparative outcome design)An established treatment, e.g. CBT vs interpersonal therapy, or CBT vs fluoxetineAnswers "which works better?"Differences between real treatments are small, so very large samples (or a non-inferiority design, 25.4) are needed
Dismantling (component analysis)The full package vs the package minus a componentWhich ingredient is activeMany arms, large n
Additive (constructive) designExisting treatment vs existing treatment plus a new componentWhether the extra component adds anythingCeiling effects if the base treatment already works well
Parametric designDifferent amounts of the same treatment (8 vs 16 sessions)Dose-responseLarge n

The most cited dismantling study: Neil Jacobson and colleagues (1996) randomised 150 depressed outpatients to behavioural activation alone, behavioural activation plus work on automatic thoughts, or full cognitive therapy (Aaron Beck's package). Full cognitive therapy did no better than behavioural activation alone, at the end of treatment or at six-month follow-up. That single dismantling result is why behavioural activation became a stand-alone treatment, and why it is used by lay counsellors in low-resource settings including India.

What a waitlist does not control. A waitlist controls for the passage of time, nothing else. If CBT beats a waitlist, the cause could be CBT's specific techniques or simply attention, hope and a caring relationship. Only an attention-placebo or an active comparator separates specific from non-specific effects. Ethics of waitlist and placebo controls: section 26.

25.4 Trial architecture: parallel, crossover, cluster; superiority, non-inferiority, equivalence

Who gets what, and when

  • Parallel-group RCT: each participant receives one condition only, and the arms run side by side. The default design.
  • Crossover RCT: each participant receives both conditions in random order (AB or BA), usually with a washout period between them, so each person is their own control (the within-subjects logic of sections 9.4 and 20). It needs far fewer participants, but only works for stable, chronic conditions and treatments whose effects wear off. It fails when there are carryover effects, which is why it is unsuitable for psychotherapy: a skill learned in CBT does not "wash out". (A crossover run on one patient is the N-of-1 trial; section 22.)
  • Cluster RCT: intact groups are randomised. Use it when the intervention works at group level (a school anti-bullying programme), or when individuals in the same setting would contaminate each other. Example: the MANAS trial in Goa (Vikram Patel and colleagues, 2010) randomised 24 primary care facilities to a lay health counsellor-led stepped-care programme for depression and anxiety or to enhanced usual care. Because people within a cluster resemble each other, the sample must be inflated by the design effect = 1 + (m − 1) × ICC, where m is the cluster size and ICC the intra-cluster correlation; analysis must respect the clustering (multilevel models).
  • Factorial RCT: two treatments tested at once in a 2 × 2 design (e.g. CBT or not × antidepressant or placebo), giving main effects and their interaction from one trial (section 10).

What the trial is trying to show

A superiority trial asks whether the new treatment is better than the control; the null hypothesis is "no difference". But sometimes a new treatment does not need to be better, only not meaningfully worse, because it is cheaper, shorter, safer or easier to deliver: internet-delivered CBT compared with face-to-face CBT, or a lay counsellor compared with a psychologist. Then you run a non-inferiority trial. You fix in advance a non-inferiority margin Δ, the largest loss of effect you would accept, and you conclude non-inferiority if the whole 95% confidence interval for (new − standard) lies above −Δ. An equivalence trial asks for the whole interval to lie between −Δ and +Δ. The figure shows how the same logic yields five different verdicts.

Two surprises. First, "not significantly different" in a superiority trial does not show equivalence (absence of evidence is not evidence of absence; trial 4 in the figure is simply inconclusive). Second, in non-inferiority trials the intention-to-treat analysis (25.7) is not the conservative choice, because dropouts and crossovers make the arms look more alike, which favours a non-inferiority conclusion; so both intention-to-treat and per-protocol results are reported, and both must agree. CONSORT has a dedicated extension for non-inferiority and equivalence trials (2006, updated 2012) and another for cluster trials (2004, updated 2012).

25.5 Efficacy versus effectiveness: explanatory and pragmatic trials

Efficacy is whether a treatment works under ideal, tightly controlled conditions. Effectiveness is whether it works in routine practice, with ordinary clinicians and ordinary, comorbid patients. (Efficiency adds cost: does it work at an acceptable price? The three words come together in Archie Cochrane's 1972 book Effectiveness and Efficiency.) The distinction is internal versus external validity (section 19) applied to treatments.

Martin Seligman (1995), in "The effectiveness of psychotherapy: The Consumer Reports study", listed what makes a study an efficacy study: random assignment to treatment and control (including placebo) conditions; a manualised treatment delivered with fidelity checks; a fixed number of sessions; well-operationalised target outcomes; blind raters and diagnosticians; patients who meet criteria for a single diagnosed disorder, with comorbid cases excluded; and a fixed follow-up. Real therapy, he argued, is of flexible length, self-correcting and aimed at several problems at once; his own evidence, a magazine readers' survey, was criticised for having no control group.

PYQ pattern. "All of the following are characteristics of efficacy studies EXCEPT: therapist flexibility is encouraged." Flexibility is the hallmark of effectiveness research; efficacy research controls therapists with a manual.

The same contrast in trial language is explanatory versus pragmatic, a distinction made by Daniel Schwartz and Joseph Lellouch (1967). An explanatory trial asks "can this work?" (selected patients, expert therapists, strict protocol, placebo control). A pragmatic trial asks "does this work in real care?" (broad eligibility, usual clinicians, flexible delivery, usual-care comparison, patient-relevant outcomes, intention-to-treat analysis). Most trials sit somewhere between; the PRECIS-2 tool (2015) scores a trial on nine domains from 1 (very explanatory) to 5 (very pragmatic). MANAS, run in routine clinics with lay counsellors and an enhanced usual-care comparison, sits near the pragmatic end.

Efficacy (explanatory) trialEffectiveness (pragmatic) trial
QuestionCan it work under ideal conditions?Does it work in everyday practice?
PatientsHomogeneous, single diagnosis, comorbidity excludedWhoever presents, comorbidity included
TherapistsTrained experts, manual, fidelity monitoredRoutine clinicians, flexible delivery
ComparisonPlacebo or attention controlUsual care or another real treatment
StrengthHigh internal validityHigh external validity

25.6 Phases of drug trials, and regulation in India

Before any human receives a new molecule there is preclinical work in the laboratory and in animals (pharmacology, toxicology; the ethics of animal work are in section 26). Clinical development then runs in phases. The sizes below are the United States Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) descriptions, which Indian textbooks also use.

PhaseWho and how manyMain purpose
Phase 0 (exploratory, "microdosing")A handful of people (often fewer than 15); a tiny sub-therapeutic dose (under 1/100 of the expected therapeutic dose)Does the drug reach its target, and how does the body handle it (pharmacokinetics)? No therapeutic or safety claims. Introduced by the FDA's exploratory guidance of 2006; optional
Phase IAbout 20 to 100, usually healthy volunteers (patients for toxic drugs such as cancer chemotherapy)Safety, tolerability and dosage: the maximum tolerated dose, side effects, pharmacokinetics
Phase IIUp to several hundred patients with the conditionFirst evidence of efficacy, the best dose, and short-term side effects; often randomised and placebo-controlled
Phase IIIAbout 300 to 3,000 (or more) patients, often multicentreConfirmatory RCTs against placebo or the standard treatment; the basis for marketing approval
Phase IVThousands of patients in routine usePost-marketing surveillance: rare and long-term adverse effects, new populations, new indications
Why phase IV is essential. A phase III programme of 3,000 patients cannot reliably detect an adverse effect that strikes 1 in 10,000. By the "rule of three", to have a good chance of seeing even one event of incidence 1/n you need roughly 3n patients. Rare harms therefore surface only after approval, through pharmacovigilance (in India, the Pharmacovigilance Programme of India) and spontaneous reports.

The Indian framework

  • Regulator: the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO), headed by the Drugs Controller General of India (DCGI), under the Directorate General of Health Services, Ministry of Health and Family Welfare.
  • Law: the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019, notified on 19 March 2019 under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940. They replaced Schedule Y (and Part XA) of the Drugs and Cosmetics Rules, 1945, which governed trials before. They require ethics committee approval (committees themselves registered with the CDSCO; composition in section 26), informed consent, and compensation for trial-related injury.
  • Registration: the Clinical Trials Registry-India (CTRI), launched by the Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) on 20 July 2007, hosted at ICMR's National Institute of Medical Statistics. Registration became mandatory from 15 June 2009, and since 2018 CTRI accepts only prospective registration (before the first participant is enrolled). CTRI is a primary register of the World Health Organization's International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. Behavioural and psychotherapy trials in India are registered there too.
  • Why registration matters: a public, time-stamped record of planned outcomes and sample size exposes unpublished trials and switched outcomes (25.13, 25.15). Journal editors (ICMJE, 2004) made registration a condition of publication for trials starting from July 2005; the US registry is ClinicalTrials.gov.

25.7 Analysing a trial: intention-to-treat, per-protocol and attrition

People drop out of trials, stop attending, or switch to the other treatment. How you handle them changes the answer.

Intention-to-treat (ITT) analysis: every randomised participant is analysed in the group to which they were randomised, whether or not they received, completed or adhered to that treatment ("once randomised, always analysed"). Per-protocol (PP) analysis: only participants who completed the treatment as specified in the protocol are analysed. As-treated analysis: participants are analysed by the treatment they actually received. Completers analysis is a form of per-protocol analysis.
Why ITT is preferred. Randomisation makes the arms comparable only as randomised. Dropping people afterwards destroys that comparability, because the people who drop out of CBT (perhaps the most depressed, or the least motivated) differ from those who drop out of the control arm. A per-protocol analysis compares the survivors of one arm with the survivors of the other, which re-introduces selection bias and usually flatters the treatment. ITT preserves randomisation, is conservative (it tends to underestimate efficacy in a superiority trial), and is pragmatic: it estimates what happens when a clinic offers the treatment, which includes the people who will not complete it.

Worked example: how per-protocol flatters

Take the trial in the figure, with "response" (a 50% fall in symptom score) as the outcome. Among the 90 CBT patients with an outcome, 60 respond; among the 93 control patients with an outcome, 40 respond. A completers analysis gives 60/90 = 67% vs 40/93 = 43%, a difference of 24 percentage points. ITT keeps all 100 in each arm and, using the conservative rule that a missing outcome counts as non-response, gives 60/100 = 60% vs 40/100 = 40%, a difference of 20 points. The 10 people lost from the CBT arm did not vanish at random: they are probably not the success stories.

Missing data and LOCF

ITT needs an outcome for everyone, so missing values must be handled. The old method was last observation carried forward (LOCF): a participant who left at week 4 is assumed to stay at their week-4 score until the end. It is simple, but it assumes no change after dropout, which is rarely true (depression improves over time; dementia worsens), and it treats an imputed value as if it were real, making confidence intervals too narrow. A 2010 US National Research Council panel advised against LOCF unless its assumptions are justified. Preferred methods are multiple imputation (Donald Rubin, 1987) and mixed-effects (multilevel) models that use all available observations, plus sensitivity analyses.

Attrition (experimental mortality, section 19) threatens a trial in two ways. Overall attrition shrinks n and power and threatens generalisability; a common rule of thumb in evidence-based medicine treats under 5% loss as little cause for concern and over 20% as a serious threat. Differential attrition (different dropout rates or reasons in the two arms) is worse, because it breaks the comparability that randomisation created. CONSORT therefore requires the flow diagram above, with reasons at every stage.

25.8 How big is the benefit: absolute and relative risk, NNT

When the outcome is an event (relapse, remission, suicide attempt, hospital admission), results come from a 2 × 2 table, the same table used for relative risk and odds ratios in observational designs (section 21.6). In a trial the rates have these names:

  • CER, control event rate = events in control arm / n in control arm.
  • EER, experimental event rate = events in treatment arm / n in treatment arm.
  • Absolute risk reduction ARR = CER − EER (also called the risk difference).
  • Relative risk (risk ratio) RR = EER / CER; relative risk reduction RRR = (CER − EER) / CER = 1 − RR.
  • Number needed to treat NNT = 1 / ARR, always rounded up to the next whole number: the number of patients you must treat, instead of giving the control, for one additional patient to benefit (or for one additional bad outcome to be prevented). Ideal NNT = 1; larger is worse.
  • Number needed to harm NNH = 1 / absolute risk increase of an adverse effect.
Andreas Laupacis, David Sackett and Robin Roberts introduced the number needed to treat in the New England Journal of Medicine in 1988, precisely because relative measures made treatments sound more impressive than they were for the individual patient.

Fully worked example

Four hundred people who have recovered from a depressive episode are randomised: 200 to maintenance CBT, 200 to treatment as usual. Over one year, 50 CBT patients relapse and 80 TAU patients relapse.

RelapsedDid not relapseTotalEvent rate
Maintenance CBT50150200EER = 50/200 = 0.25
Treatment as usual80120200CER = 80/200 = 0.40
  1. ARR = 0.40 − 0.25 = 0.15: CBT prevents relapse in 15 of every 100 patients treated.
  2. RR = 0.25 / 0.40 = 0.625; RRR = 0.15 / 0.40 = 0.375, "CBT cuts relapse by 37.5%".
  3. NNT = 1 / 0.15 = 6.67, rounded up to 7: treat seven patients with maintenance CBT to prevent one relapse that would otherwise have happened.
  4. Odds ratio (for comparison): odds of relapse with CBT = 50/150 = 0.333; with TAU = 80/120 = 0.667; OR = 0.333/0.667 = 0.50. Notice the OR (0.50) looks more dramatic than the RR (0.625); the two are close only when the event is rare.
Why the absolute figure matters. Now suppose a different outcome, suicide attempts, falls from 0.8% to 0.5% with a new treatment. The RRR is again (0.008 − 0.005)/0.008 = 37.5%, identical to the example above. But ARR = 0.003, so NNT = 1/0.003 = 333.3, rounded up to 334. Same relative reduction, a fifty-fold difference in how many people must be treated. Relative risk reductions are what advertisements quote; NNT and ARR are what a clinician needs. For harms the logic reverses: if a drug causes sexual dysfunction in 30% of patients against 10% on placebo, the absolute risk increase is 0.20 and the NNH = 5.
Clinical versus statistical significance. A p value says only whether an effect is unlikely to be zero; with 5,000 patients a trivial difference of one point on a 52-point depression scale can reach p < .001. Clinical significance asks whether the change matters to the patient's life: the effect size (Cohen's d and its benchmarks, section 8.7), the NNT, and at the level of the individual patient, whether they changed reliably and moved into the functional range (the reliable change index and clinical significance criteria of Neil Jacobson and Paula Truax, 1991, section 22).

25.9 Reporting a trial: CONSORT and the family of reporting guidelines

Readers can only judge a trial if it is reported completely: how the sequence was generated, whether it was concealed, who was blinded, how many dropped out and why. Surveys in the early 1990s found that most published trials omitted these basics, so editors and methodologists wrote checklists. CONSORT (Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials) was first published in 1996 (Colin Begg and colleagues, JAMA), revised in 2001, and revised again as CONSORT 2010, a 25-item checklist plus a four-stage flow diagram (enrolment, allocation, follow-up, analysis; the figure in 25.7). An update, CONSORT 2025, was published on 14 April 2025 simultaneously in several major journals, with a 30-item checklist and the flow diagram; older textbooks and most question banks still quote "CONSORT 2010, 25 items". CONSORT is a reporting standard: it tells you how to write a trial up, not how to design or conduct it.

CONSORT spawned a family, collected by the EQUATOR Network (Enhancing the QUAlity and Transparency Of health Research, launched 2008). The exam skill is matching the acronym to the design.

GuidelineFor which kind of studyYear(s) and size
CONSORTRandomised controlled trials1996, 2001, 2010 (25 items), 2025 (30 items)

A randomised trial of yoga vs waitlist for anxietyCONSORT
A systematic review and meta-analysis of CBT for insomniaPRISMA (register the protocol on PROSPERO)
The protocol of a trial not yet startedSPIRIT

25.10 Evidence-based practice and the hierarchy of evidence

The term evidence-based medicine was coined by Gordon Guyatt (1991, in the ACP Journal Club; the Evidence-Based Medicine Working Group's manifesto followed in JAMA in 1992), at McMaster University in Canada, where David Sackett led the movement. The definition every paper quotes is from Sackett and colleagues (1996) in the BMJ:

Evidence-based medicine is "the conscientious, explicit, and judicious use of current best evidence in making decisions about the care of individual patients." In the 2000 edition of their book, Sackett and colleagues widened it to "the integration of best research evidence with clinical expertise and patient values": the three-circle model. Best research evidence + clinical expertise + patient values and preferences, with the decision in the overlap. It is not "do whatever the RCTs say".

For psychology, the American Psychological Association adopted a policy in August 2005, published with the report of its Presidential Task Force in the American Psychologist in 2006: evidence-based practice in psychology (EBPP) is "the integration of the best available research with clinical expertise in the context of patient characteristics, culture, and preferences." Note the APA wording: patient characteristics, culture and preferences in place of Sackett's "patient values".

Empirically supported treatments (Division 12)

Before that, APA's Division 12 (Society of Clinical Psychology) set up a Task Force on Promotion and Dissemination of Psychological Procedures, appointed in 1993 by David Barlow and chaired by Dianne Chambless. Its 1995 report listed "empirically validated treatments", later renamed empirically supported treatments (ESTs), in two tiers:

  • Well-established: at least two good between-group experiments, by different investigating teams, showing the treatment superior to pill or psychological placebo or to another treatment, or equivalent to an already established treatment in adequately powered studies; or a large series of single-case experiments (n > 9) with good designs. Also required: a treatment manual and clearly specified sample characteristics.
  • Probably efficacious: two experiments showing the treatment superior to a waitlist control; or experiments meeting the well-established criteria but all from one team (no independent replication); or a small series of single-case experiments (n ≥ 3).
Label variant. In their 1998 paper "Defining empirically supported therapies", Dianne Chambless and Steven Hollon used different labels: efficacious and specific (beats placebo or an alternative treatment in independent replications), efficacious, and possibly efficacious (one supporting study, or replication only by the same team). If a question offers "well-established vs probably efficacious", it is the Task Force (Chambless and colleagues, 1995 and 1998 updates; reviewed by Chambless and Thomas Ollendick, 2001). The key idea in both: beating a waitlist is weaker evidence than beating a placebo or another real treatment.

The hierarchy (pyramid) of evidence

For questions about whether a treatment works, study designs can be ranked by how well they protect against bias. Formal levels of evidence go back to the Canadian Task Force on the Periodic Health Examination (1979); the Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine published widely used levels from 1998 (revised 2009 and 2011).

The criticisms are standard short-answer material:

  • Design is not quality. A small, unblinded RCT with 40% attrition can be worse evidence than a large, careful cohort study. The GRADE system (2004; Gordon Guyatt and colleagues, 2008) starts RCT evidence as "high" and observational evidence as "low", then downgrades for risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias, and upgrades for large effects or dose-response.
  • The right design depends on the question. For prognosis the cohort is best; for rare harms, case-control studies and phase IV surveillance; for lived experience, qualitative research (section 24), which the pyramid ignores.
  • External validity. RCT samples are selected and homogeneous (25.5). And some questions cannot be randomised (the harm of smoking or of childhood abuse).
  • A meta-analysis at the top is only as good as what goes in (garbage in, garbage out; 25.14).

25.11 Systematic reviews and meta-analysis: what they are and where they came from

Narrative (traditional) reviewSystematic review
QuestionBroad, often unstatedFocused, stated in advance (PICO)
SearchWhatever the author knows or choosesComprehensive, documented, reproducible; several databases plus unpublished ("grey") literature
SelectionUnstated; open to biasExplicit inclusion criteria applied by two reviewers independently
AppraisalVariableFormal risk-of-bias assessment of every study
SynthesisQualitative, often "vote counting" (how many studies were significant)Quantitative (meta-analysis) where possible
A systematic review is a review that uses explicit, pre-specified, reproducible methods to find, select, appraise and synthesise all the studies on one question. A meta-analysis is the statistical part: combining the effect sizes of those studies into one weighted estimate. A systematic review need not include a meta-analysis (studies may be too different to pool); a meta-analysis should sit inside a systematic review.

The steps

  1. Frame the question as PICO: Population (adults with insomnia), Intervention (CBT for insomnia), Comparison (sleep hygiene education or waitlist), Outcome (sleep efficiency). PICOS adds Study design (RCTs only).
  2. Write and register a protocol (on PROSPERO, the international register of systematic review protocols, launched in 2011, or as a Cochrane protocol) so that the methods cannot be changed after seeing the results.
  3. Search several databases (PubMed/MEDLINE, PsycINFO, Embase, the Cochrane CENTRAL register), trial registries and grey literature, without language restrictions where possible.
  4. Screen titles and abstracts, then full texts, with two reviewers working independently and their agreement checked (Cohen's kappa, section 15.2). The numbers at each stage go into the PRISMA flow diagram.
  5. Extract data on standard forms (n, means, SDs, events).
  6. Assess risk of bias in each study: sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting (the Cochrane risk-of-bias tool, RoB 2 for randomised trials; ROBINS-I for non-randomised studies).
  7. Synthesise: meta-analysis if the studies are similar enough, otherwise a structured narrative synthesis.
  8. Rate the certainty of the evidence (GRADE) and report with PRISMA.
Archibald (Archie) Cochrane (1909–1988), a British epidemiologist, argued in Effectiveness and Efficiency (1972) that health care should rest on randomised trials, and criticised medicine for having no organised, updated summaries of all relevant trials. Iain Chalmers answered: the Cochrane Collaboration was founded in 1993 (named in Cochrane's honour; renamed simply "Cochrane" in 2015) and publishes the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. Its logo is a forest plot of seven trials of corticosteroids for women about to deliver prematurely, a life-saving treatment whose benefit a timely meta-analysis would have shown years earlier.
Gene V. Glass coined the word "meta-analysis" in 1976, in his presidential address to the American Educational Research Association ("Primary, secondary, and meta-analysis of research"): the analysis of analyses. Its most famous early use was psychological. Hans Eysenck (1952), in "The effects of psychotherapy: an evaluation", had claimed that roughly two-thirds of neurotic patients improve within two years whether or not they receive psychotherapy, citing improvement rates of about 44% with psychoanalysis, 64% with eclectic therapy and 72% with custodial or general-practitioner care. Mary Lee Smith and Gene Glass (1977), in "Meta-analysis of psychotherapy outcome studies", pooled 375 controlled studies yielding 833 effect sizes and found an average effect size of 0.68: the average treated client was better off than about 75% of untreated controls (because 0.68 SD above the control mean lies at the 75th percentile of the normal curve, section 6). The extended book by Smith, Glass and Thomas Miller, The Benefits of Psychotherapy (1980), pooled 475 studies, average effect about 0.85 (better off than about 80%). Eysenck replied in 1978 that meta-analysis was "an exercise in mega-silliness".

25.12 Pooling: effect sizes, weights, fixed and random effects, heterogeneity

Step 1: a common effect size

Studies use different scales (BDI, HAM-D, PHQ-9), so each result is converted to a standardised effect size (section 8.7): Cohen's d = (Mtreatment − Mcontrol) / SDpooled; Hedges' g, the same with a correction for small-sample bias (Larry Hedges, 1981); Glass's Δ, which divides by the control group's SD (Glass's own choice, since treatment can change the spread); r for correlational studies; and the odds ratio or risk ratio for event outcomes (pooled on the log scale). They can be converted into one another, e.g. for equal groups r = d / √(d² + 4).

Step 2: weight by precision (inverse variance)

A study of 240 people estimates the effect more precisely than a study of 40, so it should count for more. The standard weight is the inverse of the variance of the study's effect size: w = 1 / v = 1 / SE². For d, v = (n₁ + n₂)/(n₁n₂) + d²/[2(n₁ + n₂)]. The pooled effect is the weighted mean, d̄ = Σwd / Σw, with standard error 1/√Σw.

From the forest plot below: Study A has n = 20 + 20 and d = 1.12, so v = 40/400 + 1.2544/80 = 0.100 + 0.016 = 0.116 and w = 8.64. Study D has n = 120 + 118 and d = 0.31, so v = 238/14,160 + 0.0961/476 = 0.0168 + 0.0002 = 0.0170 and w = 58.79. Study D counts almost seven times as much as Study A. Summing over all seven studies, Σw = 186.25 and the pooled d = 0.47, SE = 1/√186.25 = 0.073, so the 95% CI is 0.47 ± 1.96 × 0.073 = 0.33 to 0.62.

Step 3: fixed effect or random effects?

A fixed-effect model assumes all studies estimate one true effect, and that they differ only by sampling error. A random-effects model (the standard method is that of Rebecca DerSimonian and Nan Laird, 1986) assumes the true effects themselves vary from study to study (different populations, therapists, doses), forming a distribution with mean μ and between-study variance τ². Each weight becomes 1/(v + τ²), which gives small studies relatively more weight and a wider confidence interval: it estimates the average effect across a range of settings. In psychology, where no two trials are identical, random effects is usually the honest choice. For the seven studies below, τ² = 0.040, and the random-effects estimate is d = 0.50 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.72), against the fixed-effect 0.47 (0.33 to 0.62).

Step 4: heterogeneity

Are the studies telling the same story? Cochran's Q (William Cochran, 1954) is the weighted sum of squared deviations of each study from the pooled estimate, Q = Σw(d − d̄)², tested as chi-square on k − 1 df. With few studies Q has low power, so I² (Julian Higgins and Simon Thompson, 2002) is reported as well: the percentage of the total variation across studies that is due to real heterogeneity rather than chance.

I² = (Q − df) / Q × 100%, set to 0 if negative. Benchmarks from Julian Higgins, Simon Thompson, Jonathan Deeks and Douglas Altman (2003), which they called tentative: about 25% low, 50% moderate, 75% high heterogeneity. Heterogeneity is then explored with subgroup analysis or meta-regression on moderators (therapist training, severity, control type).

In this example Q = 12.00 on 6 df gives p = .06, not significant, yet I² = (12.00 − 6)/12.00 = 50%, moderate heterogeneity. That is the low power of Q in action, and the reason I² is always reported.

How to read a forest plot

  • Each row is one study. The square marks its effect size; the square's area is proportional to its weight; the horizontal line is its 95% confidence interval.
  • The vertical line of no effect is at 0 for d, g and risk differences, and at 1 for odds ratios and risk ratios. A study whose CI crosses that line is not significant on its own (Study E).
  • The diamond is the pooled estimate: its centre is the pooled effect, its width the pooled CI. If the diamond does not touch the line of no effect, the pooled effect is significant.
  • Small studies have long lines (Study A); large studies have short lines and big squares (Study D). Here five of the seven individual studies are significant, but the pooled estimate is far more precise than any of them: that is the point of meta-analysis.

25.13 Publication bias: the file drawer, the funnel plot, Egger's test, trim and fill

A meta-analysis can only pool studies it can find. Studies with significant, positive results are more likely to be submitted, accepted, published quickly, published in English and cited. Studies with null results more often stay unpublished. The published literature is therefore a biased sample of the research that was actually done, and the pooled effect is inflated. Related distortions: outcome reporting bias (within a study, only the outcomes that "worked" are reported), time-lag bias, language bias and citation bias.

Robert Rosenthal (1979), in "The file drawer problem and tolerance for null results", put the extreme form vividly: journals filled with the 5% of studies that are Type I errors, while the file drawers back in the lab hold the 95% that found nothing. His remedy was the fail-safe N: the number of unpublished null studies that would have to be sitting in file drawers to make the combined result non-significant. If that number is large (Rosenthal suggested larger than 5k + 10, where k is the number of studies), the finding is judged robust. Robert Orwin (1983) gave a version based on effect sizes. The fail-safe N is now considered weak: it assumes the missing studies average exactly zero, and it does not estimate the bias.

The funnel plot

A funnel plot (popularised by Richard Light and David Pillemer, 1984) is a scatter of each study's effect size (x-axis) against its precision, usually its standard error, with the most precise studies at the top. Large studies cluster tightly near the true effect; small studies scatter widely, equally on both sides. With no bias the cloud looks like an inverted, symmetrical funnel. If small studies with small or negative effects are missing, a corner of the funnel is empty and the plot is asymmetric.

The simulation behind the figure: 34 trials of varying size were generated with a true effect of d = 0.40. In panel A all 34 are visible: the fixed-effect pooled d is 0.38, close to the truth, and Egger's test finds no asymmetry (intercept −0.16, p = .72). In panel B, 19 of the 34 (non-significant, smaller trials) were "never published". The remaining 15 give a pooled d of 0.46, Egger's intercept is 1.91 (p < .01), and the simple average of the published effects is 0.53 against 0.37 for all trials run. The dashed lines are the pseudo-95% confidence limits, d̄ ± 1.96 × SE: about 95% of studies should fall inside them if there is no bias and no heterogeneity.

  • Egger's regression test (Matthias Egger, George Davey Smith and colleagues, 1997) puts a number on asymmetry: regress each study's standardised effect (d/SE) on its precision (1/SE). With no small-study bias the line passes through the origin; an intercept significantly different from zero signals asymmetry.
  • Trim and fill (Sue Duval and Richard Tweedie, 2000) estimates how many studies are missing, "trims" the asymmetric small studies to find the true centre, then "fills" in their mirror images on the empty side and recomputes the pooled effect.
  • Caution: asymmetry is a small-study effect, not proof of publication bias. Small trials may genuinely find bigger effects (more severe or more selected patients, more enthusiastic investigators, lower quality), and real heterogeneity or chance can also produce it. Funnel tests have little power with fewer than about 10 studies.

25.14 The Dodo bird verdict, and the criticisms of meta-analysis

In 1936 Saul Rosenzweig, in "Some implicit common factors in diverse methods of psychotherapy", argued that very different therapies seem to work about equally well because they share common factors (a relationship, an explanation, a hopeful healer). He borrowed a line from the Dodo in Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, who judges a race and declares: "Everybody has won, and all must have prizes." In 1975 Lester Luborsky, Barton Singer and Lise Luborsky reviewed comparative studies of psychotherapies ("Is it true that 'everyone has won and all must have prizes'?") and found that most comparisons showed no significant difference: the Dodo bird verdict. Bruce Wampold and colleagues' 1997 meta-analysis of direct comparisons between bona fide therapies found differences close to zero, and Wampold's The Great Psychotherapy Debate (2001) built a contextual model in which common factors (alliance, empathy, expectations, a credible rationale) do most of the work, an idea rooted in Jerome Frank's Persuasion and Healing (1961) and Edward Bordin's (1979) working alliance.

The counter-position, from the empirically supported treatments movement: specific treatments matter for specific disorders (exposure for obsessive-compulsive disorder, phobias and PTSD); comparative trials are too small to detect modest differences; and researcher allegiance colours comparative results. Exams ask for the verdict itself: different bona fide therapies tend to produce roughly equivalent outcomes, attributed to common factors such as the therapeutic alliance and empathy.

Do not confuse two "1950s to 1970s" debates. Hans Eysenck (1952) asked whether psychotherapy works at all (spontaneous remission); Smith and Glass (1977) answered with meta-analysis: yes, d ≈ 0.68. The Dodo bird verdict asks whether one therapy works better than another; Rosenzweig (1936) and Luborsky and colleagues (1975) answered: mostly not. (A parallel to Eysenck in social work: Joel Fischer's 1973 review "Is casework effective?" concluded that it had not been shown to be.)

The standard criticisms of meta-analysis

CriticismWhat it saysStandard reply
Apples and orangesIt mixes studies too different to combine: different therapies, patients, outcome measuresDefine the question and the inclusion criteria tightly; test whether the differences matter with subgroup analysis and meta-regression (if the question is about fruit, pooling apples and oranges is legitimate)
Garbage in, garbage outPooling many poor studies gives a precise but wrong answer (Eysenck's "mega-silliness" objection)Rate every study's risk of bias; run sensitivity analyses with only high-quality studies; GRADE the certainty
File drawer / publication biasThe studies found are a biased sample of those doneSearch grey literature and registries; funnel plot, Egger's test, trim and fill (25.13)
Non-independenceOne study contributes several effect sizes (Smith and Glass had 833 from 375 studies), over-weighting itOne effect per study, or multilevel (three-level) meta-analysis
Ecological (aggregation) fallacyA moderator that explains differences between studies need not apply to individualsIndividual participant data meta-analysis

25.15 The replication crisis and open science

John Ioannidis (2005) had argued in "Why most published research findings are false" that small studies, small effects and flexible analyses make most significant findings in some fields false positives. Then, in 2011, Daryl Bem published nine experiments in a leading social psychology journal claiming evidence of precognition using standard methods (if standard methods can "prove" the impossible, the methods are the problem); the fraud of Diederik Stapel came to light (section 26); and Joseph Simmons, Leif Nelson and Uri Simonsohn (2011), in "False-positive psychology", showed that combining a few common, undisclosed choices (which of two outcomes to report, adding participants after peeking, adding a covariate, dropping a condition) could raise the real false-positive rate from the nominal 5% to about 61%. They called this flexibility researcher degrees of freedom, and illustrated it with a real experiment "showing" that listening to "When I'm Sixty-Four" made people younger.

The Open Science Collaboration (2015), a project of some 270 researchers coordinated by Brian Nosek, published "Estimating the reproducibility of psychological science" in Science. They repeated 100 studies from three leading psychology journals (2008 issues). 97% of the original studies had significant results; only 36% of the replications did. The replications' mean effect size was about half the originals' (r = .20 vs .40); 47% of original effect sizes fell within the replication's 95% confidence interval, and 39% of effects were subjectively rated as replicated. The usual exam answer is "about 36% (roughly one-third) replicated".

Questionable research practices (QRPs)

PracticeWhat it is
p-hackingTrying analyses (outcomes, covariates, exclusions, transformations, subgroups) until p < .05, then reporting only that one
HARKing (Norbert Kerr, 1998)Hypothesising After the Results are Known: presenting a post hoc hypothesis as if it had been predicted in advance
Optional stoppingChecking significance as data come in and stopping when p dips below .05; each peek is another chance of a Type I error (section 8)
Selective reporting (outcome switching)Reporting only the measures, conditions or studies that "worked"; the within-study version of the file drawer
Flexible exclusion of outliersDeciding which participants to drop after seeing which choice gives significance
Rounding p valuesReporting p = .054 as "p < .05"

Leslie John, George Loewenstein and Drazen Prelec (2012) surveyed about 2,000 academic psychologists and found such practices were widespread and widely regarded as defensible. Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken (2013) added that p-hacking need not be deliberate: when analysis decisions depend on the data, a researcher who runs only one test is still walking a "garden of forking paths". QRPs are not fabrication (section 26), but they produce the same result: false findings in the literature.

The open-science remedies

  • Preregistration: a time-stamped, public plan written before data collection (hypotheses, sample size and stopping rule, primary outcome, analysis plan), on the Open Science Framework, AsPredicted, or for trials a registry such as CTRI or ClinicalTrials.gov. Deviations are allowed but must be declared, which kills HARKing and hidden p-hacking. Exploratory analyses remain welcome, labelled as exploratory.
  • Registered reports: the journal peer-reviews the introduction, methods and analysis plan before the data exist; if approved, it gives in-principle acceptance, and the paper is published whatever the results. This removes publication bias at source. First launched by the journal Cortex in 2013 (Chris Chambers).
  • Open data, materials and code, so others can check the analysis and repeat the study (APA Standard 8.14 already requires sharing data for verification, section 26).
  • Adequate power: a priori power analysis and larger samples (section 8), often through multi-site collaborations.
  • Replication: direct (exact, close) replication repeats the original procedure as closely as possible; conceptual replication tests the same hypothesis with different methods. A field needs both.
  • Institutions: the Center for Open Science (founded 2013 by Brian Nosek and Jeffrey Spies), the reporting guidelines of 25.9, and journals' transparency standards.
Recap of section 25: the RCT is the gold standard for treatment questions because random allocation balances known and unknown confounders and a control group absorbs remission, regression and expectancy; Lind (1747) ran the first controlled trial, the MRC streptomycin trial (1948, Bradford Hill) the first modern RCT. Allocation is simple, block or stratified; allocation concealment hides the next assignment from recruiters (prevents selection bias, always possible), blinding hides the actual assignment afterwards (single, double, triple; psychotherapy can blind only assessors). Waitlist and no-treatment controls control only for time, attention-placebo for common factors, active comparators answer "which is better"; dismantling removes a component (Jacobson 1996), additive designs add one. Designs: parallel, crossover (washout; fails with carryover), cluster (design effect), factorial; superiority vs non-inferiority (CI above −Δ) vs equivalence (CI within ±Δ); efficacy (explanatory, manualised) vs effectiveness (pragmatic; Martin Seligman 1995). Drug phases: 0 microdose, I safety and dose in healthy volunteers, II efficacy in patients, III confirmatory RCTs before approval, IV post-marketing surveillance; India: CDSCO/DCGI under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, registration on CTRI (ICMR 2007, mandatory 2009). Analyse by intention-to-treat; avoid LOCF. NNT = 1/ARR, rounded up; relative risk reductions flatter rare-event benefits. Report with CONSORT (2010: 25 items plus flow diagram; 2025: 30 items), PRISMA, STROBE, STARD, CARE, COREQ, SPIRIT, TREND, SCRIBE. Evidence-based practice (Sackett 1996) integrates research, clinical expertise and patient values (APA 2006); Division 12 ESTs are well-established or probably efficacious. Glass coined meta-analysis (1976); Smith and Glass (1977) answered Hans Eysenck (1952) with d = 0.68 from 375 studies. Pool by inverse-variance weights, fixed or random effects; heterogeneity by Q and I² (25/50/75%); read the forest plot's squares, CIs and diamond. Publication bias (Robert Rosenthal's file drawer, fail-safe N) shows as funnel asymmetry, tested by Egger's regression, corrected by trim and fill. Dodo bird verdict (Rosenzweig 1936; Luborsky 1975): bona fide therapies perform about equally. Replication crisis: 36% of 100 replications significant (Open Science Collaboration 2015), driven by p-hacking, HARKing (Kerr 1998), optional stopping and researcher degrees of freedom (Simmons, Nelson and Simonsohn 2011); remedies are preregistration, registered reports, open data and well-powered replication.

26 Research ethics

Every design in sections 18 to 25 involves doing something to people (or animals) for the sake of knowledge rather than for their own immediate good. Research ethics is the set of principles, codes and laws that decides when that is acceptable and on what conditions. It did not grow out of philosophy seminars; almost every rule in it was written in response to a specific scandal. So this section begins with the history, then distils the principles, then turns them into the practical questions an ethics committee will ask about your study: consent, deception, confidentiality, risk, inducements, fairness, animals, honesty in publication.

26.1 Why research ethics exists: the history

The Nazi experiments and the Nuremberg Code (1947)

During the Second World War, German physicians carried out lethal experiments on concentration camp prisoners: immersion in freezing water and exposure to simulated high altitude to study survival, deliberately infected wounds to test drugs, and twin studies at Auschwitz. At the Doctors' Trial in Nuremberg (United States v. Karl Brandt et al.), 23 defendants, most of them physicians, were tried; seven were executed. The verdict of August 1947 set out ten principles for permissible medical experiments, the Nuremberg Code, drawing partly on a memorandum by the American physician Leo Alexander.

The Nuremberg Code's ten points, in brief: (1) "The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential" (legal capacity, free choice without force or coercion, enough knowledge and understanding); (2) the experiment must yield results for the good of society unobtainable by other means; (3) it must rest on prior animal work and knowledge of the disease; (4) it must avoid all unnecessary physical and mental suffering; (5) no experiment where death or disabling injury is expected; (6) risk must never exceed the humanitarian importance of the problem; (7) proper preparations and facilities to protect the subject; (8) only scientifically qualified persons may conduct it; (9) the subject must be free to end the experiment at any time; (10) the scientist must stop if continuing is likely to cause injury, disability or death.

The Declaration of Helsinki (1964 onwards)

The Nuremberg Code was a court's verdict, and doctors outside Germany tended to treat it as a rule for barbarians, not for them. The medical profession's own statement came from the World Medical Association: the Declaration of Helsinki, adopted in June 1964 at its General Assembly in Helsinki. It distinguished research combined with patient care from non-therapeutic research, and it has been revised repeatedly: 1975 (Tokyo, which introduced review by an independent committee), 1983, 1989, 1996, 2000 (Edinburgh), 2008 (Seoul, which required trial registration), 2013 (Fortaleza), and most recently October 2024 (Helsinki), a revision that speaks of research "participants" rather than "subjects". Helsinki is the source of the rules on placebo controls (26.12) and on the primacy of the participant's welfare over the interests of science and society.

Tuskegee, the National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report (1979)

From 1932 to 1972 the US Public Health Service ran the "Tuskegee Study of Untreated Syphilis in the Negro Male" in Macon County, Alabama. About 600 poor Black men were enrolled, 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without. They were told they were being treated for "bad blood", were given free meals, transport and burial insurance, and were never told their diagnosis. When penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s, it was deliberately withheld, and the men were steered away from treatment, so that the natural course of the disease could be observed to death. A Public Health Service employee, Peter Buxtun, raised objections internally for years; the story broke through the journalist Jean Heller of the Associated Press in July 1972, and the study ended that year. (US President Bill Clinton formally apologised in 1997.)

Public outrage produced the National Research Act (1974), which required institutional review of federally funded research and created the National Commission for the Protection of Human Subjects of Biomedical and Behavioral Research. The Commission's best-known product, named after the Belmont Conference Center in Maryland where it was drafted, is the Belmont Report: completed in 1978 and published in the US Federal Register in April 1979. Its three principles (26.2) became the basis of US regulation, codified in 1991 as the Common Rule (the Federal Policy for the Protection of Human Subjects, 45 CFR 46, adopted by 15 federal departments and agencies; revised version in force from January 2019). The Common Rule requires review by an institutional review board (IRB) of at least five members, including at least one scientist, one non-scientist and one member not affiliated with the institution.

Henry K. Beecher, a Harvard anaesthetist, showed in 1966 ("Ethics and clinical research", New England Journal of Medicine) that abuse was not confined to Nazis or to one government project: he described 22 ethically questionable studies published in mainstream journals by respected investigators. The international, developing-country perspective came from the Council for International Organizations of Medical Sciences (CIOMS), working with the World Health Organization: proposed guidelines in 1982, revised in 1993 and 2002, and replaced in 2016 by the International Ethical Guidelines for Health-related Research Involving Humans, with particular attention to research in low-resource settings.

26.2 The Belmont principles, and the ethical theories behind every code

The Belmont Report reduced the field to three principles, each with an application. This mapping is the single most examined fact in research ethics.

  • Respect for persons: two convictions. Individuals should be treated as autonomous agents, and persons with diminished autonomy (children, people with severe mental illness or dementia, prisoners) are entitled to protection. Application: informed consent, which Belmont says has three elements: information, comprehension and voluntariness.
  • Beneficence: two rules, "do not harm", and "maximise possible benefits and minimise possible harms". Application: a systematic assessment of risks and benefits, which the review committee checks.
  • Justice: fairness in who bears the burdens of research and who receives its benefits. Application: fair selection of subjects. Tuskegee is the textbook violation: the burdens fell on poor Black men, while the knowledge served others.

Four principles and two ethical theories

In the same year, Tom Beauchamp and James Childress published Principles of Biomedical Ethics (1979), which gave clinical ethics its four principles ("principlism"): respect for autonomy, non-maleficence (do no harm), beneficence (do good) and justice. The difference from Belmont is that beneficence is split into two. The ICMR's 2017 guidelines (26.4) use exactly these four. A frequent question asks which list is the "four pillars of principle-based ethics": beneficence, non-maleficence, justice and respect for autonomy (not "integrity", not "respect" alone).

ApproachCore ideaIn research ethics
Deontological (duty-based; Immanuel Kant)Some acts are right or wrong in themselves, whatever their consequences; people must never be used merely as a meansDeceiving or harming a participant is wrong even if the knowledge gained is valuable; the spirit of Diana Baumrind's (1964) critique of Stanley Milgram's obedience study (1963; 26.9)
Utilitarian / consequentialist (Jeremy Bentham, John Stuart Mill)The right act produces the greatest good for the greatest number: a cost-benefit judgementThe risk-benefit analysis of ethics committees; Milgram's own defence (valuable knowledge, little lasting harm)

26.3 Professional codes: the APA Ethics Code and the BPS

The American Psychological Association adopted its first ethics code in 1952, published in 1953 as Ethical Standards of Psychologists, the first such code in psychology and, unusually, built empirically from critical incidents that members described. The current version is the Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct, adopted in 2002 (effective June 2003) and amended in 2010 and 2016 (the 2016 amendment, effective January 2017, concerned Standard 3.04 and the prohibition on psychologists' participation in torture). A draft revised code was released for public comment in December 2024 but, as of this writing, the 2002 code with its 2010 and 2016 amendments remains in force.

Structure of the APA code. An introduction and preamble; five General Principles (A to E), which are aspirational (ideals, not enforceable rules); and ten sections of Ethical Standards, which are enforceable: 1 Resolving Ethical Issues, 2 Competence, 3 Human Relations, 4 Privacy and Confidentiality, 5 Advertising and Other Public Statements, 6 Record Keeping and Fees, 7 Education and Training, 8 Research and Publication, 9 Assessment, 10 Therapy.
General PrincipleMeaning
A. Beneficence and NonmaleficenceStrive to benefit those you work with and take care to do no harm; guard against misuse of your influence
B. Fidelity and ResponsibilityEstablish relationships of trust; be aware of professional and scientific responsibilities to society; manage conflicts of interest
C. IntegrityAccuracy, honesty and truthfulness in science, teaching and practice; where deception may be justified, a serious obligation to consider its consequences and correct mistrust
D. JusticeFairness: all persons are entitled to equal access to the benefits of psychology and to equal quality of processes and services
E. Respect for People's Rights and DignityPrivacy, confidentiality and self-determination; special safeguards for people whose capacity for autonomous decisions is impaired; respect for cultural and individual differences
Count and contents. "How many General Principles?" Five. "Which is NOT one of them?" Look for an intruder such as Equity, Competence or Confidentiality (competence and confidentiality are Standards 2 and 4, not General Principles). Note also that Principle A is one principle with two names, and E is "Respect for People's Rights and Dignity", not "autonomy".

Standard 8: Research and Publication

StandardTitleWhat it requires
8.01Institutional ApprovalObtain approval where required (IRB or ethics committee) and conduct the research as approved
8.02Informed Consent to ResearchTell participants the purpose, duration and procedures; their right to decline and to withdraw; consequences of declining or withdrawing; foreseeable risks, discomfort or adverse effects; prospective benefits; limits of confidentiality; incentives; whom to contact. For intervention research also: the experimental nature of the treatment, what the control group will get, how assignment is made, available alternatives, and costs
8.03Informed Consent for Recording Voices and Images in ResearchConsent before recording, except naturalistic observation in public places, or when deception is used (consent then sought at debriefing)
8.04Client/Patient, Student, and Subordinate Research ParticipantsProtect them from adverse consequences of declining or withdrawing; when research is a course requirement or earns extra credit, offer an equitable alternative activity
8.05Dispensing With Informed Consent for ResearchOnly where research would not reasonably be assumed to create distress or harm and involves normal educational practices in educational settings; only anonymous questionnaires, naturalistic observations or archival research where disclosure would not put participants at risk and confidentiality is protected; or job/organisational effectiveness studies with no risk to employability; or where law or regulations permit
8.06Offering Inducements for Research ParticipationAvoid excessive or inappropriate financial or other inducements likely to coerce participation
8.07Deception in ResearchStrict conditions (26.6)
8.08DebriefingPromptly give participants information about the nature, results and conclusions, and correct misconceptions; if delay is justified, reduce the risk of harm; if harm occurred, take steps to minimise it
8.09Humane Care and Use of Animals in Research26.10
8.10Reporting Research ResultsDo not fabricate data; correct significant errors once discovered
8.11PlagiarismDo not present others' work or data as your own
8.12Publication CreditAuthorship only for work actually performed or substantially contributed; order reflects contribution; a student is usually first author of a multi-authored article based substantially on their dissertation
8.13Duplicate Publication of DataDo not publish previously published data as original
8.14Sharing Research Data for VerificationDo not withhold data from competent professionals who want to verify claims by reanalysis
8.15ReviewersRespect the confidentiality and proprietary rights of material submitted for review
