In Britain, the British Psychological Society publishes a separate Code of Human Research Ethics (2010, revised 2014 and 2021) built on four principles: respect for the autonomy, privacy and dignity of individuals, groups and communities; scientific integrity; social responsibility; and maximising benefit and minimising harm. Do not confuse these with the four principles of the BPS's general Code of Ethics and Conduct: respect, competence, responsibility and integrity.

26.4 Research ethics in India

The ICMR guidelines

The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR) issued India's first statement in 1980 (Policy Statement on Ethical Considerations Involved in Research on Human Subjects), then the Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Subjects (2000), the Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human Participants (2006), and the current National Ethical Guidelines for Biomedical and Health Research Involving Human Participants (2017). The 2017 guidelines apply to behavioural and social science research in health, which includes clinical psychology.

ICMR 2017: four basic principles: respect for persons (autonomy), beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. These expand into 12 general principles: (1) essentiality, (2) voluntariness, (3) non-exploitation, (4) social responsibility, (5) ensuring privacy and confidentiality, (6) risk minimisation, (7) professional competence, (8) maximisation of benefit, (9) institutional arrangements, (10) transparency and accountability, (11) totality of responsibility, (12) environmental protection.

The 2017 guidelines classify research by risk, and the category decides the type of ethics review:

ICMR risk categoryMeaning and examplesUsual review
Less than minimal riskHarm nil or not expected: anonymous data, public-domain data, meta-analysisExemption from review (decided by the committee, not the researcher)
Minimal riskNo greater than in routine daily life or routine tests: questionnaires, interviews, history taking, observation, urine or saliva samplesExpedited review (chair, member secretary and one or two members)
Minor increase over minimal risk (low risk)Routine research on children, research on people unable to consent, delaying or withholding a proven treatment in a control or placebo arm, small blood samples, social and psychological risksFull committee review
More than minimal risk (high risk)Interventional studies with drugs, devices or invasive proceduresFull committee review

Research involving deception must always go to full committee review under ICMR 2017, which describes a two-step procedure: initial consent, then debriefing after participation.

Ethics committees

ICMR 2017 (all biomedical and health research)New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019, Rule 7 (drug trials)
SizePreferably 7 to 15 membersAt least 7 members (CDSCO registration sets a maximum of 15)
IndependencePreferably 50% from outside the institution; chairperson from outside; member secretary from the institutionAt least 50% not affiliated with the institution; chairperson from outside; member secretary from the institution
MembersBasic medical scientist (preferably a pharmacologist for drug research), clinician, legal expert, social scientist / philosopher / ethicist / theologian, lay person from the communityMust include at least one lay person, one woman, one legal expert and one independent member (social scientist, NGO representative, philosopher, ethicist or theologian)
Gender"Adequate representation of age and gender"At least one woman
QuorumAt least 5, including at least one non-affiliated member (preferably the lay person)At least 5 members of the specified categories
RegistrationCommittees reviewing biomedical and health research register with the Department of Health ResearchCommittees reviewing drug trials register with the Central Licencing Authority (CDSCO); valid 5 years

Other Indian law and bodies

  • Clinical trial registration: on CTRI (launched by ICMR 2007, mandatory since 2009; section 25.6).
  • Rehabilitation Council of India (RCI): a statutory body under the RCI Act, 1992 (under the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment), which registers clinical psychologists and other rehabilitation professionals. Section 21 of the Act lets the Council prescribe standards of professional conduct, etiquette and a code of ethics, framed as regulations in 1998; misconduct can lead to removal from the register.
  • Mental Healthcare Act, 2017, Section 99 (Research): research on persons with mental illness needs their free and informed consent. If a person cannot give it but does not resist, interventional research needs permission from the State Mental Health Authority, which may allow research on the consent of the nominated representative only if the research cannot be done on people able to consent, is necessary to promote the mental health of the population represented, aims at knowledge relevant to their mental health needs, discloses all interests, and has ethics committee approval. Case notes may be used for research without consent if anonymity is secured. Consent can be withdrawn at any time.
  • Data protection: the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs digital personal data in India; for international studies, the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR, applied from 2018) may also apply.
  • Mandatory reporting: the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act, 2012 requires anyone who learns of child sexual abuse to report it, and penalises failure to report. This overrides research confidentiality (26.7).

26.5 Informed consent in practice

Informed consent is a person's voluntary agreement to take part, given with enough information to decide and the capacity to understand it. It is a process, not a signature: the information sheet is discussed, questions are answered, and consent is renewed if the study changes or the person's capacity fluctuates (as in relapsing psychosis or bipolar disorder).

Three conditionsWhat it meansThreatened by
Competence (capacity)The person can understand the information, appreciate how it applies to them, reason about it and communicate a choiceChildhood, intellectual disability, dementia, acute psychosis, intoxication
Information and comprehensionAll material facts are disclosed in a language and at a level the person understandsJargon, English-only forms for non-English speakers, long legal documents, low literacy
VoluntarinessThe choice is free of coercion and undue influencePower relationships (teacher and student, doctor and patient, warden and prisoner), large payments, fear of losing treatment

Elements of the information (combining APA 8.02, Belmont and ICMR): the purpose; the procedures and what is experimental; the expected duration; foreseeable risks and discomforts; expected benefits to the participant or to others; alternatives (especially treatment alternatives in a clinical trial); how confidentiality will be protected and its limits; that participation is voluntary; the right to withdraw at any time without penalty or loss of benefits (including the clinical care they would otherwise receive); any incentives or compensation; and a contact person for questions about the study and about participants' rights. Consent is normally written; oral consent (witnessed and recorded) is used for people who cannot read; a waiver of consent is possible only for minimal-risk research that could not otherwise be done (APA 8.05; decided by the committee).

Children: assent and parental permission

Minors cannot give legal consent, so research needs permission (consent) from a parent or legal guardian plus the child's own assent: affirmative agreement appropriate to the child's age. Mere failure to object is not assent, and a child's refusal should normally be respected even if the parent agrees (unless the research offers a direct benefit unavailable elsewhere). This follows the principle in the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) that children can express their views, including assent and dissent. ICMR 2017 is specific: no documentation of assent is needed below 7 years; verbal assent, recorded in the presence of the parents, from 7 to 12; written assent (with parental signature) from 12 to 18.

Adults with impaired capacity

Capacity is decision-specific and can fluctuate, so it is assessed for this decision at this time, not assumed from a diagnosis. A person with schizophrenia is not automatically incapable. Where capacity is absent, consent comes from a legally acceptable (authorised) representative (ICMR) or, under the Mental Healthcare Act, through the nominated representative with State Mental Health Authority permission (26.4), and the person's own assent or dissent is still sought. The research should be possible only in this population and carry low risk, and consent is sought from the person directly if they regain capacity.

Vulnerable groups

People whose ability to protect their own interests is reduced need additional safeguards: children; prisoners and others in custody; people with severe mental illness or cognitive impairment; pregnant women (risk to the fetus); the terminally ill; economically and socially disadvantaged people; and anyone in a dependent or hierarchical relationship with the researcher: students in the researcher's own class, employees, patients of the treating clinician, members of the armed forces. ICMR 2017 also lists sexual minorities and sex workers, and tribal populations. Safeguards include independent recruiters (a student should not be asked by their own teacher in class), extra committee scrutiny, an equitable alternative to participation for students (APA 8.04), and a guarantee that refusing will not affect grades or treatment.

Active and passive consent; consent online

  • Active (opt-in) consent: a parent or participant must positively agree, usually by returning a signed form. The standard.
  • Passive (opt-out) consent: participation is assumed unless the parent returns a refusal; sometimes used in school surveys. It raises response rates and reduces bias against non-responding families, but non-return may mean the letter never reached home, so committees allow it only for minimal-risk research.
  • Online research: consent is typically a click-through information page; the researcher cannot see whether it was read, cannot easily verify age or identity, and cannot ensure debriefing if the participant closes the window (so debriefing information is shown at exit). Data from public social media posts raise questions of whether "public" means "consented"; verbatim quotes can be traced by a search engine, so they are paraphrased. The Association of Internet Researchers publishes guidelines on these issues.

26.6 Deception and debriefing

Some questions cannot be studied if participants know the hypothesis: conformity, obedience, bystander intervention, the effect of expectations. Psychology therefore permits deception, under strict conditions.

APA Standard 8.07, Deception in Research. (a) Psychologists do not conduct a study involving deception unless they have determined that its use is justified by the study's significant prospective scientific, educational or applied value and that effective non-deceptive alternative procedures are not feasible. (b) Psychologists do not deceive prospective participants about research that is reasonably expected to cause physical pain or severe emotional distress. (c) Any deception that is an integral feature of the design is explained as early as is feasible, preferably at the end of the person's participation and no later than the end of data collection, and participants are permitted to withdraw their data.
  • Active deception (deception by commission): telling participants something false, e.g. a cover story about the study's purpose, false feedback on a test, a fake shock generator, a confederate posing as a participant.
  • Passive deception (deception by omission): withholding information, e.g. not mentioning the real hypothesis, or not saying that a second "unrelated" study is part of the first. Generally regarded as less serious, but still requires justification.
  • Cover story: the false explanation of the study's purpose that keeps the real hypothesis hidden (Milgram's "effects of punishment on learning").
  • Confederate (stooge): a member of the research team who pretends to be a participant or bystander and behaves according to a script (the unanimous majority in Solomon Asch's 1951 line-judging study; Milgram's "learner").

Debriefing

Debriefing is the conversation after participation in which the researcher explains the true nature and purpose of the study, answers questions and makes sure the participant leaves no worse off. David Holmes (1976), in two papers in the American Psychologist, named its two components:

  • Dehoaxing: revealing the deception and convincing the participant that the false information was false (for example, that the "learner" received no shocks and the personality feedback was invented).
  • Desensitising: helping participants deal with any negative feelings or self-knowledge the study produced (for example, that they were willing to shock someone), by explaining that most people behave the same way and that their behaviour reflects the situation, not a defect in them.

Holmes reviewed the evidence and concluded that, done carefully, both were effective. But Lee Ross, Mark Lepper and Michael Hubbard (1975) showed a problem: participants given false feedback about their ability kept part of the false belief even after being told the feedback was fake (belief perseverance). Simply announcing "it was fake" (outcome debriefing) was not enough; it worked better when the researcher also explained the process by which false beliefs persist. This is process debriefing, now the recommended standard: discuss the participant's experience, explain the deception and why it was needed, explain how such beliefs persist, check for distress, and offer withdrawal of data and contact details. Debriefing is good practice even when no deception was used.

Informed consent vs debriefing. Informed consent comes before participation and tells people enough to decide whether to take part; debriefing comes after and tells them everything, including what was concealed. "The principle under which participants are given full information about all aspects of the study after it is done" is debriefing. Debriefing does not retroactively make an unjustified deception acceptable.

26.7 Confidentiality, anonymity and privacy

AnonymityConfidentiality
DefinitionNobody, not even the researcher, can link the data to the person; no identifying information is collectedThe researcher knows who gave the data but promises not to disclose it to others, and reports only in a form that cannot identify anyone
ExampleAn online survey with no names, emails or IP addresses recordedA longitudinal study that must contact the same people again; a therapy trial; a recorded interview
Follow-up possible?NoYes
Can you withdraw a person's data later?No, it cannot be foundYes, through the code
The classic trap. A study cannot be both anonymous and longitudinal, and a face-to-face interview is never anonymous: the researcher has seen the person. Promising "anonymity" when you mean "confidentiality" is itself an ethical error. Privacy is a third, broader idea: the person's right to control access to themselves and their information, which can be violated even when data stay confidential (covert observation of private behaviour, 26.12).

Keeping data confidential

  • Coding (pseudonymisation): replace names with ID numbers and keep the key linking codes to names separately, locked or encrypted, with access limited to named researchers.
  • Secure storage: password-protected, encrypted devices; locked cabinets for paper; a stated retention period and secure destruction afterwards.
  • Reporting in aggregate: group statistics, no small cells that identify individuals (the only woman psychiatrist in a district hospital), altered details in case descriptions, pseudonyms in qualitative quotes.

Limits of confidentiality

Confidentiality is not absolute, and its limits must be stated in the consent process (APA 8.02). Researchers may have to break it when there is a serious and imminent risk of harm to the participant (active suicidal intent) or to others; the US case Tarasoff v. Regents of the University of California established a duty to warn (1974) and then a broader duty to protect (1976) identifiable potential victims of a client's violence. Breaches are also required by law: mandatory reporting of child abuse (POCSO in India), court orders and subpoenas, and certain notifiable conditions. A study screening adolescents for self-harm must therefore have a written plan for what happens when a participant discloses suicidal intent.

26.8 Risk and benefit, the right to withdraw, inducements, and fair selection

Minimal risk (US Common Rule, 45 CFR 46.102): "the probability and magnitude of harm or discomfort anticipated in the research are not greater in and of themselves than those ordinarily encountered in daily life or during the performance of routine physical or psychological examinations or tests." ICMR 2017 uses essentially the same definition and adds categories below and above it (26.4).

Risks in psychological research are rarely physical. They include psychological harm (anxiety, guilt, lowered self-esteem, re-traumatisation when interviewing survivors), social harm (stigma if a diagnosis or sexual orientation is exposed), legal harm (disclosure of drug use) and economic harm (loss of a job). Benefits include direct benefit (a trial treatment), indirect benefit (monitoring, information), and the value of the knowledge to society. The ethics committee's risk-benefit analysis asks whether the risks are minimised (the least risky design that can answer the question), whether they are reasonable in relation to the expected benefits, and whether safeguards (screening, distress protocols, stopping rules, data monitoring) are in place.

The right to withdraw without penalty, at any time and without giving reasons, is in every code since Nuremberg (point 9). In practice it also means participants can ask for their data to be removed (until it is anonymised or published), and that withdrawal must not cost them anything they were entitled to, such as their usual clinical treatment. Milgram's prods ("you have no other choice, you must go on") are the classic violation.

Inducements and coercion. Coercion is an explicit or implicit threat of harm for not participating (a prisoner fearing loss of parole, a patient fearing loss of care, a student fearing a lower grade). Undue inducement is an offer so large that it distorts judgement about risk. Reasonable payment for time and reimbursement of travel are acceptable; the larger the payment relative to the person's income, the more the committee worries, which is a real issue in low-income settings. Course credit is acceptable only if an equitable, non-research alternative is offered (APA 8.04) and the instructor does not know who declined.

Fair selection (justice) cuts both ways. Risky research must not be loaded onto convenient, powerless groups (prisoners, institutionalised children, the poor, captive students), as at Tuskegee and Willowbrook. But excluding groups (women, children, older adults, people with comorbidity, non-English speakers) from research also harms them, because treatments then go untested in the very people who will receive them.

26.9 The famous ethically controversial studies

StudyResearcher(s), yearWhat happenedThe ethical issue
Little AlbertJohn B. Watson and Rosalie Rayner, 1920An infant ("Albert B.", about 9 months old at baseline, 11 months when conditioning began) was conditioned to fear a white rat by pairing it with a loud noise; the fear generalised to other furry objectsDeliberately induced fear in an infant; never deconditioned (he left the hospital); consent from a mother who worked at the hospital is questionable
Monster StudyWendell Johnson; carried out by his graduate student Mary Tudor, University of Iowa, 193922 children at an orphans' home in Iowa; some children who spoke normally were repeatedly told their speech was defective and that they stuttered ("negative therapy")Harm to vulnerable children (orphans), deception, lasting speech and psychological problems; kept quiet until 2001; Iowa paid a settlement in 2007
Tuskegee syphilis studyUS Public Health Service, 1932–1972399 Black men with syphilis (and 201 controls) observed untreated for 40 years; told they had "bad blood"; penicillin withheldNo informed consent, deception, withholding effective treatment, exploitation of a poor minority (injustice); led to the National Research Act and Belmont
Willowbrook hepatitis studiesSaul Krugman, Willowbrook State School, New York, 1956–1971Children with intellectual disabilities were deliberately infected with hepatitis to study the disease and test gamma globulinHarm to a vulnerable group; coerced consent: when the school was "full", places were available only in the hepatitis unit for children whose parents agreed
Obedience to authorityStanley Milgram, Yale, published 196340 men told to give increasing "shocks" to a learner (a confederate) for errors; 26 of 40 (65%) went to the maximum 450 V; experimenter's prods ("The experiment requires that you continue")Deception; severe stress (sweating, trembling, nervous laughter; three had full seizures); pressure undermining the right to withdraw. Critique by Diana Baumrind (1964); Milgram replied that he had dehoaxed everyone and that in a follow-up 84% were glad to have taken part and 1.3% sorry
Tearoom TradeLaud Humphreys, 1970Covert participant observation of men having impersonal sex in public toilets, acting as "watchqueen" (lookout); noted licence plates, traced addresses, and a year later interviewed the men at home in disguise as part of a "social health survey"No consent, deception, invasion of privacy, risk of exposure when homosexuality was criminalised
Stanford Prison ExperimentPhilip Zimbardo, Stanford, August 197124 male students randomly assigned to be guards or prisoners in a mock prison; planned for two weeks, stopped after six days after guards became abusive and prisoners broke down; ended after Christina Maslach objectedHarm and humiliation; prisoners led to believe they could not leave (right to withdraw); Zimbardo's dual role as researcher and "prison superintendent". Later critiques (Thibault Le Texier, 2019) also question its demand characteristics
Maternal deprivation in monkeysHarry Harlow, University of Wisconsin, 1950s–1960s ("The Nature of Love", 1958); later isolation chamber ("pit of despair") work with Stephen Suomi, early 1970sInfant rhesus monkeys separated from mothers, raised with wire or cloth surrogates or in total isolation; showed contact comfort mattered more than feedingSevere, lasting suffering in animals; central to the growth of animal welfare and the 3 Rs
Facebook emotional contagionAdam Kramer, Jamie Guillory and Jeffrey Hancock, published 2014 (PNAS)The News Feeds of 689,003 users were manipulated for one week in January 2012 to show fewer positive or fewer negative posts; users' own posts shifted slightly in the same directionNo specific informed consent (only the platform's terms of service), no debriefing, attempts to alter mood; the journal published an editorial expression of concern
Why Stanley Milgram is the hardest case. Diana Baumrind argued that the stress and the loss of dignity were not justified, that the laboratory setting made subjects especially trusting, and that the experience could harm their self-image and trust in authority. Milgram answered that the outcome was not predictable (psychiatrists he surveyed had expected almost nobody to go to the end), that everyone was dehoaxed and reconciled with the "learner", that most were glad to have taken part, and that the knowledge was important. Under APA 8.07(b) (no deception about research expected to cause severe emotional distress) the original study could not be approved today; Jerry Burger's 2009 partial replication stopped at 150 V, the point at which the learner first demands to be let out.

26.10 Animal research

Animals cannot consent, so the ethics of animal research is about justification and welfare. William Russell and Rex Burch, in The Principles of Humane Experimental Technique (1959), proposed the framework every committee now uses, the 3 Rs:

RMeaningExample
ReplacementUse non-animal methods wherever possibleCell cultures, computer models, human volunteers, recorded data
ReductionUse the minimum number of animals that gives a valid answerPower analysis, better designs, sharing animals and data between studies
RefinementMinimise pain, distress and lasting harm; improve welfareAnaesthesia and analgesia, humane end points, enriched housing, trained handlers

APA Standard 8.09 requires psychologists to acquire, care for, use and dispose of animals in line with the law, under the supervision of a psychologist trained in their care; to minimise discomfort, infection, illness and pain; to subject animals to pain, stress or privation only when an alternative procedure is unavailable and the goal is justified by its scientific, educational or applied value; to perform surgery under appropriate anaesthesia; and, when an animal's life must be ended, to do so rapidly and with minimal pain. Reporting of animal studies follows the ARRIVE guidelines (section 25.9).

India. Animal experiments are regulated under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960 (Section 15) and the Breeding of and Experiments on Animals (Control and Supervision) Rules, 1998, through the Committee for the Purpose of Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CPCSEA). Every establishment needs an Institutional Animal Ethics Committee (IAEC). In January 2023 the committee was renamed the Committee for Control and Supervision of Experiments on Animals (CCSEA), under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying; question papers still use "CPCSEA". The Indian committee also stresses a "fourth R", rehabilitation and after-care of animals once experiments end.

26.11 Research misconduct, authorship and publication ethics

Research misconduct = FFP (US federal definition, 2000): fabrication (making up data or results), falsification (manipulating materials, equipment or processes, or changing or omitting data, so the record misrepresents the research) and plagiarism (appropriating another person's ideas, processes, results or words without credit), in proposing, performing, reviewing or reporting research. It excludes honest error and differences of opinion. Questionable research practices (p-hacking, HARKing; section 25.15) are a grey zone short of FFP that does similar damage.

Famous cases

  • Sir Cyril Burt (British educational psychologist, died 1971): reported a correlation of .771 between the IQs of identical twins reared apart, unchanged to three decimals as his sample grew from 21 to 53 pairs. Leon Kamin (1974) pointed out the implausibility; the journalist Oliver Gillie (1976) alleged fraud and that two co-authors could not be traced; Burt's biographer Leslie Hearnshaw (1979) concluded he had fabricated data. Later authors (Robert Joynson 1989, Ronald Fletcher 1991) defended him, so the case is usually described as a controversy; the data are no longer used.
  • Diederik Stapel (social psychologist, Tilburg University, Netherlands): exposed in 2011 after junior colleagues reported him; an investigation (final report 2012) found he had fabricated data in dozens of publications, often handing "collected" data sets to students. He has about 58 retractions. The case fed directly into the replication crisis (25.15).
  • Andrew Wakefield (1998, The Lancet): a paper on 12 children suggesting a link between the MMR vaccine and autism; found to be dishonest and unethical (including invasive procedures on children without proper approval), retracted in 2010, and Wakefield was struck off the UK medical register. Vaccination rates fell for years afterwards: misconduct with a public-health cost.

Plagiarism and publication ethics

  • Forms of plagiarism: copying verbatim without quotation marks and citation; patchwriting or mosaic plagiarism (stitching together lightly altered phrases from sources); paraphrasing ideas without credit; collusion (submitting jointly produced work as individual work); ghost-writing (submitting work someone else wrote); self-plagiarism (recycling your own published text as new). Correct citation is not plagiarism; that is the usual "which is NOT" answer.
  • Duplicate publication (publishing the same data twice as original, APA 8.13) and salami slicing (splitting one study into many thin papers) inflate the evidence base and can double-count participants in meta-analyses.
  • Authorship must reflect real contribution (APA 8.12). The International Committee of Medical Journal Editors requires all four: substantial contribution to conception, design, data collection or analysis; drafting or critically revising the paper; approving the final version; and accepting accountability for the work. Gift (honorary) authorship (adding a head of department who did nothing) and ghost authorship (omitting someone, such as a company writer, who did write it) both violate this. Minor contributors go in the acknowledgements.
  • Conflicts of interest: financial (industry funding, consultancy, shares in a test or app) and non-financial (allegiance to one's own therapy, 25.14) must be declared; drug-company-funded trials are more likely to report results favouring the sponsor's product.
  • Correcting the record: errors are corrected (APA 8.10) and seriously flawed papers retracted. Data sharing for verification (8.14) and preregistration make all of this easier to detect.

26.12 The ethics of particular designs

  • Withdrawal (reversal) designs (ABAB, section 22): returning to baseline means withdrawing a treatment that is working, for example stopping a successful intervention for a child's self-injury. This is acceptable for brief periods with mild behaviours, but for dangerous behaviours the ethical alternative is a multiple-baseline design, which never removes the treatment.
  • Waitlist and no-treatment controls (25.3): delaying treatment is justified when the delay is short, the condition is not dangerous, waitlisted people are monitored and can be moved to treatment ("rescue" or escape rules) if they deteriorate, and treatment is offered at the end. A waitlist is not acceptable for a person at high suicide risk.
  • Placebo controls when an effective treatment exists: the Declaration of Helsinki allows a placebo or no-intervention control only where no proven intervention exists, or where there are compelling, scientifically sound methodological reasons and the participants will not face additional risk of serious or irreversible harm. Otherwise the new treatment should be compared with the best proven one (an active comparator, or "add-on" designs where everyone receives standard care). ICMR 2017 classes delaying or withholding a proven treatment in a control or placebo arm as a "minor increase over minimal risk", which needs full committee review.
  • Equipoise: randomising patients is ethical only when there is genuine uncertainty in the expert community about which arm is better; Benjamin Freedman (1987) called this clinical equipoise. If accumulating evidence clearly favours one arm, an independent data and safety monitoring board stops the trial early.
  • Covert observation (section 23): observing people without their knowledge avoids reactivity but violates consent and possibly privacy. It is acceptable for anonymous behaviour in genuinely public places (APA 8.05 and 8.03), and controversial in private or semi-private settings: Humphreys' tearooms, or David Rosenhan's (1973) pseudopatients ("On being sane in insane places"), who deceived psychiatric hospital staff to gain admission.
  • Qualitative research and the researcher relationship (section 24): in-depth interviews create intimacy, so participants may disclose more than they intended; consent is treated as an ongoing process consent, renegotiated during the study. Interviews about trauma, abuse or suicide need a distress protocol (pause, stop, referral). A clinician who interviews their own patients holds a dual role that can make refusal feel risky and blur research with therapy. Rich description of a small community can reveal identities even with pseudonyms (deductive disclosure), so details are altered and quotes checked. Reflexivity (section 24) includes reflecting on these power relationships.
Recap of section 26: research ethics was written in response to scandals. The Nazi experiments produced the Nuremberg Code (1947; 10 points; "the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential"); the profession answered with the World Medical Association's Declaration of Helsinki (1964; latest revision October 2024). Tuskegee (US Public Health Service, 1932–72) led to the National Research Act (1974) and the Belmont Report (1979): respect for persons → informed consent (information, comprehension, voluntariness); beneficence → assessment of risks and benefits; justice → fair selection of subjects; then the Common Rule (1991; IRBs) and CIOMS guidelines. Beauchamp and Childress (1979) gave four principles (autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, justice); deontology judges acts by duty, utilitarianism by cost-benefit. The APA Ethics Code (first 1953; current 2002, amended 2010 and 2016) has five aspirational General Principles (A beneficence and nonmaleficence, B fidelity and responsibility, C integrity, D justice, E respect for people's rights and dignity) and enforceable Standards; Standard 8 covers research (8.01 approval to 8.15 reviewers; 8.07 deception, 8.08 debriefing, 8.09 animals). In India, the ICMR National Ethical Guidelines (2017; earlier 1980, 2000, 2006) give four basic and 12 general principles and four risk levels; ethics committees have 7 to 15 members, half from outside, with a lay person, legal expert and social scientist, and under the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules 2019 at least one woman; trials register on CTRI; RCI regulates clinical psychologists; Mental Healthcare Act 2017 Section 99 requires free and informed consent (or State Authority permission). Consent needs competence, information and voluntariness, with assent plus parental permission for children (ICMR: verbal 7 to 12, written 12 to 18). Deception is allowed only with significant value, no alternative, no pain or severe distress, and early explanation (APA 8.07); debriefing means dehoaxing and desensitising (Holmes 1976), ideally process debriefing. Anonymity means even the researcher cannot identify participants; confidentiality means the researcher can but will not tell, within stated limits (risk of harm, Tarasoff, POCSO). Minimal risk = no more than daily life or routine tests; the right to withdraw is absolute; avoid coercion and undue inducement; select participants fairly. Know the controversial studies (Little Albert 1920, Monster Study 1939, Tuskegee, Willowbrook, Milgram 1963 and Diana Baumrind 1964, Tearoom Trade 1970, Stanford Prison 1971, Harry Harlow, Facebook 2014), the 3 Rs (Russell and Burch 1959; CPCSEA, now CCSEA), misconduct as fabrication, falsification and plagiarism (Burt, Stapel, Wakefield), honest authorship, and the ethics of withdrawal designs, waitlists, placebo controls, covert observation and qualitative relationships.

27 Which design to use, the research-methods name index, and the traps

This section closes Part II the way sections 16 and 17 close Part I. It gives you a decision walk that ends in a design name, a one-line lookup table for the way papers describe designs, an index of every name in sections 18 to 26, and the confusable pairs that cost the most marks. Nothing here is new; each line points back to the section where it is taught properly.

27.1 Which design to use

Almost every "which design is this?" or "which design should the researcher use?" item is a single path through five questions. Ask them in order.

First, what kind of question is it? There are six kinds. To describe asks what is there and how common it is: how many college students in Bengaluru screen positive for depression? To relate or predict asks whether two variables go together: is childhood trauma associated with adult depression? To establish cause asks whether changing X changes Y: does CBT reduce BDI scores more than waiting? To study one person's change asks whether an intervention works for this particular client: does a token economy reduce this boy's tantrums? To understand meaning asks what an experience is like or how a process unfolds: what is it like to care for a son with schizophrenia? To pool studies asks what the whole body of evidence says: across 40 trials, how large is the effect of CBT for panic? The kind of question settles the family of design before anything else.

Second, for description: once or over time? One measurement of a population at one moment is a cross-sectional survey, which gives prevalence. Measuring the same people repeatedly is a longitudinal (panel) design, which shows change within people. If age differences are the point, remember that a cross-sectional comparison of age groups confounds age with cohort and a longitudinal one confounds age with time of measurement; the sequential designs of K. Warner Schaie (1965), which follow several cohorts over time, disentangle them (section 21).

Third, for relationships: where do you start? If you start from the outcome (people who already have a rare disorder, plus matched controls) and look back for exposures, it is a case-control study, the design of choice for rare outcomes, and it yields an odds ratio. If you start from the exposure and follow exposed and unexposed people forward to see who develops the outcome, it is a cohort study, which yields incidence and relative risk (prospective if followed from now, retrospective if reconstructed from old records). If you simply measure both variables on the same people, it is correlational. When the "independent variable" has already happened and cannot be manipulated (abuse, divorce, a head injury), and groups are compared on it after the fact, the design is called ex post facto (causal-comparative). None of these can prove causation on its own; for that, observational researchers use Austin Bradford Hill's (1965) nine viewpoints (strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy).

Fourth, for cause: can you manipulate, and can you randomise? If you cannot manipulate the IV, you are back to ex post facto or a natural experiment. If you can manipulate it and can randomly assign people to conditions, you have a true experiment (section 20.5): the posttest-only or pretest-posttest control group design, or the Solomon four-group design (Richard L. Solomon, 1949) when you fear that the pretest itself sensitises people to the treatment; with two or more IVs, a factorial design; in a clinical treatment test, a randomised controlled trial with blinding and intention-to-treat analysis (section 25). If you can manipulate but cannot randomise, you have a quasi-experiment (section 20.8): intact groups give the nonequivalent control group design; many observations before and after an intervention give an interrupted time series; and a cut-off score that decides who is treated gives a regression discontinuity design (Donald L. Thistlethwaite and Donald T. Campbell, 1960). Random assignment, not manipulation, is the line between true and quasi-experiments.

Fifth, one case or many? If the question is about one person's change and you can take repeated measurements, use a single-case experimental design (section 22). If the treatment can be withdrawn and the behaviour is reversible, the ABAB reversal design is the strongest. If withdrawal is unethical or the behaviour will not reverse (a skill once learned), use a multiple-baseline design across behaviours, settings or participants. If the goal is reached in steps (cigarettes cut from 20 to 15 to 10 a day), use a changing-criterion design; to compare two treatments quickly in one client, an alternating-treatments design. If you only want to describe one person richly, without manipulation, it is a case study (sections 21 and 24). For questions of meaning, choose the qualitative approach by its object (section 24): phenomenology or IPA for lived experience, grounded theory for a theory of a process, ethnography for a culture, and mixed methods when you need numbers and meaning together. To pool many studies, do a systematic review and, where the studies are similar enough, a meta-analysis (section 25).

The five questions, in order.
1. What kind of question? Describe, relate, cause, one person's change, meaning, or pooling studies.
2. Can the IV be manipulated? No means non-experimental (correlational, ex post facto, cohort, case-control).
3. Can people be randomly assigned? Yes means a true experiment; no means a quasi-experiment.
4. One case or many? One person with repeated measurement means a single-case design; many means a group design.
5. Is time a dimension? Once means cross-sectional; repeatedly means longitudinal; several cohorts over time means sequential.
Answer those and only one design is left standing.

27.3 The traps

Each item below is a confusable pair or a misstatement that papers use as a distractor. Read each until the distinction is automatic.

  1. Random selection vs random assignment. Random selection decides who enters the study and buys external validity (section 7.2). Random assignment decides who gets which condition and buys internal validity (section 19). A trial can have random assignment without random selection, and a survey the reverse.
  2. Mediator vs moderator. A mediator is the mechanism, caused by X and passing its effect to Y (stress → rumination → depression). A moderator changes the strength or direction of the X–Y relation and is an interaction ("social support buffers stress"). Neither is a confound, which causes both X and Y (Baron and Kenny, 1986).
  3. Internal vs external validity. Internal: did X really cause the change in Y in this study? External: does the result generalise to other people, settings and times? Tight control raises the first and often lowers the second.
  4. Ecological vs external validity. Ecological validity (Brunswik's term, now used for realism of setting) is one part of external validity; population validity is the other (Bracht and Glass, 1968). A study can generalise across people yet still use an artificial setting.
  5. Validity of a test vs validity of a study. Content, criterion and construct validity (section 15.3) are properties of a measure. Statistical conclusion, internal, construct and external validity (Cook and Campbell) are properties of a study. Social validity (section 22.9) is a third thing: whether consumers find goals and outcomes acceptable and important.
  6. What each control controls. A no-treatment control group controls history, maturation, testing and instrumentation; only random assignment controls selection; blinding controls expectancy; counterbalancing controls order effects.
  7. Maturation vs history. Maturation is change inside participants with time (growing older, tired, recovering naturally). History is an outside event between measurements (a festival, an exam, a news story). Testing is the effect of an earlier test; instrumentation is a change in the measuring instrument or observers.
  8. Regression to the mean. People selected for extreme scores score nearer the mean on retest even with no treatment, because part of their extremity was error (Francis Galton, 1886). It is controlled by a randomly assigned control group drawn from the same extreme pool, not by matching or a bigger sample.
  9. Hawthorne vs demand characteristics vs Pygmalion vs John Henry. Hawthorne: participants change because they are observed. Demand characteristics (Orne, 1962): cues lead participants to guess the hypothesis and act on it. Pygmalion (Rosenthal and Lenore Jacobson, 1968): the experimenter's or teacher's expectation changes the participant's performance. John Henry: the control group works harder to compete. Placebo: improvement from expecting treatment.
  10. Single-blind vs double-blind. Single-blind: participants do not know their condition. Double-blind: neither participants nor the experimenters or assessors know. Double-blinding controls both experimenter bias and participants' expectancy effects, which is the past-paper answer. Blinding is not allocation concealment: concealment hides the next assignment from recruiters before allocation (preventing selection bias, and always possible); blinding hides the assignment after it (in psychotherapy trials usually only the assessors can be blind).
  11. Solomon four-group: what it is for. It controls, and measures, pretest sensitisation (the interaction of testing and treatment, an external-validity threat), by crossing pretested vs not with treated vs not (Solomon, 1949). It does not exist to control maturation or selection; an ordinary randomised control group already does that.
  12. Quasi vs true experiment. The dividing line is random assignment, not manipulation. Quasi-experiments usually do manipulate the IV, but on intact groups. "Two classes, radio on in one" is a quasi-experiment.
  13. Ex post facto vs experiment. In ex post facto (causal-comparative) research the IV has already happened and groups are chosen by it (abused vs non-abused children); nothing is manipulated, people select themselves into the conditions, and causal claims are weak.
  14. "One-shot case study" vs case study. Campbell and Stanley's one-shot case study (X O) is a pre-experimental group design, the weakest of all. A qualitative or clinical case study (sections 21 and 24) is an in-depth study of one case. Same words, different things.
  15. Case study vs single-case experiment. A case study describes, with no manipulation and no baseline. A single-case experiment (ABAB, multiple baseline) has repeated measurement, a baseline and planned manipulation, and can show causation.
  16. ABAB ethics and reversibility. ABAB is the strongest single-case demonstration but needs a treatment that can ethically be withdrawn and a behaviour that will reverse. When either fails (self-injury, a learned skill), use a multiple baseline. AB alone is only quasi-experimental; BAB has no initial baseline.
  17. Cross-sectional vs longitudinal confounds. Cross-sectional comparisons confound age with cohort (the past-paper answer to "a disadvantage of cross-sectional studies"). Longitudinal designs confound age with time of measurement and suffer attrition and practice effects. K. Warner Schaie's sequential designs separate age, cohort and time.
  18. Prospective cohort vs case-control. A cohort study starts from exposure and follows forward to outcome; a case-control study starts from outcome and looks back to exposure. For a rare outcome, case-control; for a rare exposure, cohort. A retrospective cohort built from old records is still a cohort study, because it runs from exposure to outcome.
  19. Odds ratio vs relative risk. Relative risk needs incidence, so it comes from cohort studies and trials; a case-control study can only give an odds ratio, which approximates the relative risk when the outcome is rare (Cornfield, 1951). A ratio of 1 means no association.
  20. Prevalence vs incidence. Prevalence is the proportion who have the condition at a time (cross-sectional surveys). Incidence is the rate of new cases over a period (cohort studies).
  21. Intention-to-treat vs per-protocol. ITT analyses everyone in the group they were randomised to, whatever they actually received, so it preserves randomisation and gives a conservative, real-world estimate. Per-protocol analyses only those who followed the protocol and can be biased.
  22. Efficacy vs effectiveness. Efficacy is whether a treatment works under ideal, controlled conditions (an explanatory trial with selected patients and manualised therapists); effectiveness is whether it works in routine practice (a pragmatic trial). A waitlist control answers only "better than time passing?"; an attention-placebo control asks "better than the common factors?".
  23. The file drawer problem. Rosenthal (1979): non-significant studies stay unpublished "in the file drawer", so the published literature overstates effects. It is publication bias, detected by funnel-plot asymmetry and addressed by the fail-safe N and preregistration. It is not about lost data.
  24. Statistical vs clinical significance. A significant p value says a difference is unlikely to be chance; it does not say the change matters to the patient. The reliable change index and clinically significant change (Jacobson and Truax, 1991) answer that.
  25. Content analysis vs thematic analysis. Content analysis (Berelson, 1952) codes manifest content into categories fixed in advance and counts them, with inter-coder reliability. Thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006) interprets patterns of meaning in six recursive phases.
  26. IPA vs descriptive phenomenology. Descriptive phenomenology (Husserl, Giorgi, Colaizzi) brackets and seeks the essence. IPA (Smith, 1996) interprets through a double hermeneutic and stays idiographic.
  27. Grounded-theory coding order. Open → axial → selective (Strauss and Corbin, 1990). Axial coding "weaves the data back together"; selective coding finds the core category. Theoretical sampling is decided during analysis; purposive sampling is planned in advance.
  28. Trustworthiness parallels. Credibility – internal validity; transferability – external validity; dependability – reliability; confirmability – objectivity (Lincoln and Guba, 1985).
  29. Explanatory vs exploratory sequential. Explanatory = QUAN → qual (numbers first, interviews explain them). Exploratory = QUAL → quan (interviews first, usually to build a tool).
  30. Belmont's three principles. Respect for persons (autonomy, informed consent, protection of those with diminished autonomy), beneficence (do no harm, maximise benefits, assess risks) and justice (fair selection of participants and fair sharing of burdens and benefits). Confidentiality and debriefing are rules that serve these, not extra principles. The APA code has its own list: five general principles, A to E.
  31. Anonymity vs confidentiality. Anonymous data cannot be linked to the person even by the researcher. Confidential data can be linked, but the researcher promises not to disclose them. A named interview cannot be anonymous; it can be confidential.
  32. Informed consent vs debriefing; dehoaxing vs desensitising. Consent comes before participation; debriefing comes after and explains the full purpose. When deception was used, debriefing has two jobs (David Holmes, 1976): dehoaxing, revealing the deception and why it was needed, and desensitising, removing any distress or harmful self-beliefs the study caused.
  33. Nuremberg vs Helsinki vs Belmont. Nuremberg Code, 1947, after the Nazi doctors' trial, centred on voluntary consent. Declaration of Helsinki, 1964, by the World Medical Association, for medical research. Belmont Report, 1979, in the United States after the Tuskegee syphilis study, with three principles. In India the reference is the ICMR guidelines of 2017.

27.4 How to attack Part II

  1. Learn sections 19 and 20 first, and learn them perfectly. Campbell and Stanley's eight internal and four external threats, which control handles which threat, and the R, X, O notation answer more research-methods items than anything else, because "which threat is this?" and "which design controls it?" are the two most repeated question forms.
  2. Then walk the tree in 27.1 until you can classify any one-paragraph study description in ten seconds: question type, manipulation, random assignment, number of cases, time. Identification items ("A researcher tests two intact classes...") are free marks once the walk is automatic.
  3. Memorise the fixed numbers. 8 internal and 4 external threats; Campbell and Stanley's 3 pre-experimental, 3 true and 10 quasi-experimental designs; Solomon's 4 groups; Thurstone's 11 piles; Guttman's reproducibility of .90; focus groups of about 6 to 10; COREQ's 32 items; CONSORT 2010's 25 items (30 in the 2025 update); PRISMA 2020's 27 items; PND above 90% as very effective; |RC| above 1.96; Belmont's 3 principles; the APA's 5 general principles; 1947, 1964, 1979 and 2017 for Nuremberg, Helsinki, Belmont and the ICMR guidelines.
  4. Learn the names in 27.2. Campbell, Stanley, Cook, Fisher, Solomon, Orne, Robert Rosenthal, Landsberger, K. Warner Schaie, Bradford Hill, Baer, Wolf and Risley, Thurstone, Likert, Guttman, Osgood, Bogardus, Jacob Moreno, Glaser and Strauss, Braun and Clarke, Lincoln and Guba, and Glass are the ones that recur.
  5. Drill the traps in 27.3 as pairs. Cover the right-hand half of each item and say the distinction aloud. Random selection vs assignment, mediator vs moderator, Hawthorne vs Pygmalion, cohort vs case-control and explanatory vs exploratory are asked almost every year.
  6. Do not skip sections 24 and 26. Qualitative methods and ethics are short, pure recall and usually the least prepared. Grounded-theory coding order, the six phases of thematic analysis, Lincoln and Guba's four criteria, Belmont's three principles and the difference between debriefing and informed consent are all repeat items.
  7. Then sit the real papers. Work the research-methods items in the PYQ Real 2024, PYQ Real 2025, IHBAS 2024, RML 2025, JEMAS 2025 and SGT papers, then the MET mocks. Every item you miss will map back to a numbered section of Part II.
Recap of section 27: choose a design by asking, in order, what kind of question it is (describe, relate, cause, one person's change, meaning, pooling), whether the IV can be manipulated, whether people can be randomly assigned, whether there is one case or many, and whether time matters. Description leads to cross-sectional, longitudinal or sequential designs (Schaie, 1965); relationships to case-control (from outcome; odds ratio), cohort (from exposure; relative risk) or correlational and ex post facto designs, judged by Bradford Hill's (1965) viewpoints; causes to true experiments (random assignment; Solomon's four groups for pretest sensitisation; factorial for interactions; RCTs) or quasi-experiments (nonequivalent groups, interrupted time series, regression discontinuity); one person's change to ABAB, multiple baseline, changing criterion or alternating treatments; meaning to phenomenology, IPA, grounded theory, ethnography or mixed methods; pooling to systematic review and meta-analysis. The name index runs from Bacon and Mill through Popper, Kuhn and Bridgman, Fisher, Campbell and Stanley, Cook and Campbell, Orne and Rosenthal, Solomon, Schaie and Bradford Hill, B. F. Skinner, Sidman and Baer, Wolf and Risley, the scaling pioneers, the qualitative founders, Glass and Rosenthal on meta-analysis, to Nuremberg (1947), Helsinki (1964), Belmont (1979) and ICMR (2017). The traps are pairs: selection vs assignment, mediator vs moderator, internal vs external, test vs study validity, maturation vs history, Hawthorne vs demand vs Pygmalion, quasi vs true, case study vs single-case experiment, cohort vs case-control, OR vs RR, ITT vs per-protocol, content vs thematic analysis, explanatory vs exploratory, anonymity vs confidentiality, and consent vs debriefing.
